item.title: THE SHU PARADOX
item.category: Organizational Learning · Expert Voice · Strategic Leadership
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: When an organization fears the misuse of expertise so much that it pushes expertise away—and later discovers it cannot handle reality without it.
item.content:encoded:
Article 89 · Organizational Learning · Expert Voice · Strategic Leadership

THE SHU PARADOX

When an organization fears the misuse of expertise so much that it pushes expertise away—and later discovers it cannot handle reality without it.

In Suikoden II, Shu is remembered as an exceptionally capable strategist who once studied under Mathiu. Their relationship offers a useful lens for a dilemma that appears in real organizations: what happens when leaders recognize that someone has valuable expertise, but distrust the way that expertise might be used?

The tension is not simply “ethics versus intelligence.” It is a harder question: how do we prevent expertise from being abused without disabling the very capability we need to solve difficult problems?

1. First, what does the original story actually establish?

Konami’s official Suikoden II character description says Shu studied under Mathiu but was expelled because he tried to use his exceptional military skills for his own career. That is the clearest official summary of the conflict. It establishes both Shu’s exceptional ability and Mathiu’s objection to its intended use.

The anime scene shown in the reference screenshots appears to dramatize Mathiu’s warning and Shu’s reaction. However, the official character summary does not reproduce that dialogue. I could not verify the exact wording of the scene against a full, accessible copy of the Japanese novelization. Therefore, this article treats the exchange as an adaptation-inspired reading—not as a verified verbatim quotation from the novel.

The Suikoden II novelization is commonly catalogued as a four-volume series by J. S. Hori; Volume 2 is listed as ISBN 4840217793. The bibliographic record helps identify the book, but it does not independently verify the precise Mathiu–Shu dialogue.

Canon versus interpretation: Canonical basis: Shu’s exceptional military skill and his expulsion for seeking personal advancement, as stated by Konami. Interpretation: the anime’s warning can be read as a debate about restraint, agency, and the duty to use expertise responsibly. The organizational analogy below is an application of that theme, not a claim that the game depicts a modern workplace.

2. The disagreement: Mathiu and Shu are protecting different things

Mathiu’s position can be understood as a warning about purpose: exceptional ability must not become an instrument of private ambition. Shu’s apparent frustration in the anime can be read from another angle: if other actors are already using strategy to outmaneuver or destroy one another, why should the person capable of responding be told to hold back?

These are not necessarily mutually exclusive principles. Mathiu is concerned about the ends for which power is used; Shu’s dilemma concerns the cost of refusing to act when others continue to act.

Conceptual interpretation of the character conflict—not a diagram from the game or novel.

The danger on Mathiu’s side is moralizing restraint until it becomes paralysis. The danger on Shu’s side is treating the existence of hostile actors as permission to use any means necessary. Responsible leadership must avoid both.

3. The organizational version: leaders panic about reality, then sideline the people who understand it

Now translate the dilemma into an organization. A team faces a complex problem: the operating environment is changing, risks are accumulating, and existing plans are not working. Leaders ask for solutions—but the person who understands the system, can challenge assumptions, or has the technical ability to respond may already have been marginalized.

Sometimes this happens because the expert is difficult, blunt, politically inconvenient, or unwilling to endorse a preferred narrative. Sometimes the expert has behaved poorly or has conflicts of interest. Sometimes leaders have legitimate concerns about how the expertise might be used. Those possibilities must be assessed rather than assumed away.

The organizational failure occurs when leaders treat a concern about a person’s motives as a reason to discard the person’s knowledge altogether—without testing the evidence, setting safeguards, or creating a way for the expertise to contribute responsibly.

The contradiction: “We need someone who understands this problem” can coexist with “we do not want to hear from the person who understands it.” The result is not necessarily a lack of talent. It may be a failure to listen, evaluate, and govern talent.

This is especially costly in complex environments. No single leader can personally know everything. Organizations depend on people closest to the data, the operations, the technology, the communities, and the risks to surface information that senior decision-makers may not possess.

4. What research says about silencing expertise

Employee voice and organizational silence

Organizational researcher Elizabeth W. Morrison describes employee voice as voluntarily communicating suggestions, concerns, information about problems, or work-related opinions upward. Silence withholds potentially useful information from the organization. Her review shows that whether people speak up depends on individual motivations and organizational conditions—not simply whether they have something useful to say.

Psychological safety is not comfort or agreement

Edmondson and Bransby’s 2023 review explains that psychological safety matters because organizations need candid sharing of information, questions, concerns, and diverse expertise. People may stay quiet when they fear being seen as ignorant, incompetent, or intrusive. Psychological safety does not mean lowering standards or avoiding disagreement; it means making interpersonal risk-taking possible so the team can learn.

Inviting input but ignoring it can make things worse

Research on “pseudo voice” warns that asking employees for opinions without intending to consider them can be experienced as managerial disregard. A feedback channel is not meaningful if contributions disappear without acknowledgement, explanation, or action.

Leaders need to listen and respond, not merely collect feedback

A 2024 conceptual review of safety listening synthesizes research on what organizations do after someone raises a concern. It highlights that failures to listen to people who call attention to risks are implicated in safety incidents. The relevant question is not only whether people can speak, but whether decision-makers genuinely process and respond to what they hear.

5. What should an organization do instead?

The research does not recommend giving every expert unchecked authority. It points toward conditions where relevant information can surface, be examined, and influence decisions. A practical approach is to separate three questions that organizations often collapse into one:

  1. Is the expertise real and relevant? Evaluate demonstrated competence, evidence, work samples, and track record.
  2. Is the proposed use legitimate? Examine purpose, proportionality, conflicts of interest, foreseeable harm, and who benefits or bears the risk.
  3. What safeguards make responsible use possible? Define scope, decision rights, review, documentation, and accountability.

A practical governance sequence synthesized from research on employee voice, psychological safety, and safety listening. It is not a single validated intervention protocol.

Build structured dissent into decisions

Before a high-stakes decision, assign someone to challenge the assumptions, invite independent technical review, and ask what evidence would change the decision. This prevents disagreement from being treated as disloyalty and helps distinguish useful dissent from obstruction.

Give experts a channel that reaches decision-makers

Use clear escalation routes, written risk notes, technical review panels, and protected ways to raise concerns. Leaders should acknowledge input and explain the disposition. A suggestion need not be accepted, but it should be considered in good faith.

Keep power bounded by purpose and oversight

Expertise should inform decisions, not grant an individual unlimited authority. Define the legitimate objective, proportionality, limits, review points, and accountability. If an expert has a conflict or has acted improperly, address that conduct directly while preserving access to relevant knowledge through appropriate safeguards.

Do not confuse challenge with disloyalty

A person who questions a plan may be trying to prevent failure. Leaders should test the substance of the challenge before judging its tone or presumed motive. Equally, experts should present evidence clearly, disclose uncertainty, and remain open to correction.

6. The real lesson: restraint must not become institutional helplessness

Mathiu’s warning matters: talent can become dangerous when it serves ego, status, or private ambition. But a modern organization can make the opposite mistake: it can become so anxious about the risks of expertise that it excludes the very people who could help it respond to reality.

Shu’s dilemma, read through the anime scene, asks a question worth carrying into organizational life: if others continue acting strategically, is it enough for us to declare our own restraint virtuous—even when people depend on us to respond?

The answer is not to abandon ethics or to imitate the worst actor. It is to preserve capability while governing its use. Do not demand that experts become silent to prove they are trustworthy. Ask them to make their reasoning transparent, accept scrutiny, and use their skills within legitimate boundaries. And require leaders to listen, assess, and explain their decisions.

Do not discard the strategist because strategy can be misused. Establish the rules that make strategy serve the mission—and hold everyone, including the strategist and the leadership, accountable to them.
The organizational paradox: An institution cannot complain that reality is out of control while systematically silencing the people who understand it. Ethical restraint should govern expertise—not replace it with institutional helplessness.

Sources and further reading

  1. KONAMI — Suikoden II official character profile. Official description of Shu: formerly studied under Mathiu, expelled for attempting to use exceptional military skills for his own career. This is the primary official source for the character background summarized here. https://www.konami.com/games/suikoden/rem/1_2/us/en-us/about_2
  2. Hori, J. S. — Genso Suikoden II novelization, Volume 2. Japanese novelization bibliographic listing: ISBN 4840217793; author and volume details are catalogued here. The full text was not available for direct verification of the anime dialogue. Volume 2 bibliographic entry
  3. Morrison, E. W. (2014). “Employee Voice and Silence.” Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, 1, 173–197. Review of upward voice, silence, antecedents, and organizational consequences. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-031413-091328
  4. Edmondson, A. C., & Bransby, D. P. (2023). “Psychological Safety Comes of Age: Observed Themes in an Established Literature.” Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, 10, 55–78. Review of psychological safety, collaboration, candid information sharing, and diverse expertise. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-120920-055217
  5. Detert, J. R., & Edmondson, A. C. (2011). “Implicit Voice Theories: Taken-for-Granted Rules of Self-Censorship at Work.” Academy of Management Journal. Studies how beliefs about the risks of speaking up contribute to workplace silence. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.61967925
  6. de Vries, G., Jehn, K. A., & Terwel, B. W. (2012). “When Employees Stop Talking and Start Fighting: The Detrimental Effects of Pseudo Voice in Organizations.” Journal of Business Ethics, 105, 221–230. Discusses the harm when managers invite input without intending to consider it. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10551-011-0960-4
  7. Pandolfo, A. M., Reader, T. W., & Gillespie, A. (2024). “Safety Listening in Organizations: An Integrated Conceptual Review.” Reviews organizational responses to safety-related voice and the consequences of failing to listen. https://doi.org/10.1177/20413866241245276
  8. Edmondson, A. C. (2003). “Speaking Up in the Operating Room: How Team Leaders Promote Learning in Interdisciplinary Action Teams.” Journal of Management Studies, 40(6), 1419–1452. Examines how leaders influence speaking up and learning in interdisciplinary teams. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-6486.00386

Evidence note: these studies support the importance of voice, psychological safety, and listening; they do not prove that a particular organization has sidelined a particular expert, nor that every dissenting employee is correct. The Shu–Mathiu diagram is an interpretive model. The recommendations are a practical synthesis of the cited research, not a claim that one standardized intervention has been tested as a package.

item.title: TRANSACTIONAL RECIPROCITY: WHEN KINDNESS BECOMES AN UNWRITTEN CONTRACT
item.category: Social Psychology · Transactional Reciprocity · Moral Indebtedness · Professional Ethics
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: Why I hesitate to ask friends for help unless absolutely necessary. Gratitude, moral indebtedness, hidden expectations, and the invisible social contracts that can turn kindness into leverage over someone's future decisions.
item.content:encoded:
Article 90 · Social Psychology · Reciprocity · Professional Ethics · Human Relationships

TRANSACTIONAL RECIPROCITY: WHEN KINDNESS BECOMES AN UNWRITTEN CONTRACT

Why I would rather give help than ask for it, and why I prefer clear agreements over invisible debts.

Why am I reluctant to ask friends or other people for help unless it is absolutely necessary?

It is not because I dislike helping others. Quite the opposite.

I simply don't want a favor to become an invisible debt that someone can collect years later.

I believe there is a difference between gratitude, reciprocity, and transactional obligation.

This is also why organizations like the United Nations have rules governing gifts and benefits: to protect integrity, independence, impartiality, and prevent conflicts of interest or undue influence over professional decisions.

Let me explain.

1. When a favor becomes an unwritten contract

Imagine someone helps you through a difficult period in your life.

You genuinely appreciate it. You are grateful, and you never forget what they did.

But several years later, that person approaches you with a request:

"My child needs a job. Can you help get them into your organization?"

Now you face a dilemma.

There might be other candidates who are more qualified, more experienced, and more deserving of the opportunity.

Do you prioritize the child because of your personal debt to their parent?

If you do, you might be unfair to other candidates.

If you refuse, you might be accused of being ungrateful.

This is precisely why I am cautious about accepting favors.

Gratitude should not automatically become a lifelong obligation to fulfill someone else's requests.

A favor that was originally presented as unconditional kindness can gradually become a source of leverage. The recipient may discover that the original assistance came with expectations that were never explicitly communicated.

The distinction: Remembering someone's kindness is healthy. Being expected to surrender future professional judgment because of that kindness is a different matter.

2. There is nothing wrong with a transparent professional exchange

For example, I might help someone prepare several project proposals, develop applications, write code, and deliver the actual working products.

In return, I might ask for a professional recommendation letter.

I consider that reasonable.

Why?

Because the work has been delivered. The applications and code are already in their hands. There is a tangible contribution, and the request for professional recognition is transparent.

I am not asking for an undefined personal favor. I am asking for professional recognition based on the actual contribution I made.

There is a difference between a mutually understood exchange and an undefined obligation that suddenly appears years later.

I don't mind reciprocity.

I mind hidden expectations.

My preference:
"I help you with this, and you help me with that."

Both parties understand the arrangement. No guessing, no emotional accounting, and no collecting favors several years later.

3. The problem with saying "I helped you, but you keep asking for more."

Consider humanitarian assistance.

Imagine refugees who have lost almost everything.

An organization provides food, drinking water, and temporary accommodation.

But are those the only things human beings need?

What about sanitation, healthcare, reproductive health, education, psychological well-being, social interaction, and recreational activities?

Survival is not the same as living with dignity.

If the organization cannot provide everything, that is understandable. Resources are limited, and priorities must be established.

But imagine the organization starts complaining:

"We have already given them food and shelter. Why are they asking for more?"

This is where I see a dangerous misunderstanding.

Providing basic assistance does not mean the recipient must stop having other legitimate human needs.

The recipient is not automatically being ungrateful simply because the initial assistance was insufficient.

Of course, assistance has limits. But those limits should be communicated honestly rather than turning legitimate needs into a moral accusation against the recipient.

Humanitarian assistance is not a personal favor that gives the donor ownership over the recipient's expectations. It is a response to human needs, guided by dignity, accountability, and available resources.

There is an important distinction between recognizing resource constraints and making recipients feel guilty for having needs.

4. Not every relationship should operate like a transaction

I also recognize that different relationships have different expectations.

I have a different perspective when asking for help from my parents, siblings, or someone I genuinely love, such as a husband or wife.

Even when there are expectations or personal interests involved, I can accept that kind of reciprocity differently.

Why?

Because family and intimate relationships are built around ongoing mutual commitment, shared responsibilities, and emotional bonds.

They are not necessarily equivalent to professional relationships or ordinary friendships.

I don't expect every relationship to be completely free of self-interest.

But I do expect some clarity about what kind of relationship and obligation we are entering.

Not every exchange needs to be calculated. A healthy family relationship, for example, often involves generalized reciprocity: people give and receive over time without keeping an exact record of every contribution.

However, that does not mean every friendship or professional relationship should operate under the same expectations.

5. The real issue: Gratitude versus indebtedness

Research in social psychology distinguishes between gratitude and indebtedness.

They are related, but they are not identical.

Gratitude is appreciating what someone has done for you.

Indebtedness is feeling that you owe someone something in return.

And when someone perceives that a favor was given strategically, with an expectation of future repayment, the resulting obligation can feel more like pressure than genuine appreciation.

This is an important distinction. Someone can appreciate a person's generosity while simultaneously feeling uncomfortable about the obligation to repay it.

The problem becomes more complicated when the expected repayment is never communicated.

One person believes they have given unconditional assistance. The other person may feel they have entered an informal contract without knowing its terms.

Years later, both parties may have completely different understandings of what happened.

This is why I prefer to be careful when asking for favors.

I would rather find a professional solution, pay for a service, or solve a problem independently than create an undefined social obligation.

I don't want someone to feel that I owe them something they never explicitly told me about.

And I don't want to use my past kindness as leverage over someone else's future decisions either.

6. Why professional organizations regulate gifts and favors

This issue is not limited to personal relationships. It also matters in professional institutions.

Organizations such as the United Nations maintain ethical rules concerning gifts, benefits, outside interests, and conflicts of interest.

Why?

Because professional decisions should not be influenced by personal favors, financial interests, relationships, or expectations of future reciprocity.

Imagine an employee who receives substantial personal assistance from a contractor, supplier, government representative, or another individual seeking to influence an official decision.

Even if the employee believes they can remain objective, the situation can create a conflict of interest or the appearance of undue influence.

It can undermine public trust.

The issue is not necessarily that every gift is corrupt or every favor is suspicious. The concern is that personal generosity can create obligations, dependencies, or perceptions that compromise professional independence.

This is why transparent procedures, disclosure requirements, and restrictions on certain gifts and benefits matter.

Professional integrity requires more than having good intentions. It also requires avoiding situations that can compromise, or appear to compromise, independent judgment.

7. Why I prefer to give rather than ask

And perhaps this explains why I tend to help people more often than I ask them for help.

When I help someone, I know what I am offering, what I am contributing, and where my boundaries are.

I don't have to worry about someone bringing up an old favor years later, questioning my decisions, or expecting something in return that was never discussed.

There is also an interesting psychological dynamic: people who receive substantial help may develop a sense of indebtedness. Sometimes, they become uncomfortable disagreeing, setting boundaries, or refusing future requests because they perceive themselves as being indebted to the giver.

I recognize that this is not necessarily a healthy foundation for every relationship, and I don't expect people to remain silent simply because I helped them.

But it illustrates why I am more comfortable being the giver than the recipient.

Personally, I would rather avoid that psychological burden altogether.

My preferred arrangement is simple: direct and transparent reciprocity.

You help me with something, and I help you with something in return.

"I help you with this, and you help me with that."

No mysterious obligations. No emotional accounting. No collecting favors several years later.

If we agree on an exchange, we both know what we are getting into.

And if someone genuinely wants to help me without expecting anything in return, I appreciate that. But I would rather not make a habit of depending on other people's generosity.

Perhaps I am overly cautious, but I value relationships where people can freely say yes, freely say no, and never have to wonder what an old favor will cost them in the future.

I would rather have a clear agreement than an invisible debt.

8. The difference between helping and controlling

There is one final distinction worth making.

Helping someone should not give us ownership over their future decisions.

If I help someone, I should not expect to control whom they hire, whom they marry, what opportunities they pursue, or which decisions they make years later.

Likewise, if someone helps me, I should not automatically be expected to surrender my professional judgment or personal autonomy.

We can acknowledge past generosity without turning it into a permanent instrument of influence.

And this principle should apply in both directions.

I don't want to be controlled by someone's generosity, and I don't want my generosity to become a tool for controlling someone else.

My principle:
I want people to help me because they genuinely want to, not because they expect something from me. And I want to help others without making them feel that they owe me their future.

My point is simple

  • You can be grateful without being permanently indebted.
  • You can help someone without owning their future decisions.
  • You can accept assistance without surrendering your right to say no later.
  • You can acknowledge someone's kindness without sacrificing fairness toward other people.
  • You can establish reciprocity without creating hidden obligations.
Kindness should build relationships, not create invisible contracts that can be enforced whenever the benefactor wants.

I would rather have a clear agreement than an invisible debt.

References and further reading

  1. Gouldner, A. W. (1960). "The Norm of Reciprocity: A Preliminary Statement." American Sociological Review. A foundational explanation of reciprocity as a social norm. Raw link: DOI
  2. Greater Good Science Center, UC Berkeley. Articles on gratitude, indebtedness, and the psychology of giving and receiving. Raw link: Greater Good Magazine
  3. Big Think. "'Don't Mention It': Yeah, Right!" Discusses hidden expectations and the social obligations attached to favors. Raw link: Big Think
  4. Cleveland Clinic. "How To Recognize (and Stop) a Guilt Trip." Explains how guilt can be used to influence another person's decisions and boundaries. Raw link: Cleveland Clinic
  5. Sphere Association. The Sphere Handbook. Humanitarian principles and minimum standards concerning dignity, assistance, accountability, and essential human needs. Raw link: Sphere Handbook
  6. United Nations Ethics Office. Guidance on ethics, gifts, outside interests, and conflicts of interest. Raw link: UN Ethics Office

Conceptual note: Transactional Reciprocity is used here as an editorial framing for exchanges involving explicit or implicit expectations of repayment. It is not presented as a standalone psychological diagnosis or universally established scientific theory. Gratitude, indebtedness, and reciprocity can have healthy as well as unhealthy forms. This article focuses on situations where expectations are unclear, disproportionate, or used as leverage.

item.title: WHAT IS A RESOURCE, REALLY?
item.category: Human Resources · Political Patronage · Organizational Accountability
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: When people hear the word resources, they often think of money, oil, minerals, land, or other natural resources. But there is another resource without which most organizations cannot turn budgets, infrastructure, or plans into results: human capability.
item.content:encoded:
Article 88 · Human Resources · Political Patronage · Organizational Accountability

WHAT IS A RESOURCE, REALLY?

The Politics of Gratitude: When Loyalty Becomes More Valuable Than Expertise

When people hear the word resources, they often think of money, oil, minerals, land, or other natural resources. But there is another resource without which most organizations cannot turn budgets, infrastructure, or plans into results: human capability.

People do not simply occupy positions. They interpret evidence, solve problems, build systems, maintain institutional memory, make decisions, and deliver services. Human beings are not interchangeable line items. Their knowledge, judgement, experience, and ability to learn are part of an organization’s real capacity.

And yet, the way some organizations allocate money can reveal a strange contradiction: they may spend generously to preserve political relationships, while treating professional expertise as an expense to be minimized.

1. The contradiction: expensive connections, discounted expertise

Consider a pattern—not a claim about every organization, country, or political appointment:

  1. An organization is willing to spend substantial money on a person connected to a powerful official, political ally, family, or inner circle.
  2. The appointment may preserve access, reward loyalty, fulfill an obligation, or strengthen a relationship.
  3. When the organization needs a specialist whose work is genuinely important, the hiring conversation suddenly becomes about finding the lowest possible price.
  4. The specialist’s expertise is described as “support,” “nice to have,” or replaceable—even when the organization knows the role is critical.
  5. The decision is shaped less by the value and risk of the work than by who should receive the opportunity or whose relationship must be protected.

This is the paradox: the organization may understand the value of expertise, yet its incentives reward something else. It is not necessarily that leaders cannot recognize skill. Sometimes skill simply does not deliver the same immediate political or relational return as patronage.

A necessary distinction: a low offer alone does not prove favoritism. Pay can be constrained by a salary scale, procurement rules, budget limits, or a poorly designed job description. The concern is the pattern: discretionary spending for connections alongside persistent underinvestment in capabilities the organization says it needs.

2. What forces can push an organization toward this?

Patronage is not always one person making one obviously corrupt decision. It can emerge from a chain of pressures. A politician may need allies; an executive may need political cover; a manager may fear retaliation; a hiring process may be opaque; and the costs of poor technical decisions may be delayed or borne by someone else.

Conceptual systems map—not a claim that every appointment follows this exact sequence. Multiple pressures can reinforce one another.

Several well-established concepts help describe these dynamics:

  • Political patronage: positions or benefits are distributed through political relationships rather than solely through role-related merit.
  • Clientelism: a reciprocal exchange in which a benefit is made conditional on political support or loyalty.
  • Nepotism: favoritism toward relatives.
  • Cronyism: favoritism toward friends or close associates.
  • Organizational capture: decisions are bent toward a narrow group’s interests rather than the organization’s stated purpose.

These terms overlap, but they are not identical. A political appointment is not automatically clientelism; the key issue is whether benefits and loyalty are exchanged, whether merit is displaced, and whether the process is accountable.

3. Why can an ordinary appointment be valued more than an expert?

One answer is that organizations can be operating with two different “value systems” at once.

Relational benefits can be immediate and visible: someone is pleased, an alliance is maintained, a promise is fulfilled. The value of expertise may be less visible at first. A specialist can prevent a failure that never happens, improve a decision that would otherwise be poor, or build a system whose benefits arrive months later.

This creates a familiar organizational trap: the cost of hiring an expert is visible today; the cost of not having expertise may appear much later. When decision-makers are rewarded for short-term relationships and not held accountable for long-term performance, the incentives can become badly misaligned.

It is also possible to undervalue expertise because it is difficult to assess. If leaders do not know how to distinguish high-quality technical work from a polished presentation, they may fall back on price, familiarity, credentials, or personal trust. That is a management problem—not proof that expertise has no value.

4. The research: this is not merely a personal impression

Research documents that political connections can affect who is hired and how public organizations select employees. For example, Colonnelli, Prem, and Teso’s study of Brazil’s public workforce from 1997 to 2014 found that political connections were an important determinant of public employment, that patronage played a role, and that political considerations led to the selection of less competent individuals in the setting they studied.

That finding should be interpreted carefully: it is evidence from a specific country, period, and research design—not a universal claim about every political appointment. Still, it illustrates the risk when political connections substitute for competence.

OECD guidance on public integrity emphasizes merit-based, transparent recruitment and objective qualification and performance criteria. It also notes that patronage and nepotism can undermine integrity and, in extreme cases, create roles to reward allies rather than meet real organizational needs.

Meanwhile, the OECD’s guidance on senior public service recruitment recognizes a genuine tension: political responsiveness matters, but appointments also need leadership assessment, transparency, accountability, and safeguards against undue political influence.

5. If we cannot reject the appointee, what should we do?

Here is the practical question. Suppose someone has already been appointed. Perhaps the appointment was political. Perhaps rejecting the person is not within your authority—or is simply not feasible.

Do we give up? Do we silently accept that they do not understand the role?

I would argue for a different response: do not confuse accepting the appointment with accepting incompetence. If the person holds the responsibility, they must learn the responsibility.

That does not mean humiliating them, shouting at them, or pretending that every gap can be solved through pressure. It means building a disciplined learning and accountability process. “Pecut” should mean a demanding standard, structured practice, direct feedback, and consequences for refusing to learn—not abuse.

The goal is capability, not punishment. The assessment should match the actual duties and be fair, documented, and proportionate.

Step 1 — Make the job requirements explicit

Do not rely on vague expectations such as “be a good leader” or “understand the sector.” Translate the role into observable capabilities: what must this person know, explain, decide, produce, and be accountable for?

Step 2 — Diagnose before prescribing

Ask the person to explain the core concepts, walk through a realistic case, or review a sample deliverable. A knowledge gap, a lack of experience, a language barrier, and a refusal to learn are different problems. They require different responses.

Step 3 — Create a learning contract

Agree on a mentor, learning materials, practice assignments, deadlines, and the evidence that will demonstrate progress. A title should not exempt someone from learning; it should make the learning expectations clearer.

Step 4 — Coach, practise, and challenge

Use real work. Ask the appointee to defend a decision, explain the evidence, identify uncertainty, and respond to feedback. Repeat the cycle. A demanding leader does not merely say “you should know this.” They create the conditions and insist that the person reaches the required standard.

Step 5 — Assess performance, not loyalty or confidence

Someone may sound confident and still misunderstand the subject. Someone may be inexperienced and learn quickly. Use work samples, scenario-based assessments, transparent criteria, and feedback from relevant experts.

Step 6 — Keep accountability real

If the person meets the standard, give them greater autonomy. If they are improving but not there yet, provide additional support and time where appropriate. If they repeatedly refuse to learn or cannot safely perform essential duties, restrict decision authority, redesign the role, or pursue reassignment through fair and lawful procedures.

My principle: if we cannot always control who gets appointed, we must at least insist on what the appointment requires. Political selection cannot be a permanent exemption from professional standards.

6. Expertise is not a luxury item

Imagine an organization working in science but failing to understand scientific evidence. Imagine a public health leader who cannot distinguish a strong study from a weak one. Imagine a monitoring and evaluation manager who cannot explain indicators, data quality, or the limits of causal claims.

Should we be embarrassed? Yes—not because people begin their careers knowing everything, but because a position carries a duty to learn what is necessary to do the job responsibly.

There is a difference between “I do not know yet” and “I do not need to know.” The first can be the beginning of professional growth. The second can become a risk to the entire organization.

And the same standard should apply to how we pay people. If expertise is essential, compensation should reflect the required level of skill, responsibility, scarcity, and impact—within transparent and defensible pay structures. Paying the lowest possible amount is not automatically efficient if it increases delivery risk, turnover, rework, or the likelihood of failure.

7. Human resources means developing human capability

We cannot claim to value people while treating their knowledge as disposable. Nor can we claim to value expertise while refusing to invest in it.

A healthy organization should be able to answer:

  • What capabilities do we actually need?
  • Are people selected and paid using clear, role-related criteria?
  • Can we explain why a position exists and what value it creates?
  • Do appointees receive support to learn—and are they held accountable for doing so?
  • Can professional experts speak honestly when evidence contradicts political preference?

These are not anti-politics questions. They are questions about whether an organization can remain competent, trustworthy, and useful while navigating political realities.

Being appointed is not the same as being competent. Being connected is not the same as being qualified. And being grateful to someone who gave you an opportunity does not exempt you from the responsibility to do your job properly.

The appointment may be political. The responsibility is still professional.

That is what we lack—not necessarily resources or money, but a consistent commitment to developing human capability.

So before asking how much an organization should spend on its resources, perhaps we should ask a more fundamental question:

Do we even understand what a resource is?

Research and further reading

  1. Colonnelli, E., Prem, M., & Teso, E. (2020). “Patronage and Selection in Public Sector Organizations.” American Economic Review, 110(10), 3071–3099. Study of Brazil’s public workforce; reports political connections as a major determinant of employment and political considerations selecting less competent individuals in the studied setting. Raw link: AEA
  2. OECD (2020). “Merit.” OECD Public Integrity Handbook. Explains merit-based recruitment, objective criteria, transparent processes, and risks from patronage and nepotism. Raw link: OECD
  3. OECD (2021). “Special focus: Managing the senior level public service.” Public Employment and Management 2021. Discusses leadership competency assessment, transparency, accountability, and balancing political responsiveness with merit and stability. Raw link: OECD
  4. OECD Recommendation on Public Integrity (2017). Recommends fair, open, merit-based recruitment and selection, with objective criteria and accountability. Raw link: OECD Legal Instruments
  5. Trantidis, A. (2025). “Clientelism.” Cambridge Elements in Political Economy. Defines clientelism as conditional provision of resources or advantages in exchange for political support. Raw link: Cambridge University Press
  6. Kuipers, N. (2026). “Bureaucratic Selection and Weberian Values: Lab-in-the-Field Evidence from Indonesia.” The Journal of Politics, 88(1), 234–249. An Indonesia-focused experiment examining merit-based selection, patronage, and bureaucratic values. Raw link: DOI
  7. León, A., & Santos, K. (2026). “Political accountability and bureaucratic selection.” Journal of Public Economics, 255, 105580. Reports that anti-corruption audits improved skill-task matching, with mechanisms including political accountability, recruitment effort, and reduced patronage. Raw link: DOI

Evidence and framing note: research findings are summarized in context and do not establish that every politically appointed person is unqualified, that every low salary offer is favoritism, or that one training approach works for all roles. The diagrams are conceptual models authored for this article, not empirical causal estimates.

item.title: Why Effort Changes the Opportunity to Solve a Problem: Samsung, Nokia, and the Psychology of Repair
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: Effort does not guarantee success, but relevant and sustained effort can create opportunities to diagnose problems, reduce harm, rebuild trust, and adapt. Explore the Samsung Galaxy Note7 recall, Nokia's smartphone decline, and the psychology of effective repair.
item.content:encoded:
Psychology • Strategy • Conflict Repair • Systems Thinking

Effort does not guarantee success. But relevant, sustained effort can change what is possible: it creates more opportunities to understand a problem, test solutions, reduce harm, and rebuild trust.

When a conflict remains unresolved, people sometimes say, “If it is meant to be, things will work out,” or “Time will heal everything.” Those statements may offer comfort, but they can also hide an important question: what is anyone actually doing to make a better outcome possible?

Problems do not all require the same response. A small misunderstanding may need one honest conversation. A serious breach of trust may require accountability, repeated evidence of change, and time. The size and nature of the damage should shape the kind of effort used to repair it.

Effort matters not because suffering proves sincerity, but because meaningful action can create opportunities that passive waiting leaves unused.

1. Effort changes the opportunity—not the guarantee

Imagine a conflict as a situation with several possible paths. One path is avoidance: do nothing, hope emotions fade, and assume the other person will eventually move on. Another is repair: clarify what happened, listen to the impact, accept responsibility, propose a relevant remedy, and follow through.

Repair does not guarantee reconciliation. The other person may still decline to continue the relationship, and that choice must be respected. Yet active repair can create opportunities that did not exist before: an opportunity to correct misinformation, understand the harm, demonstrate accountability, or make an informed decision about the future.

Low or misdirected effortLeaves important questions unanswered, relies on assumptions, and may allow avoidable damage to continue.
Relevant, sustained effortCreates more chances to learn what went wrong, test a remedy, respond to feedback, and show that change is real.
OutcomeStill depends on many factors: the severity of harm, timing, context, the quality of the response, and whether both people want to participate.

2. Interactive model: how effort can change the opportunity for repair

Select each stage in the diagram. Notice that effort does not magically jump straight to forgiveness. It creates intermediate opportunities, and each one can succeed or fail.

Selected: Conflict. Effort begins by acknowledging that something needs attention.

This diagram is a conceptual model for reflection, not a validated mathematical formula or a guarantee of a particular outcome.

3. Case study: Samsung Galaxy Note7—accepting a costly remedy

In 2016, Samsung's Galaxy Note7 phones were found to have a battery-related fire hazard. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission's recall notice described risks of overheating and catching fire, and offered consumers a refund or replacement remedy. Samsung announced that it had stopped sales and would voluntarily replace devices, then worked with regulators and retail partners on the recall process.

In the United States, Samsung's exchange program offered customers choices that included exchanging the Note7 for a Galaxy S7 or S7 edge, with a refund of the price difference, or taking part in the replacement process. When replacement devices also presented safety concerns, Samsung stopped production and sales and expanded the recall to include both original and replacement devices.

That is a useful example of costly corrective action. A company could not responsibly solve a safety problem with a reassuring slogan alone. It needed to stop sales, coordinate logistics, give customers a practical remedy, investigate the failure, and accept commercial consequences.

What the example shows: the company created a more credible path to consumer protection by taking concrete action, not merely by saying that customer safety mattered.

Samsung's response was not flawless, and the replacement-device problem showed that the first corrective action was insufficient. This makes the case more instructive, not less: effort must include learning and adjustment. A costly first response is not enough if evidence shows that the underlying risk remains.

Samsung's 2017 sustainability report later described extensive investigation, including testing more than 200,000 devices and 30,000 batteries, and said it had worked to identify the causes of the battery failures. These figures are reported by Samsung itself, so they should be understood as the company's account of its investigation.

The lesson is not that every organisation should always choose the most expensive response. The lesson is that when the potential harm is serious, a proportionate response may require accepting substantial cost to protect people and address the damage.

4. The contrasting case: Nokia and the cost of a delayed strategic response

Nokia is often described as a company that “ignored customers” or simply refused to innovate. That is too simplistic. Its decline in the smartphone market had multiple causes, including organisational conflict, strategic decisions, a fragmented software environment, and the industry's shift from hardware-led competition toward operating systems, apps, and platform ecosystems.

Research discussed by INSEAD notes that Nokia was initially dismissive of the iPhone and Android challenge while its Symbian operating system was ageing and its app ecosystem struggled to match competitors. A separate study of Nokia's decline describes how organisational design and strategic choices made it harder for the company to respond effectively to the transition.

Nokia did try to respond, including through its Windows Phone partnership with Microsoft. But effort is not automatically effective just because an organisation is busy. If a response arrives late, relies on risky assumptions, or does not meet what users and developers need, it may fail to recover the opportunity that has already shifted elsewhere.

Important correction: Nokia did not simply “go bankrupt.” Its handset business was sold to Microsoft; Nokia continued as a company and focused more heavily on network infrastructure and other businesses. The more accurate lesson is that it lost its former dominance in mobile phones, not that the entire company disappeared.

This contrasts with the Note7 recall in a useful way. Samsung's safety crisis demanded immediate corrective action to reduce direct harm. Nokia's platform crisis demanded earlier strategic adaptation, stronger software execution, and a more effective response to a changing ecosystem. Different problems require different kinds of effort.

5. The opposite case: Takata—when denial and concealment magnify a crisis

The Takata airbag scandal shows a much darker kind of failure than simply choosing the wrong strategy. Certain airbag inflators could rupture and propel metal fragments into vehicle occupants, causing serious injuries and deaths. According to the U.S. Department of Justice, Takata admitted that from around 2000 through 2015 it supplied false or manipulated test data that concealed the true performance of certain inflators from automakers. Even after failures in the field included ruptures, injuries, and deaths, the company continued withholding accurate information.

This distinction matters: Takata's failure was not merely that a product had a defect. Products can fail despite responsible design and testing. The deeper failure was the response to known risk—concealing information that customers and regulators needed to make decisions, rather than confronting the problem transparently and quickly enough.

What made the crisis worse? When a safety-critical problem is concealed or downplayed, the organisation loses time that could have been used to warn people, investigate the cause, coordinate repairs, and reduce further harm. The delay does not simply preserve the original problem; it can enlarge the consequences.

In January 2017, Takata agreed to plead guilty to wire fraud. In February 2017, it was sentenced to pay US$1 billion in criminal penalties, including restitution for injured individuals and recall-related costs incurred by automakers. The company filed for bankruptcy in 2017 as the airbag crisis and related liabilities overwhelmed it.

The U.S. government reported that Takata's conduct involved a long-running scheme to falsify test information, and that defective inflators were linked to injuries and deaths. This is stronger evidence than a general claim that the company merely “did not try.” The documented issue was a failure of honesty, disclosure, accountability, and timely action in the face of known safety risks.

What responsible effort could have enabledEarly disclosure, transparent testing, prompt regulator engagement, warnings, root-cause investigation, and a coordinated remedy before the crisis expanded further.
What concealment did insteadIt deprived customers and automakers of accurate information, undermined trust, complicated the response, and exposed the company to severe legal and financial consequences.
The central lessonWhen people depend on you for safety, effort must include truthfulness and accountability—not merely working harder to protect the organisation's image.

Takata is not proof that one decision alone caused the company's collapse. Its downfall had multiple legal, operational, and financial causes. But the official case record supports a clear conclusion: the prolonged deception and failure to disclose known problems were central to the crisis and its consequences.

6. Three cases, three different lessons

Samsung Note7A severe product-safety crisis prompted recalls, customer remedies, and further investigation. The case illustrates costly corrective action and the need to adjust when the first remedy proves insufficient.
NokiaThe company lost smartphone market leadership amid a complicated transition involving strategy, software, organisational challenges, and ecosystem competition. Its story is better described as delayed or ineffective adaptation—not simply a refusal to make an effort.
TakataA prolonged scheme to falsify or withhold safety-test information made a dangerous product crisis worse. Its case highlights the consequences of concealment and failures of accountability.

These cases are not a controlled experiment, and they should not be reduced to “high effort equals success” or “low effort equals bankruptcy.” They involve different industries, risks, and circumstances. Their value is in showing how the quality of a response—whether it is timely, honest, relevant, and sustained—can change the range of outcomes available.

7. Why effort can change the odds: five mechanisms

It improves diagnosis.
Effort spent listening, investigating, and checking evidence reduces the chance of solving the wrong problem.
It creates options.
People who explore alternatives can discover routes that passive waiting never reveals.
It reduces ongoing harm.
In safety or trust crises, timely action can limit further damage while a fuller solution is developed.
It creates observable evidence.
Promises describe intentions. Actions and follow-through give others evidence to evaluate.
It enables adaptation.
When the first attempt fails, feedback and continued work make correction possible.

These mechanisms explain why effort can improve the probability of an effective solution. They do not mean that effort alone controls outcomes. A well-executed plan can still fail because of external constraints, insufficient resources, incompatible goals, or damage that cannot be reversed.

8. Effort must match the damage—and the actual problem

Consider three examples:

A misunderstandingRelevant effort might mean clarifying what was said, listening without interruption, and correcting a false assumption.
A breach of trustRelevant effort might mean admitting what happened, answering reasonable questions, changing the behavior, and remaining consistent over time.
A product safety failureRelevant effort may require stopping sales, recalling the product, providing refunds or replacements, investigating the cause, and preventing recurrence.

Notice that the amount of effort is not the only issue. Its direction matters. An expensive gift may do little to repair a repeated breach of trust. A public apology may do little to protect consumers if the dangerous product remains in circulation.

The right question is not simply “How much effort was made?” It is “Was the effort proportionate to the harm, directed at the real cause, and sustained long enough to make a difference?”

9. A practical framework for evaluating effort

Use these questions when assessing a conflict, a project failure, a customer complaint, or an organisational crisis:

What exactly was damaged?
Identify the harm, its scale, who experienced it, and whether it is continuing.
Who has responsibility to act?
Separate the responsibility to repair harm from the separate question of whether the affected person chooses to forgive or continue.
What action would address the cause?
Choose a remedy that fits the actual problem rather than a symbolic gesture that merely looks impressive.
What obstacles are real?
Account for safety, resources, time, access, and other constraints. Look for reasonable alternatives rather than demanding reckless sacrifice.
What evidence would show progress?
Define observable signs: a corrected process, a kept commitment, fewer repeat incidents, clearer communication, or improved user outcomes.
What happens if the first attempt fails?
Review the evidence, acknowledge shortcomings, and adapt the response. Do not assume that good intentions make an ineffective remedy sufficient.

10. In relationships, effort is not a test of suffering

There is a risk in talking about effort: people may interpret it as a demand to prove love through dramatic gestures, unlimited availability, or unsafe sacrifices. That is not the point.

Showing up uninvited, lying to provoke a reaction, manufacturing an emergency, or ignoring someone's boundaries is not a healthy way to measure care. These behaviours can create pressure and confusion rather than genuine repair.

More useful evidence includes whether someone takes initiative, communicates honestly, makes realistic plans, follows through, accepts responsibility, and changes the behaviour that caused the problem. If circumstances prevent a planned action, proposing a reasonable alternative can also show commitment.

And the person who was hurt retains the right to say no. Effort can create an opportunity for repair; it does not create an entitlement to forgiveness, access, or reconciliation.

Conclusion: Effort changes what becomes possible

The Samsung Note7 case illustrates how a company can respond to a serious product safety problem with costly corrective action. Nokia's smartphone decline illustrates a different risk: when a changing environment demands a timely and effective strategic response, fragmented or poorly aligned decisions can allow an opportunity to disappear. Neither case is a simple morality tale, and neither proves that effort guarantees success.

Together, they point to a broader principle. Effective effort creates opportunities to diagnose, act, learn, and adapt. Insufficient or misdirected effort can leave problems unresolved or allow them to grow. The key is not effort for its own sake, but effort that matches the scale and nature of the problem.

Time does not recall a product. Good intentions do not fix a broken process. And wanting a relationship to heal does not, by itself, rebuild trust. Meaningful effort is the bridge between recognising a problem and creating a real opportunity to solve it.

This article uses business cases as illustrations of a general problem-solving principle. Corporate outcomes have multiple causes; the cases should not be interpreted as proof that effort alone caused success or failure.

Further Reading

  • Samsung — Official Statement on Galaxy Note7 (September 2, 2016): announcement of stopped sales and a voluntary replacement programme.
  • U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission — Galaxy Note7 Recall: safety hazard, recall details, and consumer remedies.
  • Samsung — Expanded Note7 Recall (October 13, 2016): recall expansion to original and replacement devices.
  • Samsung Sustainability Report 2017: the company's account of its Note7 investigation and corrective measures.
  • INSEAD Knowledge — The Strategic Decisions That Caused Nokia’s Failure: analysis of Nokia's strategic and organisational challenges.
  • London Business School — The Rise and Fall of Nokia: case overview of Nokia's smartphone-era decline and sale of its handset business.
  • U.S. Department of Justice — Takata Pleads Guilty and Is Sentenced to Pay $1 Billion: official summary of the admitted fraud scheme, withheld test data, injuries, deaths, and criminal penalties.
  • NHTSA — Takata Air Bag Recall Spotlight: recall information and consumer safety guidance.

item.title: Your Brain Has a Task Manager: How Stress and Lies Can Overload Thinking
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: Explore one interactive brain pathway from problem to stress to concealment. Watch the brain glow as simulated cognitive demands rise, and see why overload may make details easier to miss and statements harder to keep consistent.
item.content:encoded:
Cognitive Psychology • Stress • Working Memory • Systems Thinking

Your brain is not literally a CPU, and IQ is not a battery percentage. But the computer analogy can help explain a useful idea: when attention and working memory are occupied by competing demands, fewer resources may remain available for the task in front of you.

Imagine you are trying to finish a difficult project. You must analyse information, remember instructions, solve errors, make decisions, and meet a deadline. Now add stress: you worry about failure, anticipate criticism, and replay every possible consequence. Then add concealment: you must remember what you told different people, which details you left out, and how to keep explanations consistent.

The original task has not become easier. You have simply added more processes for your mind to manage.

The central idea: maintaining a complicated lie can add cognitive demands. Under pressure, those demands may compete with the attention, working memory, and control needed to do the original work. This is a conceptual explanation—not a way to calculate anyone's IQ or detect lies from appearance.

1. One interactive brain: from a problem to cognitive overload

Use this single visual to follow the chain: a problem demands attention; stress adds worry and threat-monitoring; hiding the problem can add another task—maintaining a story. When the illustrative demand reaches the model's 100-unit reference, there may be no “headroom” left for unexpected details. Real people may then overlook information, contradict earlier statements, or make faulty connections—not because a lie always causes this, but because competing demands can strain attention and working memory.

Adjust the same live model

50
20
20
10

Total illustrative demand: 100 / 100 units · Remaining headroom: 0

At the reference limit: no headroom remains in this toy model.

The “100 units” are a teaching metaphor, not a measurement of IQ, brain energy, or an individual's mental capacity. When the model reaches the limit, it illustrates competition between demands—not a biological brain hitting a literal 100% cap.

3. Why stress can make thinking harder

Stress can redirect attention toward threats, consequences, and uncertainty. Some of that monitoring may be useful: noticing a real deadline or safety risk can help you respond. But persistent worry can also compete with the task you are trying to complete.

Think of a developer debugging an application. The developer needs to inspect logs, test hypotheses, and keep several technical details in working memory. If they are also worrying constantly about being blamed, they may find it harder to stay focused on the evidence. That does not prove their intelligence has fallen. It means the situation is demanding more from their attention and control.

Stress affects people differently. Its effects depend on intensity, duration, context, experience, and the task. The CPU analogy is useful for explaining competition between demands, but the brain does not literally allocate a neat percentage to “stress.”

4. Why maintaining a lie can add more processes

A simple false statement may be brief. A sustained deception can be more complicated, especially when a person has to keep multiple details consistent or conceal information from different people. Possible extra demands include:

  • Constructing a version: deciding what to say instead of reporting what happened.
  • Monitoring consistency: remembering what was said previously and to whom.
  • Inhibiting the truth: stopping a well-practised or spontaneous truthful response from coming out.
  • Tracking the listener: watching questions and reactions to decide whether the story needs further explanation.
  • Managing consequences: anticipating discovery, judgement, or punishment.
  • Justifying the choice: creating reasons that make the behaviour feel acceptable to oneself.

These processes are not equally present in every lie, and lying is not always more demanding than truth-telling in every context. Familiar, rehearsed, or low-stakes lies may be produced with little apparent effort. The strongest claim is narrower: complicated deception can impose extra cognitive demands, and competing tasks can interfere with some forms of dishonest responding.

The background-process problem: the original problem is still running. The person now also has to manage the cover story. When attention is already strained, that extra work may make it harder to analyse, communicate, and correct the original problem.

5. What does the research say?

A study by van ’t Veer, Stel, and van Beest, published in Judgment and Decision Making, tested whether cognitive load affected dishonest reporting. In an experiment with 173 participants, people memorised either a short or a longer string of letters while reporting die-roll outcomes, one of which affected payment. In the high-load condition, the researchers did not detect the same pattern of dishonest reporting for the paid roll that appeared in the low-load condition.

The authors interpreted the result as evidence that limited cognitive capacity can interfere with certain forms of dishonesty. The study does not establish a universal law that every lie consumes a fixed amount of mental capacity, nor does it show that a person's resource use can be calculated as a percentage. Its findings are specific to the experimental setup and should be read alongside the broader, mixed research on deception and cognitive load.

Research on deception has also examined response time, pupil dilation, working memory, and brain activation. These measures can indicate differences in cognitive processing at group level, but no single cue reliably proves that a particular person is lying. A person who pauses, looks nervous, or struggles to explain something may be stressed, confused, tired, or afraid—not necessarily dishonest.

6. IQ is not a CPU percentage

The “100% resource” idea is a metaphor, not an IQ equation. IQ scores are standardised scores from specific tests; they are not a live gauge showing how much of someone's intelligence is available at a given moment. There is no scientifically valid conversion such as “50% resource remaining = 50% IQ.”

A more accurate way to express the idea is: your underlying ability may remain the same, while your performance on a particular task can be affected by distraction, stress, fatigue, competing memory demands, or uncertainty. Even that varies from person to person and task to task.

Use the analogy carefully: “I have less attention available for this task right now” is much more defensible than “my IQ has dropped by 50%.” The first describes a temporary performance challenge; the second makes an unsupported measurement claim.

7. How to stop running unnecessary background processes

1. Pause before reacting

When pressure rises, take a short pause if the situation allows. A slower response can give you time to separate facts from fears and choose the next action deliberately.

2. Put the facts outside your head

Write down the actual problem, what is known, what remains uncertain, and the next step. Notes and checklists reduce the need to keep every detail active in working memory.

3. Replace a complicated cover story with a clear update

If you made a mistake, say what happened, what the impact is, what you have done so far, and what you will do next. You do not have to explain endlessly, and honesty does not require sharing irrelevant private details.

4. Ask for time or support when needed

If you are too overwhelmed to answer accurately, say that you need a little time to check the facts. If distress is severe or persistent, consider reaching out to someone you trust or a qualified professional.

5. Fix the original issue

Correct the error, communicate the risk, or ask for help with the task. Concealment may feel protective in the moment, but it can make the practical problem harder to diagnose and repair.

Conclusion: stop hiding, start solving

The processor analogy helps us picture how several demands can compete for limited attention and working memory. A difficult task already requires effort. Stress can add worry and threat-monitoring. A sustained lie can add the need to construct, remember, and maintain a consistent account.

That extra cognitive work may leave fewer resources for the original task—not because the person's IQ has literally dropped, but because their attention is divided. The interactive monitor above is only an illustration of this principle, not a diagnostic tool or a measurement of any individual's brain.

Do not spend the attention you need to solve a problem on maintaining a second problem created by hiding the first one. Be clear about what happened, focus on what can be corrected, and take one step at a time.

Sources and further reading

  • van ’t Veer, A. E., Stel, M., & van Beest, I. — “Limited capacity to lie: Cognitive load interferes with being dishonest.” Judgment and Decision Making, 9(3), 199–206 (2014). The main experimental source on cognitive load and dishonest reporting.
  • University of Amsterdam research repository record. A related academic source supplied for further reading.
  • Frontiers in Psychology — article on deception and cognitive processing. Further context on the cognitive processes involved in deception.

Evidence note: the numerical resource bars are invented for educational illustration. The cited research supports a relationship between cognitive load and some dishonest behaviour under specific experimental conditions; it does not validate the percentages used in this simulation or establish a universal brain-resource formula.

item.title: How to Become a Modern-Day Great Sage: Cultivating the Mind in the Age of Information Overload
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: What if the Great Sage was not simply someone who emptied the mind and waited for enlightenment, but someone who deliberately cultivated attention, knowledge, emotional discipline, and practical skill? A modern framework for becoming a lifelong learner in an age of information overload.
item.content:encoded:
Living Heritage · Cognitive Development · Lifelong Learning

How to Become a Modern-Day Great Sage

What if the Great Sage was not simply someone who emptied the mind and waited for enlightenment? What if the ancient image of the hermit, the cultivator, and the scholar described a disciplined process of developing the mind—reducing distractions, studying deeply, training deliberately, and learning to act with wisdom?

Article 85 · By Angga Conni Saputra · October 28, 2026

Ancient metaphors. Modern lessons. A wiser way to learn.

1. The Hypothesis: Perhaps the Sage Was Cultivating More Than Stillness

In stories about ancient sages, we often encounter a familiar scene: a person retreats to a mountain, leaves behind ordinary distractions, meditates, reads scrolls, practices for years, and eventually acquires extraordinary knowledge or insight.

One interpretation focuses on emptiness: the sage clears the mind, abandons worldly desires, and waits for enlightenment or guidance to arrive. That may capture part of the meaning in some spiritual traditions, but it does not tell the whole story of the metaphor.

Here is an alternative hypothesis—not a claim that every ancient tradition meant exactly this, but a modern interpretation worth exploring:

Perhaps the Great Sage is not someone who empties the mind of knowledge, but someone who clears away what prevents the mind from learning.

Under this interpretation, retreat is not the final destination. It is a method for reclaiming attention. Emotional discipline is not the rejection of human feeling. It is the ability to feel without being controlled by every impulse. Reading scrolls is not decorative storytelling. It represents the deliberate acquisition of knowledge. Cultivation is the repeated practice that turns knowledge into capability.

The metaphor becomes surprisingly contemporary when we consider our current environment: endless notifications, fragmented attention, algorithmic feeds, emotionally provocative content, and a constant supply of information that is easy to consume but not always easy to understand or remember.

We might call some of this brainrot or information overload. These terms should not be treated as clinical diagnoses, and digital media is not inherently harmful. The central concern is whether our habits leave enough time and attention for reflection, sustained learning, and meaningful practice.

The Great Sage Hypothesis: A modern sage deliberately protects attention, reduces unproductive mental noise, develops emotional self-regulation, studies reliable sources, practices useful skills, tests assumptions, and integrates what they learn into sound judgment.

This is a working framework inspired by ancient metaphors and informed by modern learning research. It is not a historical claim about the original meaning of every sage, hermit, or cultivator in every culture.

2. Four Metaphors, One Developmental Path

The four stages are a practical interpretation of the metaphors—not a universal historical doctrine.

1. The Hermit: protect attention

Reduce avoidable distractions and create periods for focused thought. The aim is not social isolation; it is intentional control over where attention goes.

2. The Cultivator: practice

Choose abilities worth developing, work on specific weaknesses, seek feedback, and repeat the practice. Exposure alone is not mastery.

3. The Scholar: understand

Read, compare sources, ask why, identify uncertainty, retrieve ideas from memory, and explain concepts in your own words.

4. The Great Sage: integrate

Use knowledge with judgment. Consider context, trade-offs, ethics, uncertainty, and consequences before deciding what to do.

3. First Principle: Clear the Noise, Not the Mind

The phrase “empty your mind” can be misunderstood as a call to stop thinking. For this framework, a more useful interpretation is to reduce the dominance of mental habits that repeatedly hijack attention.

Jealousy, envy, anger, resentment, anxiety, and desire are normal human experiences. The goal is not to erase emotions or pretend that nothing matters. Emotions can provide important signals. The task is to notice them, understand what they are telling us, and avoid letting a passing impulse make every decision.

Try a simple three-question pause when a strong emotion appears:

  1. What am I feeling? Name the emotion without immediately judging yourself.
  2. What triggered it? Separate observable facts from assumptions and interpretations.
  3. What response serves my values and goals? Choose a response rather than automatically obeying the first impulse.

Attention also needs protection from the environment. Put the phone out of reach during a focused learning session, turn off non-essential notifications, and decide in advance what you intend to learn before opening a feed or browser.

Practical rule: Do not ask only, “How much information did I consume today?” Ask, “What can I now explain, remember, evaluate, or do that I could not do before?”

This is not a claim that all entertainment or social media degrades cognition. Digital tools can teach, connect, and inspire. The key is whether use is deliberate and balanced, or whether it repeatedly displaces the activities you value.

4. Second Principle: Train Both Divergent and Convergent Thinking

A modern Great Sage needs more than a large collection of facts. Complex problems often require two complementary modes of thinking.

Divergent thinking generates a range of possible ideas, interpretations, or solutions. It asks: What else could be true? What alternatives have I overlooked? How might this problem be approached differently?

Convergent thinking evaluates and narrows those possibilities. It asks: Which options fit the evidence? What constraints matter? What are the costs, risks, and trade-offs? Which choice is most defensible?

These modes are not enemies, and they are not necessarily separate stages that occur only once. Creative work often alternates between generating ideas, evaluating them, discovering gaps, and returning to exploration. Research reviews also suggest that divergent thinking draws on multiple executive processes, including flexible attention and working memory; the exact relationships are complex and not fully settled.

Further reading: Divergent thinking and the core executive functions: a state-of-the-art review (2022); Metacontrol of human creativity: the neurocognitive mechanisms of convergent and divergent thinking (2020); and the OECD discussion of divergent and convergent thinking.

Try Invergent: a deliberate thinking workout

If you want to practice switching between divergent and convergent thinking, try Invergent, an experimental, browser-based thinking toolkit designed to help users deliberately move between exploring possibilities and making decisions.

It combines divergent thinking to expand the possibility space, convergent thinking to evaluate options using constraints and trade-offs, and switching exercises to practice moving between exploration and selection. Its lightweight, data-driven design uses an editable JSON question bank, heuristic profiles, and timed learning sessions to support reflection and practice.

Use case: Divergent & Convergent Thinking Practice — a small mental workout for generating alternatives, evaluating them, and switching modes intentionally.

Open Invergent →

Treat it as a practice tool, not a validated clinical assessment or a guarantee of increased intelligence. Its value comes from the quality of the questions, your effort, and what you learn from reflecting on your answers.

5. Third Principle: Do Not Confuse Information with Learning

Modern life makes it easy to collect links, save videos, highlight passages, and accumulate notes. These activities can be useful, but they do not prove that learning has occurred.

Learning is more convincing when you can retrieve an idea without looking, explain it in your own words, apply it to a new problem, or notice when it does not fit the evidence.

A major review by Dunlosky and colleagues evaluated ten common learning techniques. It found strong support for practice testing and distributed practice, while techniques such as rereading and highlighting alone often had lower utility when used as primary strategies. A later review in Nature Reviews Psychology also emphasizes the benefits of spacing learning over time and retrieving information from memory.

Sources: Dunlosky et al. (2013), Improving Students’ Learning With Effective Learning Techniques; Carpenter, Pan & Butler (2022), The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice.

Retrieve

Close the source and write down what you remember. Then compare your recall with the original and correct the gaps.

Space

Return to important material over multiple sessions rather than trying to absorb everything in one marathon session.

Explain

Ask “why?” and “how?” Connect a new idea to examples, mechanisms, counterexamples, and concepts you already understand.

Apply

Use the concept in a real task, a worked example, a small experiment, or a problem that differs from the original example.

For example, after reading about cognitive flexibility, do not stop at underlining the definition. Put the source away and explain what it means. Then identify an occasion when you changed your mind because of new evidence, and another occasion when you should have considered more alternatives.

That process turns reading into retrieval, explanation, and application. It also exposes the difference between familiarity—“I have seen this before”—and actual recall.

6. Fourth Principle: Practice Deliberately, Not Merely Frequently

The cultivator metaphor is especially useful here. Repeating an activity can improve performance, but repetition alone is not a magic formula. Practice becomes more informative when it targets a specific skill, includes feedback, and gives you a chance to correct errors.

Research on expert performance has examined the role of deliberate practice: structured activities designed to improve performance, often involving effortful work on weaknesses and informative feedback. The details vary by domain, and practice is not the only factor behind expertise. Access to instruction, prior knowledge, motivation, opportunity, health, and other circumstances also matter.

Further reading: Ericsson et al. (1993), The Role of Deliberate Practice in the Acquisition of Expert Performance; Ericsson & Harwell (2019), Deliberate Practice and Proposed Limits on the Effects of Practice.
