Perhaps the real “magic trick” is not convincing everyone that we were right. Perhaps it is building something useful enough to demonstrate a better way.

Related article

The Shortcut Problem: Why Doping, Gambling, Cheating and Corruption Follow the Same Behavioural Logic

This companion article explores the behavioural pattern behind shortcuts, immediate rewards, delayed costs, present bias, and the design of better alternatives.

Read Article 73 ↗

Further Reading

  • U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Why Quitting Smoking Is Hard: nicotine dependence and routines that can make quitting difficult.
  • NHS — Managing Nicotine Withdrawal Symptoms: cravings and common withdrawal symptoms after stopping smoking.
  • UNDP — Systems & Portfolios: approaches to addressing interconnected development challenges.
  • UNDP — System Change Guidebook: a practical guide to portfolio approaches and system change.
  • Harvard Business Review — When a Team Member Speaks Up and It Doesn’t Go Well: communicating concerns in organisations.
  • Harvard Business Review — Building a Culture Where Employees Feel Free to Speak Up: creating conditions in which staff can raise concerns.
  • International Labour Organization — 10 Ways to Recognize Modern Slavery: indicators of exploitation and coercive labour conditions.

This article offers a systems-thinking perspective, not a diagnosis of any individual. Behaviour depends on context, and claims about responsibility or exploitation require case-specific evidence.

item.title: The Architecture of Human Thinking: Eight Cognitive Approaches, How to Train Them, and Why Teams Need All of Them
item.category: Cognitive Science, Inclusive Leadership & Human Resource Management
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: Human thinking draws on complementary processes—not fixed cognitive types. Explore eight practical lenses, evidence-informed learning strategies, metacognition, a worked organisational case, and tools for testing assumptions and coordinating cognitive diversity in teams.
item.content:encoded:
Cognitive Science • Inclusion • Human Resource Management

Humans are not unique because everyone thinks in the same way. We are unique because we bring different combinations of attention, experience, reasoning, imagination, knowledge, and judgement to the same problem.

Some people quickly generate alternatives. Others detect inconsistencies, connect events across a system, recognise familiar patterns, or ask whether the evidence supports the conclusion. A team needs more than one of these contributions—especially when the problem is complex, unfamiliar, or socially consequential.

Divergent and convergent thinking are useful starting points, but they are not a complete map of human cognition. The eight approaches below are a practical learning framework, not eight fixed personality types or a validated diagnostic test. They overlap, can coexist in the same person, and can be strengthened through practice.

The aim is not to label people. It is to understand which thinking moves a task requires, practise the moves we underuse, and design teams in which different contributions can work together.

What this framework is—and what it is not

The eight approaches are best understood as lenses or moves in a thinking process, not as a complete taxonomy of the mind. They are grouped here because they help people ask different kinds of questions when solving problems. They do not all operate at the same conceptual level: divergent and convergent thinking describe ways of working with alternatives; deduction, induction, and abduction describe forms of inference; analytic and holistic thinking describe different emphases in representing a problem; and detail-focused and context-sensitive thinking describe attentional emphases.

This matters because a useful framework should help people reason more carefully, not imply more scientific certainty than it has. There is no claim that these eight lenses are exhaustive, independent, mutually exclusive, or suitable for diagnosing an individual's cognitive profile. Other capabilities—such as working memory, inhibition, domain knowledge, language, emotion regulation, and cognitive flexibility—also influence performance.

InputsEvidence, observations, prior knowledge, lived experience, questions, constraints, and the quality of available information.
Thinking movesAttend, interpret, generate options, decompose, connect, infer, compare, question, test, and revise.
OutputsA clearer explanation, a decision, an action, a forecast, a model, a new question, or a record of what remains uncertain.
ContextTime, fatigue, incentives, stress, tools, social power, expertise, consequences, and feedback can all change which approach is useful.

Use the framework diagnostically for the task, not diagnostically for the person. Ask “Which thinking move is missing from our process?” rather than “What type of thinker is this person?”

Explore the eight approaches

Select a node in the diagram to jump to its explanation and exercise. The map illustrates complementary approaches, not a ranking or a psychological test.

The diagram links to the numbered explanations below. It is a navigational learning aid, not a ranking, test, or permanent classification.

1. Divergent and convergent thinking: create options, then make a choice

Divergent thinking expands possible ideas and solutions. Convergent thinking evaluates alternatives against evidence and criteria to arrive at a defensible choice. They are complementary phases, not rival identities.

Practise: take a problem such as low participation in training. Spend five minutes listing plausible causes and interventions without judging them. Then shortlist options using cost, feasibility, inclusion, and expected effect. Record why you rejected alternatives.

Watch out for: endless ideation without decisions, or premature closure that dismisses alternatives before the problem is understood.

2. Analytic and holistic thinking: inspect parts and context

Analytic thinking separates a problem into parts, variables, or claims. Holistic thinking attends to relationships, circumstances, and the wider situation. Strong analysis may need both.

Practise: break an implementation failure into people, process, technology, budget, and incentives. Then map links between them and ask which relationships might explain the outcome. Check whether the apparent cause remains plausible in the wider context.

Watch out for: getting lost in details, or using complexity as a substitute for testing an explanation.

3. Intuitive and reflective thinking: notice the first answer, then test it

Intuition can produce rapid judgements from experience and recognised patterns. Reflective thinking slows down to examine evidence, assumptions, and alternative explanations. Familiar situations may reward speed; unfamiliar or high-stakes decisions deserve more checking.

Practise: record your first prediction before reviewing evidence. Later compare it with the outcome. For important decisions ask: “What evidence would change my mind?” and “What is the strongest alternative explanation?”

Watch out for: treating a gut feeling as proof, or assuming a long analysis must be correct.

4. Linear and systems thinking: follow the sequence and map feedback

Linear thinking is useful for ordered steps and straightforward causal chains. Systems thinking examines interactions, feedback, delays, incentives, and side effects. Many situations require both a process map and a system map.

Practise: map a late-reporting process. Then ask what reinforces the delay: workload, interface design, connectivity, incentives, duplicate data entry, or slow feedback. Test one leverage point and check for side effects.

Watch out for: assuming every relationship is causal, or making a model too complex to guide a decision.

5. Deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning: apply rules, learn patterns, propose explanations

Deduction applies a rule or premise to a case. Induction infers patterns from observations. Abduction proposes a plausible explanation for an observation. Abduction creates hypotheses, not proof.

Practise: apply a rule to one case (deduction); compare several cases for a recurring pattern (induction); generate several possible reasons for an unexpected result (abduction). Find evidence that could distinguish the explanations.

Watch out for: overgeneralising from few examples, confusing correlation with cause, or treating the first plausible story as truth.

6. Abstract and concrete thinking: move between principles and practice

Abstract thinking forms concepts, models, and general principles. Concrete thinking attends to specific cases, observable details, and actions. A strategy that cannot be translated into practice remains incomplete; an action without a guiding model may solve only the immediate case.

Practise: summarise an incident as a general principle, find an example that supports it and one that may challenge it, then translate the principle into an observable action.

Watch out for: abstract jargon without a workable plan, or overfitting to one example.

7. Analogical and causal reasoning: borrow insights carefully and test mechanisms

Analogical reasoning uses similarities between cases to suggest solutions. Causal reasoning asks what mechanism connects a factor to an outcome and what else might explain it. Analogy generates hypotheses; causal testing checks whether the comparison holds.

Practise: find a similar case, state precisely what is similar and different, then identify competing causes and evidence or a small experiment that could distinguish them.

Watch out for: assuming two situations share the same cause because their surface features look alike.

8. Detail-focused and context-sensitive thinking: detect signals and interpret meaning

Some tasks reward close attention to discrepancies and exceptions. Others require context—social dynamics, timing, incentives, or changes in the environment—to understand what a detail means. This is a practical distinction, not a claim that people belong to two fixed perceptual types.

Practise: review a case twice. First list only observable details. Then list context and several interpretations. Separate observations from inference and note what extra evidence is needed.

Watch out for: missing a critical detail because the overall story feels convincing, or overinterpreting one detail outside its context.

These approaches overlap—and that is the point

The eight approaches are not mutually exclusive boxes. A person can be analytical and holistic, intuitive and reflective, creative and rigorous. Ask what thinking the situation requires and whether the team is using enough complementary approaches.

Other cognitive capabilitiesCognitive flexibility switches strategies; metacognition monitors one's own thinking; probabilistic reasoning evaluates uncertainty; pattern recognition detects regularities; executive functions support attention, working memory, inhibition, and planning.
Skills are not identitiesPerformance changes with knowledge, practice, fatigue, incentives, tools, environment, and task demands. Use observations and work samples rather than inferring a permanent profile from one incident.
Not a learning-style testPreference for text, diagrams, discussion, or hands-on work does not prove that a person can learn best only through that format. Match methods to the task and test transfer to performance.

From accessing information to applying judgement

Accessing information, understanding it, remembering it, reasoning with it, making a judgement, and applying it to a new situation are related but distinct activities. A person may find a source without evaluating it, understand a sentence without knowing whether its claim is well supported, remember a fact without recognising when it applies, or make a confident decision without testing an alternative explanation.

ActivityCore questionEvidence of progress
AccessCan I locate relevant information and establish where it came from?Relevant sources are traceable; dates, authorship, and context are checked.
ComprehendCan I explain the claim accurately in my own words?The explanation preserves the original meaning and important qualifications.
RememberCan I retrieve the key idea when I need it?I can recall the idea without simply rereading the source.
ReasonHow do the evidence, assumptions, logic, and alternative explanations fit together?My conclusion follows from the evidence and makes its assumptions visible.
JudgeHow strong is the conclusion, what remains uncertain, and what would change my mind?Confidence is proportionate to evidence; relevant trade-offs are explicit.
Apply and transferCan I use the knowledge responsibly in a different situation?I adapt the principle to context rather than copying a solution mechanically.

Reading is valuable because it can supply concepts, evidence, vocabulary, and examples. Memorisation is valuable because accessible knowledge supports reasoning. Neither activity automatically guarantees sound judgement. The bridge is deliberate practice: explaining, comparing, connecting, testing, applying, and reviewing the consequences of a conclusion.

Applied Thinking Lab: why are field reports arriving late?

Consider a hypothetical organisation where field reports are frequently late. The observed problem is a delay; “staff are careless” is only one possible interpretation, and not a conclusion established by the observation. The purpose of the lab is to demonstrate how complementary approaches can improve the inquiry before the organisation commits to a solution.

Case boundaries

Known: reports arrive after the expected deadline in several reporting cycles.

Not yet known: whether the main constraint is connectivity, workload, confusing forms, training, incentives, duplicate entry, supervisory feedback, or a combination.

Decision to make: identify a feasible intervention to test, while avoiding blame before the causes are understood.

Step 1 — Define the problem before explaining it

Agree on what counts as “late,” which reports and periods are included, the baseline rate, and how the data are collected. Separate direct observations (submission timestamps, missing fields, connectivity logs) from interpretations (“the team lacks motivation”). Check whether the measure itself is reliable and whether some sites are missing from the data.

Step 2 — Generate competing hypotheses

HypothesisWhat might be observed if it is true?Useful check
Connectivity or device constraintsDelays cluster in low-connectivity locations or around upload failures.Compare timestamps, location conditions, offline records, and successful sync times.
Duplicated or confusing reporting stepsRepeated data entry, validation errors, and abandonment cluster around particular fields.Observe the workflow and ask users to complete a typical report while narrating the steps.
Workload or poorly timed deadlinesDelays peak during high-volume periods or competing field activities.Compare workload and deadline patterns across teams and weeks.
Insufficient feedback or unclear valueStaff submit late when previous submissions receive no acknowledgement or use.Examine feedback timelines and ask submitters what happens after submission.
Skills or guidance gapErrors and delays are concentrated around tasks that are poorly understood.Use a practical work sample and observe whether clear guidance changes performance.

These are hypotheses, not findings about a real organisation. More than one may be true, and another explanation may be missing. The table illustrates a disciplined way to connect each explanation to evidence that could distinguish it from the others.

Step 3 — Apply different lenses to the same case

DivergentGenerate multiple plausible causes and interventions before choosing a favourite explanation.
AnalyticBreak reporting into preparation, entry, validation, submission, review, and feedback; locate where delay accumulates.
Holistic and systemsMap how workload, connectivity, incentives, form design, and supervisory behaviour interact over time.
DeductiveIf a rule or process requirement applies, determine what should happen when the stated conditions hold.
InductiveLook for repeated patterns across sites, weeks, and types of report without assuming a small sample proves a universal rule.
AbductivePropose the explanation that best fits a particular unexpected delay, then compare it with other plausible explanations.
ReflectiveAsk what evidence would change the initial impression and actively seek disconfirming cases.
Concrete and abstractInspect an actual late report, then identify the general process principle it illustrates—without assuming one case represents every site.

Step 4 — Make the system visible, but do not mistake a diagram for proof

A simple causal map might propose that confusing forms increase correction work, correction work consumes time, and time pressure then increases rushed entries and further corrections. This would be a hypothesised reinforcing loop, not yet an established causal relationship. Interviews, process observation, time-stamped records, or a small controlled change can help test whether the proposed links are real in this context.

Step 5 — Choose a test, not an irreversible grand solution

Prioritise interventions using transparent criteria such as expected benefit, feasibility, cost, equity, reversibility, risk, and the strength of evidence. For example, one team might pilot an offline-saving feature or remove a duplicate field, depending on what the evidence indicates. Define the baseline, expected outcome, time window, and possible unintended effects before the pilot begins.

Step 6 — Review results and update the explanation

Compare actual results with the prediction. If submission timeliness improves but data quality deteriorates, the change is not an unqualified success. If the pilot has little effect, reconsider the hypothesis rather than automatically blaming implementation. Record what was learned and whether the result may generalise to other teams.

Case-study lesson: the strongest answer is not necessarily the most complicated one or the first plausible story. It is the explanation that survives meaningful checks and supports a decision proportionate to the evidence and consequences.

A repeatable protocol for difficult questions

The following sequence is a practical workflow for using the eight lenses. It is not a rigid algorithm: high-stakes decisions may require returning to earlier steps, consulting specialists, or pausing until better evidence is available.

1. FRAMEWhat exactly is the question, decision, or outcome? What is in scope, out of scope, and still unknown?
2. OBSERVEWhat do we know directly? Which parts are records, measurements, testimony, interpretation, or assumption?
3. GENERATEWhat plausible explanations, options, or interpretations have not yet been considered?
4. TESTWhat evidence would distinguish the alternatives? What observation would weaken the preferred explanation?
5. SYNTHESISEHow do the parts, broader context, mechanisms, uncertainty, and practical constraints fit together?
6. DECIDEWhich option best meets explicit criteria, and who owns the action? What are the risks and reversibility?
7. REVIEWWhat happened compared with the forecast? What should be retained, changed, or investigated next?

Metacognition: monitor the quality of your own thinking

Metacognition is the ability to monitor and regulate aspects of one's own cognition. In practical terms, it includes noticing confusion, estimating how confident a conclusion should be, recognising when attention has narrowed, choosing a different strategy, and checking whether the result matches reality. Confidence is useful information, but it is not the same as accuracy. A person can be confident and mistaken or uncertain and correct.

One practical method is a decision journal. Before making a consequential prediction or decision, record the question, current evidence, assumptions, plausible alternatives, confidence, and the outcome you expect. Later, compare the result with the prediction. This helps distinguish a good process from a lucky outcome and makes recurring blind spots easier to notice.

  1. State the claim precisely. Avoid vague predictions such as “the project will go well.” Specify an observable outcome and a time frame.
  2. Record confidence. Use words or a probability estimate, but explain what supports it. Do not invent precision when the evidence does not justify it.
  3. Write a rival explanation. Ask what else could produce the same observation.
  4. Name the evidence that would change your mind. If no imaginable evidence could change your view, consider whether the claim has become unfalsifiable or identity-protective.
  5. Review the result honestly. Identify whether the miss came from weak evidence, faulty assumptions, poor execution, luck, or an outcome that could not reasonably have been predicted.
Three-minute reflection

After completing an important task, answer: What did I assume? What did I overlook? Which part of my reasoning was strongest? What evidence changed my view? What would I do differently next time?

Common failure modes—and a practical countermeasure for each

Failure modeWhat it can look likeCountermeasure
Premature closureSelecting the first plausible answer before alternatives have been considered.Generate at least two credible alternatives and compare what evidence each predicts.
Confirmation biasSearching mainly for information that supports an existing belief.Ask someone to make the strongest case against the conclusion; search for disconfirming evidence.
Availability and vividnessTreating a memorable example as if it represents the typical case.Check base rates, denominators, and whether the example is representative.
Correlation–causation errorAssuming two things are causally linked because they appear together.Consider reverse causality, confounding factors, timing, mechanism, and alternative designs.
Overfitting one caseTurning an unusual experience into a universal rule about people or systems.Compare several cases, look for exceptions, and state the boundary conditions of the claim.
Analysis paralysisCollecting more information after the next useful decision would already be clear.Set a decision threshold, a deadline, and criteria for what additional evidence would be worth its cost.
False certainty from a modelConfusing an elegant diagram or numerical output with reality itself.Label assumptions, check sensitivity, validate against observations, and update the model.
Outcome biasJudging a decision only by whether it worked out, rather than by what was knowable at the time.Review both process and outcome, separating controllable choices from chance.

These are common reasoning risks, not diagnoses or proof that an individual is irrational. Anyone can fall into them, particularly under uncertainty, pressure, fatigue, or strong incentives.

How to train thinking instead of merely collecting information

Reading supplies concepts and evidence. Memorisation makes knowledge available when needed. Both matter—but neither guarantees that we can judge evidence, connect ideas, or apply knowledge in a new situation.

  1. Retrieve before rereading. Close the source and explain the main idea from memory, then check what you missed.
  2. Ask better questions. What is the claim? What evidence supports it? What assumptions does it need? What other explanation fits?
  3. Use contrasting cases. Compare similar cases with different outcomes, or different cases that may share a mechanism.
  4. Make a model. Draw a causal map, decision tree, or concept map to make relationships visible.
  5. Apply the idea. Use it to solve a problem, forecast an outcome, or design a small experiment.
  6. Seek disconfirming evidence. Invite a colleague to challenge your argument and revise it when warranted.
  7. Review outcomes. Compare forecasts with reality. Keep a decision log of assumptions, confidence, evidence, and lessons.
A weekly exercise: choose one real problem. Generate alternatives; break it into parts; map the system; formulate competing explanations; identify distinguishing evidence; run a small test; and record what changed. One practical cycle can exercise many approaches.

How organisations can coordinate cognitive diversity

This connects directly to Human Resource Management, team design, organisational learning, and inclusive leadership. A team does not benefit from difference merely because different people are present. The environment must let them contribute, challenge ideas, coordinate decisions, and learn from outcomes.

1. Design around the taskMap the thinking moves the challenge requires before assigning roles. Do not infer competence from seniority, identity, or simplistic labels.
2. Create safe challengeInvite questions and dissent; respond respectfully; separate criticism of an idea from judgement of a person. Psychological safety does not mean every idea is accepted.
3. Clarify decision rightsAgree who proposes, advises, decides, and implements. Give people autonomy within clear boundaries for ethics, safety, resources, and accountability.
4. Use complementary stagesOpen up the problem before converging on an option. Test the decision, monitor outcomes, and reopen it when evidence warrants.
5. Evaluate real contributionUse work samples, observable behaviours, feedback, and results. Do not use this informal framework as a hiring filter or a reason to deny opportunities.
6. Reward learningRecognise early risk detection, process improvement, assumption testing, knowledge sharing, and evidence-based revision.

Using the framework in Human Resource Management and learning design

For HRM, the framework is useful as a planning aid rather than a personality instrument. Start with the job, decision, or capability gap and define the behaviours that good performance requires. Then design learning activities that give people opportunities to practise those behaviours with feedback.

HRM or organisational taskThinking moves to practisePossible evidence of application
Learning Needs AnalysisSeparate symptoms from causes; compare evidence from performance data, work samples, observation, and staff feedback.A needs statement tied to observed capability gaps rather than assumptions about motivation.
Training designMove from abstract concepts to concrete examples, retrieval, practice, feedback, and transfer.Learners can perform a realistic task after training, not merely report that the session was enjoyable.
Performance improvementMap workflow, test alternative explanations, and identify constraints outside the individual's control.Improvements are linked to measurable outcomes and monitored for unintended effects.
Team compositionIdentify the work required—generation, quality assurance, synthesis, implementation, and review—and ensure the process covers it.Roles and review steps are explicit; contribution is assessed from work and behaviour.
Leadership developmentInvite dissent, explain decision criteria, admit uncertainty, and revise conclusions when credible evidence changes.Team members raise risks earlier, decisions have traceable reasoning, and lessons influence later work.
Knowledge managementCapture not only final answers but also evidence, assumptions, failed hypotheses, and conditions where a solution works.Colleagues can reuse the lesson without blindly copying a context-specific intervention.

Evaluation should match the desired outcome. A knowledge quiz may measure recall, but it does not by itself establish good judgement in a live situation. A scenario exercise may examine reasoning but still not prove transfer to the workplace. Where feasible, combine knowledge checks, realistic work samples, observations, follow-up measures, and contextual feedback.

A lightweight rubric for reviewing an argument

DimensionEmergingDevelopingStrong
Problem framingThe question is vague or shifts during the discussion.The scope is mostly clear, but key terms or constraints remain unresolved.The question, scope, definitions, and decision owner are explicit.
EvidenceClaims rely mainly on assertion or isolated examples.Relevant evidence is cited, but limitations or gaps are not consistently addressed.Evidence is traceable, relevant, appropriately qualified, and compared with alternatives.
ReasoningConclusions do not clearly follow from premises or observations.Most links are explained, but assumptions or rival explanations may be missed.Assumptions are visible; competing explanations and causal limits are considered.
UncertaintyConfidence is presented as certainty, or uncertainty is used to avoid deciding.Some uncertainty is acknowledged but not linked to actions or thresholds.Confidence is proportionate; unknowns, decision thresholds, and update conditions are explicit.
LearningOutcomes are not reviewed or lessons are recorded only informally.Some follow-up occurs, but the original prediction or baseline is unclear.Results are compared with the forecast; lessons inform the next cycle.

Use the rubric for coaching and development, not as a validated psychometric scale or a stand-alone basis for hiring, promotion, or disciplinary decisions. Adapt it to the task and involve relevant stakeholders.

What Google's Project Aristotle adds

Google's team-effectiveness work, widely known through Project Aristotle, examined how teams work together. Google re:Work highlights five dynamics associated with effective teams: psychological safety, dependability, structure and clarity, meaning, and impact. Psychological safety concerns whether team members feel safe taking interpersonal risks, such as asking questions, admitting mistakes, or expressing a different view.

This connects to cognitive diversity, but should not be overstated. Google's framework does not prove a team needs exactly eight cognitive styles, nor that diversity alone guarantees success. It points to conditions that help people contribute: they can speak up, depend on each other, understand expectations, and see why their work matters.

A team member who notices a hidden risk is useful only if they can raise it. A creative suggestion helps only if the team can evaluate it. A sound decision becomes an outcome only when responsibilities and follow-through are clear.

Explore Google's guide to team effectiveness ↗

From controlling people to designing conditions for contribution

Coordination is not the same as domination. Organisations need standards, legal and ethical boundaries, clear responsibilities, and decisions. But not every detail of how someone thinks or works needs to be dictated from above.

Good management clarifies the objective, non-negotiable constraints, resources, decision rights, and measures of success—then gives people appropriate room to use their judgement. When decisions affect how people work, involve them meaningfully where possible. Participation does not remove all role obligations; it makes autonomy and boundaries more transparent.

Inclusion is not making everyone think alike. It is building a system in which different ways of thinking can challenge assumptions, complement one another, and contribute to a shared outcome.

A 60-minute workshop for individuals or teams

The article can be turned into a practical session without requiring participants to memorise terminology. Choose a real but manageable problem, and keep the purpose on improving the inquiry rather than proving who is the smartest person in the room.

TimeActivityOutput
0–5 minutesFrame the problem and agree on what is known, unknown, and within scope.A shared problem statement.
5–15 minutesGenerate possible explanations or solutions independently before discussing as a group.A broad list of options, including minority views.
15–25 minutesGroup options into themes, identify assumptions, and separate observations from interpretations.A map of explanations and assumptions.
25–38 minutesChoose the strongest competing hypotheses and state what evidence each predicts.A testable evidence plan.
38–48 minutesCompare options using agreed criteria, risks, feasibility, equity, and reversibility.A reasoned provisional decision.
48–55 minutesIdentify a small next test, its owner, the timeline, the measure, and the review date.An action-and-learning plan.
55–60 minutesReflect on which thinking moves were used or absent, and whose contribution was missed.One process improvement for the next discussion.

Facilitator reminder: do not assign participants permanent labels such as “the intuitive one” or “the systems thinker.” Rotate responsibilities, make space for independent thinking before group convergence, and ask quiet participants for input without forcing disclosure. A productive discussion is not one with no disagreement; it is one where disagreement can be examined constructively and the decision process remains transparent.

Learning to think is more than reading

Reading can introduce unfamiliar ideas, provide access to research, and challenge assumptions. Memorisation makes important facts and concepts available. Both matter. But neither guarantees that we can evaluate evidence, distinguish correlation from causation, notice blind spots, or apply knowledge to a new situation.

Learning to think means practising: asking, comparing, connecting, testing, explaining, creating, deciding, and revising. The measure is not how many pages we have read or terms we can repeat. It is whether we can use knowledge responsibly and adapt when the situation changes.

Human uniqueness is not a problem for management to eliminate. It is a reality that thoughtful organisations can learn to coordinate.

Different minds. Shared purpose. Better questions. More defensible decisions.

That is the opportunity: not to rank human beings by a preferred style, but to expand what individuals and teams can notice, understand, and accomplish together.

Further reading and research foundations

The sources below support specific parts of the discussion. They do not validate this exact eight-approach framework as a complete or standardised model. The framework is a practical synthesis created for reflection and application; individual constructs should be interpreted according to the methods and limits of the cited work.

  • Google re:Work — Understand team effectiveness: an organisational guide describing psychological safety, dependability, structure and clarity, meaning, and impact. Treat it as an applied framework, not evidence that every team needs these eight cognitive lenses.
  • Runco, M. A., & Acar, S. (2012). Divergent Thinking as an Indicator of Creative Potential. Creativity Research Journal. Reviews the role and limits of divergent-thinking measures; divergent thinking can indicate aspects of creative potential but does not guarantee creative achievement.
  • Diamond, A. (2013). Executive Functions. Annual Review of Psychology. Reviews executive functions including inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility, which support goal-directed thinking and behaviour.
  • Yeung, N., & Summerfield, C. (2012). Metacognition in human decision-making: confidence and error monitoring. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B. Reviews confidence judgements and error monitoring as aspects of metacognition.
  • Carpenter, S. K., Pan, S. C., & Butler, A. C. (2022). The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice. Nature Reviews Psychology. Reviews evidence for spaced learning and retrieval practice.
  • Agarwal, P. K., Nunes, L. D., & Blunt, J. R. (2021). Retrieval Practice Consistently Benefits Student Learning: a Systematic Review of Applied Research in Schools and Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. Reviews applied classroom research on retrieval practice.
  • Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D., & Bjork, R. (2008). Learning Styles. Psychological Science in the Public Interest. Reviews the evidence for the claim that instruction should be matched to diagnosed learning-style preferences; the article cautions that the required evidence for the meshing hypothesis was lacking.
  • Edmondson, A. (1999). Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams. Administrative Science Quarterly. Reports a study of 51 work teams and examines links among psychological safety, learning behaviour, and team performance. It does not imply that all ideas should be accepted without scrutiny.
  • Baugh Littlejohns, L., Hill, C., & Neudorf, C. (2021). Diverse Approaches to Creating and Using Causal Loop Diagrams in Public Health Research. Public Health Reviews. A scoping review discussing the use and limitations of causal loop diagrams for understanding complex systems.
  • Carey, G., Malbon, E., Carey, N., Joyce, A., Crammond, B., & Carey, A. (2015). Systems science and systems thinking for public health: a systematic review of the field. BMJ Open. Reviews how systems methods have been applied in public health.
  • Gentner, D., & Smith, L. (2013). Analogical Learning and Reasoning. In The Oxford Handbook of Cognitive Psychology. Reviews how relational similarities between cases can support inference and learning.

This article is an educational framework, not a validated cognitive assessment. The eight approaches support reflection and team design, not permanent classification. Effectiveness depends on context, leadership, task design, resources, and how the team actually works together.

item.title: Thinking with Living Heritage: How Cultural Knowledge Can Strengthen Critical and Systems Thinking
item.category: Living Heritage, Critical Thinking & Systems Thinking
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: Living heritage is more than a tradition to preserve. It is a living process of observing, remembering, interpreting, testing, and adapting knowledge across generations. Discover how cultural practices can inspire contextual reasoning, systems thinking, critical inquiry, and more inclusive problem-solving—without romanticising the past.
item.content:encoded:
Living Heritage • Critical Thinking • Systems Thinking

Living heritage is not only something communities inherit and preserve. It is also a living process of observing, remembering, interpreting, testing, and adapting knowledge across generations.

When people hear the word heritage, they may picture monuments, costumes, dances, ceremonies, or objects kept in a museum. Yet much of cultural heritage lives through practice: the way knowledge is taught, a craft is learned, a story is retold, a community organises collective work, or people interpret changes in their environment.

UNESCO uses the term living heritage for intangible cultural heritage that is transmitted between generations and continually recreated in response to communities’ environments, history, and interactions with nature. Its value lies not only in a visible cultural expression, but also in the knowledge, skills, meanings, and relationships carried through it.

That perspective offers an interesting lesson for anyone who wants to think more carefully. Living heritage can help us ask: How do people learn from repeated experience? How do they recognise patterns? How does knowledge change when circumstances change? And how can different kinds of knowledge work together when a community faces a new problem?

Living heritage can be understood not merely as something to know about, but as a way to investigate how knowledge is created, shared, challenged, and adapted.

1. Think in Context, Not in Isolated Facts

A fact rarely explains an entire situation. A practice that makes sense in one place may work differently somewhere else because ecology, livelihoods, history, social relationships, and available resources differ.

For example, imagine a coastal community whose members pay close attention to seasonal winds, tides, cloud formations, or changes in marine life. These observations may have developed through repeated interaction with a particular environment. Their meaning cannot be separated from where they were observed, by whom, and under what circumstances.

A systems thinker asks how those observations connect with fishing practices, household income, local rules, weather patterns, technology, and exposure to risk. Rather than treating a traditional practice as an isolated item, the thinker investigates the relationships that make it meaningful.

Isolated-fact question“What does this community traditionally do?”
Contextual question“Under what conditions did this practice develop, what purpose does it serve, and how is it changing?”
Systems question“Which social, environmental, and economic relationships help explain why the practice works—or no longer works—as expected?”

This way of thinking is useful beyond heritage. Policies, technologies, and management methods also succeed or fail within specific contexts. A solution cannot be evaluated well if we ignore the conditions that shape its results.

2. Look for Patterns Across Time

Living heritage is transmitted through generations, but transmission is not simply the copying of an unchanged instruction. People teach, practise, remember, reinterpret, and adapt. Each generation may preserve some elements while adjusting others in response to new circumstances.

This invites a form of temporal thinking. Instead of asking only what is happening today, we can ask what has changed, what persists, what conditions accompanied earlier changes, and which explanations remain plausible.

In an illustrative coastal example, fishers’ observations might provide clues about how local conditions have varied over time. Those observations should not automatically be treated as a complete forecast. They can instead help generate questions: Have seasonal patterns shifted? Are the observations comparable across years? Have equipment, fishing locations, or reporting practices changed too?

Think critically: a remembered pattern is a valuable lead for inquiry, not automatic proof of a causal relationship. Ask what was observed, how consistently it was observed, what may have changed, and what other evidence is available.

Comparing lived experience with environmental measurements, historical records, or other forms of evidence can produce a richer account than relying on only one source. It also helps prevent us from confusing a pattern that people remember with a pattern that has been independently established.

3. Recognise That Knowledge Is Distributed

No single person necessarily holds all the knowledge needed to understand a complex issue. A craftsperson may understand materials through years of practice. An elder may remember earlier community responses to a crisis. Young people may recognise changing communication habits. Farmers, fishers, performers, healers, educators, and researchers may each contribute different observations, methods, and questions.

These forms of knowledge are not interchangeable, and none should be romanticised. The point is that complex problems often require contributions from people who see different parts of the situation.

Living heritage reminds us to ask not only, “What information do we have?” but also, “Who knows something relevant, how did they learn it, and whose experience is missing from this conversation?”

Experience-based knowledgeWhat people notice through repeated practice, direct observation, and work in a particular setting.
Documented knowledgeWhat is recorded in reports, archives, measurements, research, and formal procedures.
Relational knowledgeWhat becomes visible through trust, dialogue, shared activity, and understanding how people depend on one another.

Good analysis does not ask one form of knowledge to perform every task. It creates a process for comparing contributions, exploring disagreements, and clarifying what each source can and cannot establish.

4. Use Stories and Practices to Generate Better Questions

Stories, sayings, demonstrations, and rituals can carry accumulated interpretations of experience. They can help people remember a warning, communicate a value, or make an abstract relationship easier to discuss. A story can function as a starting model: it points our attention toward a pattern that may deserve closer examination.

But an analogy is not proof. Two situations may look similar while differing in the mechanisms that shape their outcomes. A story about cooperation, for instance, may inspire a team to coordinate better—but the team still needs to examine incentives, roles, resources, and the possibility of disagreement.

A useful thinking sequence is to begin with the cultural expression, identify the idea or relationship it appears to convey, ask where that insight may apply, and then test the comparison against the new context.

Let heritage widen the questions we ask. Let evidence help us judge which answers are defensible.

5. Learn from Practice, Not Only from Explanations

Some knowledge is difficult to communicate fully through a written instruction. Craftsmanship is a clear example: a learner may need to observe a skilled practitioner, handle materials, make mistakes, receive feedback, and repeat a process before developing reliable judgement.

This is not a reason to reject documentation or formal education. It is a reminder that knowing the description of an activity is different from knowing how to perform it under real conditions.

The same distinction appears in professional learning. Reading about stakeholder engagement is not the same as facilitating a difficult discussion. Studying risk management is not the same as responding to an unexpected event. A sound learning design combines explanation with observation, guided practice, reflection, and feedback.

A practical lesson: when a task depends on situated judgement, ask what learners need to observe, practise, discuss, and reflect on—not only what information they need to memorise.

6. Preserve the Capacity to Change

One of the most important features of living heritage is that it can be recreated as communities respond to changing circumstances. Safeguarding a practice therefore does not necessarily mean freezing it in one version or requiring every generation to reproduce it identically.

The same principle matters in thinking. A method that once worked may become less useful when the environment changes. A solution should be understood in relation to the conditions under which it was developed, rather than treated as a universal rule.

At the same time, flexibility should not become an excuse to change a practice without listening to the people who carry it. Communities should be able to participate meaningfully in decisions about how their heritage is documented, transmitted, interpreted, or adapted.

Critical thinking also means recognising that not every inherited practice is automatically fair, safe, or appropriate in every situation. Cultural knowledge deserves serious and respectful engagement, not unquestioning acceptance. Questions of human rights, mutual respect, community agency, and sustainable development matter when considering safeguarding and change.

Two mistakes to avoid: treating tradition as infallible simply because it is old, and dismissing community knowledge simply because it is not expressed in a formal scientific format. Both approaches close down inquiry before it begins.

7. A Practical Method: Think with Living Heritage

The following sequence can help turn cultural knowledge into a respectful and evidence-informed learning process. It is a practical framework, not a universal formula.

Observe the practice in context.
What happens, where does it happen, who participates, and which environmental or social conditions matter?
Listen to the knowledge holders.
Ask participants how the practice is learned, what it means to them, and what changes they have experienced. Do not assume one person speaks for an entire community.
Identify the underlying relationships.
Look for recurring patterns, dependencies, constraints, values, feedback loops, and the problems the practice helps people navigate.
Generate questions, not premature conclusions.
Use stories, observations, and experience to develop hypotheses. Make clear what is known, what is interpreted, and what remains uncertain.
Compare evidence and test the explanation.
Where appropriate, compare accounts with records, measurements, other experiences, or a small practical test. Investigate contradictions rather than hiding them.
Reflect, adapt, and share the learning.
Discuss what the inquiry suggests with the people involved. Consider who benefits, possible unintended consequences, and whether the interpretation respects community agency.

8. Worked Example: Planning a Coastal Learning Activity

Imagine a team preparing a learning activity about coastal environmental change. The team initially plans to deliver a presentation based only on a set of maps and technical slides. The information may be useful, but the team does not yet know whether the material addresses the questions residents consider most important.

A living-heritage-informed approach would not replace environmental science with tradition. It would improve the inquiry by bringing different forms of observation into conversation.

Start with local questionsInvite community members to describe the environmental changes they have noticed, which observations matter to their livelihoods, and what they want the activity to help them decide.
Map different evidenceRecord local observations alongside available maps, measurements, historical records, and expert assessments. Keep the source and uncertainty of each claim visible.
Investigate agreements and gapsAsk which findings support one another, which appear to conflict, and whether differences could be explained by location, timing, measurement, or experience.
Co-design a useful responseDevelop the learning activity with participants, then collect feedback on whether it improves understanding, supports decisions, and responds to the needs they identified.

The benefit is not simply that the activity becomes more culturally engaging. The thinking process itself improves: the team questions its assumptions, widens its evidence base, makes uncertainty visible, and checks whether the intended intervention fits the context.

9. What This Means for Foresight, Education, and Evaluation

For foresight, living heritage can prompt researchers to look beyond formal reports for signs of how people interpret change in everyday life. Stories, skills, social practices, and local observations may raise questions that conventional datasets do not capture. Those signals still need to be assessed for relevance, corroboration, uncertainty, and potential bias.

For education, living heritage can connect learning to familiar practices and relationships. Community-recognised ways of transmitting knowledge can complement formal learning, provided that participation is respectful and the content is developed with those involved.

For monitoring, evaluation, and learning, this perspective encourages us to distinguish between delivering an activity and changing how people understand or respond to a problem. A workshop may be completed successfully without participants gaining greater confidence, using the knowledge, or influencing a decision. Evaluation should therefore examine the mechanism between the activity and the intended outcome.

OutputPeople attended a learning session or a cultural knowledge-sharing activity took place.
Intermediate changeParticipants compare evidence, exchange knowledge, recognise uncertainty, or develop a shared understanding of a problem.
Outcome to investigatePeople use the learning in decisions, adapt a practice where appropriate, or gain a meaningful role in shaping a response.

These outcomes cannot be assumed. They need to be observed and assessed in context, with attention to who participates, whose knowledge is heard, and whether the resulting decisions make a real difference.

10. The Questions Worth Taking Forward

When encountering a cultural practice or a piece of inherited knowledge, try asking:

What problem, relationship, or value does this practice help people understand?
How was the knowledge developed, transmitted, and adapted over time?
Whose experience is represented—and whose perspective may be missing?
What does this knowledge help us notice, and what can it not establish on its own?
How could we test an interpretation while respecting the community and the context?
What should be preserved, what may need to adapt, and who should participate in that decision?

Conclusion: Heritage Can Teach Us How to Think, Not Just What to Remember

Living heritage connects memory with practice, knowledge with relationships, and continuity with change. Approached thoughtfully, it can encourage contextual reasoning, pattern recognition, systems thinking, practical learning, and better questions about whose knowledge informs a decision.

But learning from heritage requires more than admiration. It requires listening, careful interpretation, transparent uncertainty, evidence-informed testing, and respect for the people who sustain the practice. We should neither turn cultural knowledge into a decorative anecdote nor treat it as unquestionable truth.

For me, the deeper lesson is that thinking is not merely the act of collecting information. It is the work of connecting observations, exploring relationships, questioning assumptions, learning from others, and revising our understanding when the context changes.

Living heritage reminds us that knowledge survives not by remaining untouched, but by being meaningfully learned, practised, questioned, and carried forward.

Further Reading

  • UNESCO — What Is Intangible Cultural Heritage?: an overview of living expressions, knowledge, and skills transmitted across generations.
  • UNESCO — Frequently Asked Questions on Living Heritage: explains how living heritage evolves and is recreated in response to changing environments.
  • UNESCO — About Living Heritage and Education: discusses intergenerational transmission and the relationship between living heritage and learning.
  • UNESCO — Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage: the 2003 Convention, including the definition of intangible cultural heritage and safeguarding.

This article proposes a learning framework inspired by the concept of living heritage. The examples are illustrative; any real application should be developed with the relevant communities and supported by context-specific evidence.

item.title: Living Heritage as Propaganda: Foresight & Information Analysis
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: What if an existing cultural story could change economic behaviour—and, at a much larger scale, become a demographic or geopolitical instrument? Starting with the real history of the apple proverb, this foresight exercise explores how living heritage, narrative amplification, social norms and systemic effects can interact. The evidence stops where the What-If begins.
item.content:encoded:
What if one of the most powerful tools for changing an economy is not a subsidy, a tax, or a new law—but a story people already believe?

That is the question behind this foresight experiment.

I am interested in a specific mechanism: take an existing fact, practice, proverb, memory, or living heritage; attach it to a simple narrative; amplify the narrative through trusted cultural channels; and observe what happens when the story begins to influence behaviour at scale.

The word “propaganda” is intentionally provocative here. I am not using it to mean that every persuasive communication is evil or false. A government campaign can use persuasion to protect public health, sustain livelihoods, preserve a vulnerable cultural practice, or help a community survive an economic shock. A commercial actor can use the same psychological mechanism for profit. A state can also use it for strategic influence.

The mechanism is morally ambiguous. The direction, transparency, evidence, consent, and consequences determine whether the persuasion becomes public-interest communication, marketing, manipulation, or something more coercive.

Part I — Start With an Apple 🍎

The story begins with one of the most familiar health sayings in the English language:

“An apple a day keeps the doctor away.”

It is tempting to tell a dramatic story in which a collapsing apple industry invented the phrase and used it to manipulate the public.

That would be too neat—and historically misleading.
The saying predates modern apple-industry advertising. The earliest known printed form is a 1866 reference to a Pembrokeshire proverb: “Eat an apple on going to bed, And you’ll keep the doctor from earning his bread.” The familiar wording was recorded later, with a 1913 source noting the modern version.

In other words, the evidence supports a more interesting chain:

Existing folklore
An older cultural saying links the apple with health and avoiding the doctor.
Narrative compression
The idea becomes shorter, rhythmic, memorable and easier to repeat.
Commercial amplification
Apple producers and associations later place the story inside advertising and branding.

The distinction matters. The apple industry did not invent the proverb according to the historical evidence I can verify. But the industry absolutely did learn how useful the narrative could be.

HistoryLink's account of Washington apple farming describes increasingly aggressive advertising in the early twentieth century. A 1914 Skookum apple advertisement used the slogan “An apple a day keeps the doctor away” alongside an image of a healthy-looking child. The industry also developed related slogans such as “The Health Fruit” and “Nature's Toothbrush.” In 1928, the Washington Boxed Apple Bureau helped further the campaign. HistoryLink concludes that these campaigns helped turn Washington apples into a national product.

But the same historical source also shows why we should not simplify the story into “advertising saved a bankrupt industry.” During the Great Depression, apple prices collapsed; growers were advised not to pick some varieties, the Wenatchee Valley was declared an economically stricken area in 1935, and some orchardists survived with government loans and stimulus payments.

So the historically defensible formulation is:

The apple industry inherited an existing cultural narrative, amplified it commercially, and embedded it into a broader market-building strategy. That is not the same as inventing a false medical fact to rescue a collapsing industry.

That distinction is exactly why this is useful for information analysis.

Part II — Then Someone Tested the Story

Now the story gets even more interesting.

A 2015 JAMA Internal Medicine study examined the conventional wisdom directly. The researchers analysed 8,399 eligible US adults from NHANES data; 753 were classified as daily apple eaters, defined as consuming at least the equivalent of one small apple per day.

In the crude comparison, 39.0% of apple eaters had no more than one physician visit during the previous year, compared with 33.9% of non-apple eaters. That looks like a win for the proverb.

But after adjusting for sociodemographic and health-related characteristics, the association was no longer statistically significant: OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.93–1.53, P = .15. The authors concluded that the evidence did not support the claim that eating an apple a day keeps the doctor away.

Important nuance: this study did not show that apples are “bad”, useless, or nutritionally equivalent to every other food. It tested a much narrower proposition: whether daily apple consumption was associated with avoiding physician visits. That specific claim was not supported after adjustment.

And that creates a wonderful foresight puzzle:

How can a statement become culturally powerful without being a precise scientific proposition?

Because stories do not have to reproduce an entire evidence base.

They only have to preserve a memorable association:

APPLE → HEALTH → GOOD HABIT

Once the association is culturally stable, it can travel across generations without every person checking the original evidence.

Part III — Could It Have Been a Banana?

Now replace the object.

🍎 Apple.

🍌 Banana.

The question is not whether apples and bananas are nutritionally identical. They are not.

The question is whether a different fruit could occupy the same narrative position.

Yes.

A banana can be framed as healthy. A banana can be local. A banana can be part of a food tradition. A banana can support farmers. A banana variety can be associated with a place, a seasonal practice, a family recipe, a festival, or a transmission of agricultural knowledge.

So imagine two sentences:

“An apple is a healthy fruit.”
“Buying our local banana helps keep a living agricultural tradition alive.”

The second sentence contains much more than nutrition.

It contains identity, memory, belonging, economic solidarity and moral meaning.

That is where the living-heritage connection begins.

Part IV — From Food to Living Heritage

UNESCO treats intangible cultural heritage as something communities, groups and individuals create, maintain and transmit. Foodways can sit inside that living system: not only the food itself, but the knowledge, practices, skills, rituals, relationships and meanings surrounding it.

This matters economically. UNESCO's guidance on the economic dimensions of safeguarding intangible cultural heritage explicitly explores how economic activity can support living heritage and sustainable development, while also warning that commercialization can undermine the viability of the heritage if it is poorly managed.

That produces a much more sophisticated model than:

“Sell more products.”

Instead:

Living practice → narrative → identity → behaviour → demand → livelihood → transmission → living heritage

Now imagine a farming community facing falling prices and younger generations leaving agriculture.

A conventional campaign might say:

“Please buy local.”

A heritage-based campaign could say:

“When you buy this product, you are not only buying food. You are helping a living tradition remain economically viable for the next generation.”

The factual ingredients may remain ordinary.

The meaning changes.

Part V — My Working Concept: Heritage Narrative Engineering

I use the term Heritage Narrative Engineering here as a working foresight concept, not as an established academic label.

The idea is simple:

1. Existing fact
Something observable or evidence-supported already exists.
2. Existing heritage
A community already has practices, memories, symbols or cultural associations.
3. Narrative selection
One meaning is made especially salient.
4. Social reinforcement
Media, institutions, families, schools, celebrities or peers repeat the association.
5. Behaviour
People buy, eat, marry, participate, avoid, support or reject differently.
6. System effect
The aggregated behaviour changes markets, norms or institutional incentives.

The crucial point is that the narrative does not necessarily change the underlying fact. It changes what the fact means to people.

That is why the mechanism can be used for both benevolent and harmful purposes.

Part VI — Propaganda Is Not Automatically Evil

The word propaganda often implies deception. Historically, however, persuasive communication has also been used for public-interest goals.

Consider the UK's 5 A Day campaign. The underlying nutritional message was not “eat apples”; it was to increase fruit and vegetable consumption. A 2011 evaluation estimated that the programme increased fruit and vegetable intake by about 0.3 portions per day on average over the study period, although effects varied across income groups.

The UK campaign therefore demonstrates a useful mechanism: a simple, memorable narrative can change behaviour even when the audience is not processing the entire scientific literature behind the recommendation.

The same broad mechanism can be used in the opposite direction.

Tobacco companies historically used entertainment media to make smoking socially attractive and normal. Research based on previously secret industry documents found tobacco companies working with product-placement firms, placing tobacco products and signage in positive situations, providing free cigarettes to actors, and encouraging favourable images of actors smoking.

That is a very different ethical case from a public-health campaign.

Yet the behavioural machinery is recognisably similar:

Salience
Make the behaviour visible.
Association
Attach it to desirable people, emotions or identities.
Repetition
Make the association familiar.
Norm formation
Make the behaviour feel ordinary or expected.
The same narrative technology can be used to sell a cigarette, increase vegetable consumption, preserve a farming livelihood, or manipulate a population.

That is why I call propaganda a double-edged sword.

Part VII — Now Scale the Mechanism Up

Food is low stakes compared with demography.

But what happens when the object of narrative influence is not “what fruit should I eat?” but:

“What kind of life should I live?”

Marriage?

Children?

Career?

Migration?

Family formation?

Now narrative becomes a possible demographic variable.

This is where the following analysis deliberately shifts from documented evidence to a hypothetical scenario.

WHAT IF?What if narratives surrounding marriage, childlessness and family formation were deliberately amplified across a society because the resulting behaviour created long-term strategic value?
⚠ WHAT IF?

What if neighbouring states deliberately planted narratives to reduce birth rates in a rival society?

This is not a claim. It is a deliberately provocative foresight stress-test: the matrix separates documented evidence from interpretation and hypothetical escalation.

Narrative Influence Matrix
Click a node or a signal row to inspect the evidence boundary.
FORESIGHT SIGNALS (10)Row 2 — click any signal card to open the same evidence modal.
Documented
Evidence-supported
Interpretation
What If?
Extreme scenario
Signal detail
Open source
Want to run your own horizon scan?
Open the full Horizon Scan AI tool and build your own matrix.
Open Horizon Scan AI →

Part VIII — State A: The Demographic Cliff

I will not name the country in this article.

Readers can identify it from the data.

Total population, 2024
51.75 million
Total fertility rate, 2024
0.75
Projected population, 2072
36.22 million
Projected share aged 65+, 2072
47.7%

These are official national statistics. The same official source says the country's total fertility rate was 0.75 in 2024 and projects the population to fall from 51.75 million in 2024 to 36.22 million in 2072, while the share aged 65 and over rises from 19.2% to 47.7%.

The demographic story is also visible in marriage attitudes. Official survey reporting shows a substantial shift in how younger people view marriage and childbearing, while research on national surveys has found rising shares of never-married young adults reporting uncertain or negative intentions toward marriage. Importantly, this does not mean that people have been “brainwashed”. Economic structures, housing costs, labour-market insecurity, gender relations, work culture and changing values can all influence family formation.

The military dimension is another signal. Reuters reported that active-duty military personnel in this country fell by about 20% between 2019 and 2025, to around 450,000, amid a sharp decline in the number of enlistment-age males.

The point is not “population decline equals collapse.” It is that demographic change can propagate through multiple systems:

Fewer births → smaller youth cohorts → smaller working-age population → ageing → fiscal pressure → labour constraints → military manpower pressure → changing strategic options.

Part IX — State B: The Same Demographic Problem, A Different Narrative

Now consider a neighbouring state with a very different political system and a much larger emphasis on collective mobilisation.

Again, I will not name it.

In 2023, its leader publicly called for measures to prevent the birth rate from falling during a national meeting of mothers—the first such national mothers' meeting in 11 years. External reporting cited UNFPA data placing its total fertility rate around 1.8 in 2023.

Whether the policy is effective is a separate question.

The important foresight observation is that the state is openly treating birth rates as a national concern and using public narrative to reinforce the social role of mothers and childrearing.

That is already enough to demonstrate the mechanism exists in the world.

It is not evidence that this state is secretly exporting those messages to its neighbour.

Important evidence boundary: I have found evidence of domestic pro-natalist messaging and policy in this state. I have not found credible evidence establishing a coordinated programme to export anti-marriage or childfree narratives into another country in order to engineer demographic collapse.

Part X — State C: The Demographic Superpower Is Also Aging

A third regional power complicates the picture.

Its population at the end of 2025 was about 1.40489 billion. Births fell to 7.92 million, deaths were 11.31 million, and the natural population growth rate was -2.41 per thousand. People aged 60 and over accounted for 23.0% of the population.

The government is simultaneously trying to create a more “birth-friendly society” through childcare, parental leave, cost reduction and policies intended to address declining births and marriage. Reporting has also described campaigns encouraging single people to date, marry and have children.

Again, this is a real demographic policy response—not proof of an external influence operation.

And that is exactly what makes the scenario interesting.

Part XI — The What-If: What If the Narrative Crossed the Border?

Now we enter my subjective foresight scenario.

WHAT IF?What if an external actor deliberately amplified narratives already attractive to people inside State A—messages that framed marriage as unnecessary, parenthood as a burden, or childlessness as a superior lifestyle—because the long-term demographic effects would reduce the target state's economic and strategic capacity?

I am not claiming this is happening.

I am asking whether the system dynamics are plausible enough that a serious foresight team should at least know how to recognise the pathway.

The pathway would look something like this:

Narrative penetration
↓
Norm shift
↓
Behavioural change
↓
Lower marriage / fertility
↓
Smaller cohorts
↓
Ageing + labour contraction
↓
Fiscal / military pressure
↓
Strategic vulnerability

The final step—territorial seizure or economic capture—is not a forecast. It is one extreme branch in a scenario tree. Real outcomes would depend on many other variables: alliances, productivity, migration, automation, military technology, political cohesion, international law, economic resilience and the target state's ability to adapt.

Part XII — The Provocative Question

What makes the scenario uncomfortable is that the “weapon” would not need to invent a new belief.

It could simply amplify a belief already emerging organically.

That is much more difficult to detect.

A fabricated story can sometimes be debunked.

A genuine social trend cannot be “debunked” just because someone fears its consequences.

A society may genuinely decide:

  • Marriage is optional.
  • Children are optional.
  • Career should come first.
  • Individual autonomy should dominate family obligation.

Those can be legitimate choices.

The foresight question is different:

What happens if an external actor learns how to systematically accelerate a trend that the target population is already generating by itself?

That is a much more sophisticated information-security problem than traditional propaganda posters.

Part XIII — How I Would Analyse It in Horizon Scanning

This is where the interactive Horizon Scanning tool becomes useful.

Instead of asking the reader to accept my conclusion, the matrix lets them inspect the signals and move them themselves.

LayerQuestionExample
ObservedWhat is actually happening?Fertility rate, population projection, policy announcement.
Evidence-supportedWhat relationship has research documented?Demographic ageing affects labour supply and fiscal pressure.
InterpretationWhat pattern might these signals suggest?Demography may become a strategic constraint.
What If?What hypothetical intervention could alter the trajectory?External narrative amplification.
Extreme scenarioWhat is the far-end consequence?Severe economic or strategic vulnerability.

This separation is deliberate.

Good foresight does not hide the jump from data to imagination.

It labels the jump.

Part XIV — Why This Analysis Is Subjective

This article is a foresight exercise, not a prediction.

Two analysts can use the same demographic data and produce different scenarios because they can assign different weights to:

Economic adaptation
Automation, productivity, migration and delayed retirement may offset population decline.
Social adaptation
Marriage and family norms may change without creating systemic collapse.
Political adaptation
Governments may redesign welfare, housing and labour policies.
Strategic adaptation
Military technology may reduce dependence on raw manpower.
Narrative effects
Social attitudes may shift faster—or much slower—than demographic models assume.
External influence
Foreign actors may matter, or the observed changes may be overwhelmingly domestic.

That is why I would rather say:

“Here is one plausible pathway I can construct from the available signals.”

Not:

“This is what will happen.”

Part XV — Confirmation Bias Is Part of the Experiment

There is another uncomfortable admission.

This article intentionally foregrounds signals that are relevant to the scenario.

That is useful for a What-If exercise, but dangerous if the reader mistakes it for a complete evidence review.

Selective evidence can produce a persuasive story even when the overall evidence is mixed.

In other words:

A good narrative can be analytically useful and still be biased.

The answer is not to eliminate subjectivity. That is impossible.

The answer is to make the assumptions visible.

Part XVI — The Living Heritage Paradox

Now return to the apple.

A local agricultural tradition can be used to protect farmers.

A food story can encourage healthier consumption.

A cultural narrative can help a community preserve knowledge between generations.

These can be positive uses of persuasion.

But once we discover how powerful narrative framing can be, we must ask:

Who controls the story?

Who chooses which part of the heritage becomes visible?

Who benefits economically?

Who is excluded?

Who is allowed to correct the narrative?

And what happens if the story is more successful than the evidence behind it?

That is the central governance problem of turning living heritage into an economic or political instrument.

Part XVII — My Position

I do not think persuasion itself should automatically be treated as immoral.

If a farming community is genuinely at risk of disappearing, a public campaign that helps consumers understand the heritage value of local production may be worthwhile.

If a population needs to eat more vegetables, a memorable campaign may be more effective than a 60-page nutrition report.

If smoking is socially normalised through entertainment, governments may reasonably use equally powerful communication techniques to denormalise it.

But the line becomes dangerous when:

Evidence is deliberately distorted.
Important uncertainty is hidden.
People are treated as targets instead of participants.
Manipulation becomes coercion.
A cultural community loses control over its own heritage.
A narrative is exported to weaken another population.

Part XVIII — Propaganda Is a Double-Edged Sword

PROPAGANDA IS A DOUBLE-EDGED SWORD.

The same mechanism that can protect a farmer can manipulate a consumer. The same storytelling technique that can strengthen public health can also normalise harmful behaviour. The same narrative power that can preserve a living heritage can also be turned into an instrument of strategic influence.

It can be used for people.

It can be used against people.

It can protect.

It can distort.

It can strengthen a community.

It can quietly weaken one.

That is why I would not recommend reaching for this kind of influence casually.

Use persuasive narrative when there is a legitimate reason, keep the factual foundation honest, involve the communities affected, and understand the possibility of unintended consequences.

And as citizens, analysts, practitioners and policymakers, we should learn to recognise the mechanism before the mechanism begins making decisions for us.

The dangerous question is not only “Is this story true?”
It is also: “What behaviour does this story make easier—and who benefits if that behaviour spreads?”

Foresight Disclaimer

This is an exploratory foresight and information-analysis exercise. It is not a prediction, accusation, or claim of coordinated action by any specific government, state, community or population. State labels are intentionally anonymised in the scenario, while the underlying statistics are drawn from real public sources. The article deliberately separates documented evidence from analytical interpretation and hypothetical “What If?” scenarios. Different analysts may reach different conclusions from the same data because assumptions, weighting, framing and selected signals differ. The scenario should therefore be read as a stress-test of one possible pathway—not as a statement of what is happening.

Closing question

What if the next strategic resource is not oil, data or chips—but the stories a society repeats about itself?

Key References & Reading

Phrase origin — Pembrokeshire proverb and later wording
https://www.phrases.org.uk/meanings/an-apple-a-day.html
JAMA Internal Medicine — Apple consumption and physician visits
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/2210883
HistoryLink — Apple farming in Washington
https://www.historylink.org/File/21288
UNESCO — 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of Intangible Cultural Heritage
https://ich.unesco.org/en/convention
UNESCO — Guidance Notes: Economic dimensions of intangible cultural heritage safeguarding
https://ich.unesco.org/en/guidance-notes-01383
UK 5 A Day evaluation — Journal of Health Economics
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167629610001372
Tobacco industry and Hollywood — Tobacco Control / PMC
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1766059/
State A demographic indicators — national statistics
https://kostat.go.kr/boardDownload.es?bid=11760&list_no=436776&seq=1
State A population projections — 2022–2072
https://www.kostat.go.kr/boardDownload.es?bid=11748&list_no=439555&seq=5
State A military manpower — Reuters
https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/south-koreas-military-has-shrunk-by-20-six-years-male-population-drops-2025-08-10/
State B birth-rate messaging — Yonhap
https://en.yna.co.kr/view/AEN20231204002000315
State C population statistics — National Bureau of Statistics
https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202601/t20260119_1962328.html
State C birth-friendly policy — Reuters
https://www.reuters.com/world/china/china-improve-childbirth-policies-boost-support-elderly-2024-03-05/
