State C marriage and childbirth campaign — Financial Times
https://www.ft.com/content/5fdf42e1-2975-4c99-9031-a9f73c2251be
State A marriage statistics — national statistics
https://kostat.go.kr/boardDownload.es?bid=11774&list_no=436185&seq=1
State C population decline in 2025 — official statistics
https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202602/t20260228_1962661.html

Sources are provided for verification and further reading. Historical claims are separated from the author's scenario interpretation.

item.title: Living Heritage: When Foresight Is Right — but Still Wrong
item.category: Living Heritage, Strategic Foresight & Context Blindness
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: A foresight model can have good data, a real signal and a plausible causal mechanism, yet still miss the outcome because context changes the pathway. This article explores Context Blindness through career decisions, El Niño, critical technology dependencies, living heritage, hidden variables, structured dissent and resilience.
item.content:encoded:
One of the most dangerous mistakes in foresight is not being completely wrong. It is being almost right — because the model correctly sees the signal, but misses a contextual variable that changes how the signal becomes an outcome.

I use Context Blindness here as a working label for that failure mode: a situation where analysis captures the visible relationship between variables but does not sufficiently represent the surrounding conditions that make the relationship hold.

The core idea

A correct signal does not guarantee a correct outcome when the context is part of the causal system.

1. The easiest example: “Angga wants to become a Director.”

Imagine a foresight exercise about my career.

The researcher has good information:

  • I have a clear aspiration to become a Director.
  • The aspiration is stable.
  • I have repeatedly expressed it.
  • Leadership responsibility is part of the desired trajectory.

The data is correct.

Then someone builds this inference:

The mistake is subtle.

The forecast did not misunderstand my aspiration.

It misunderstood the relationship between aspiration and choice.

Wanting a position does not mean accepting every version of that position under every condition.

A better formulation is:

Acceptance = f(position, compensation, responsibility, authority, risk, institutional protection, resources, timing, alternatives)

So:

Director role A
Salary + authority + resources + institutional protection + clear mandate.
Potentially consistent with the aspiration.
Director role B
Title + high responsibility + weak resources + personal exposure + unclear authority.
The same title can generate a completely different decision.

Same signal. Different context. Different outcome.

2. Context blindness is not the same as “bad data”

This distinction matters a lot.

There are at least three different ways a forecast can fail:

Bad data
The underlying observation is inaccurate, incomplete or outdated.
Bad inference
The data is reasonable, but the causal interpretation is weak.
Context blindness
The inference is plausible, but relevant conditions or interacting variables were omitted.

The third category is particularly dangerous because it can survive a lot of conventional quality checks.

The spreadsheet may be clean.

The regression may be sound.

The trend may be genuine.

The interview data may be real.

The methodology may be documented.

And yet the world can still surprise you.

Sometimes the model is not wrong about what it sees. It is incomplete about what surrounds what it sees.

3. Climate gives us a beautiful example: El Niño ≠ deterministic weather

A common simplification is:

El Niño → Indonesia becomes dry → drought.

There is a real basis for the association. NOAA describes El Niño as being typically associated with suppressed rainfall and drier-than-normal conditions over Indonesia. But NOAA also explicitly notes that teleconnections are likely, not certain. ENSO operates through coupled ocean-atmosphere dynamics and large-scale atmospheric teleconnections, while actual weather remains the result of interacting processes at multiple scales.

So when somebody says:

“El Niño was predicted. Why did it rain?”

the better answer is not automatically “the forecast failed.”

The more rigorous question is:

Which level of the causal chain was being forecast — the climate tendency, the seasonal anomaly, or the local weather event?

That distinction is critical.

A seasonal tendency can be correctly forecast while a particular afternoon storm still happens.

The signal was not necessarily false.

The mistake may have been expecting a population-level tendency to dictate every individual observation.

4. The same idea becomes extreme in technology: a critical dependency can disappear

Now consider a technological thought experiment.

Suppose a severe disruption damages or interrupts the infrastructure required for advanced semiconductor manufacturing for a prolonged period.

The question is not simply:

“Do humans still know what a computer is?”

Of course they do.

The deeper question is:

“Can the industrial system still reproduce the components required to build the computer?”

Advanced lithography illustrates why this matters. ASML describes EUV as part of a complex ecosystem involving lithography systems, sources, manufacturing, supply-chain capabilities, customer support and precision technology. ASML itself describes securing unique supply-chain capabilities as important to business continuity.

And that is where living heritage suddenly becomes relevant to technological foresight.

5. Why “living heritage” belongs in this conversation

UNESCO's 2003 Convention defines intangible cultural heritage as practices, representations, expressions, knowledge and skills recognized by communities and transmitted across generations, while also being constantly recreated in response to environment, history and interaction with nature. UNESCO's living-heritage guidance also emphasises that communities themselves are central to creating, maintaining and transmitting it.

That wording matters:

Living heritage is not simply a frozen archive of obsolete things.

It is knowledge that remains meaningful because people continue to practise, transmit and recreate it.

That creates a fascinating foresight question:

What capabilities exist today that modern systems have hidden from us because we rarely need them?
Food systems
Drying, salting, smoking, fermentation and other preservation practices can become more relevant under refrigeration or logistics disruption.
Craft & repair
Local knowledge of materials, tools and maintenance may matter when industrial replacement chains become slower or unavailable.
Navigation & landscape knowledge
Place-based knowledge can provide redundancy when digital positioning or communications are unreliable.
Ecological practices
Knowledge of seasons, water, crops and local environments may provide adaptation options under changing conditions.

These are not necessarily better than modern systems.

They are different pathways.

And from a resilience perspective, alternative pathways can matter.

This is an inference from the nature of living heritage and systems resilience — not a claim that UNESCO classifies heritage elements as technological “backup systems”.

6. The surprising lesson: the future may sometimes need the past

That sentence is the bridge between living heritage and foresight.

We tend to imagine technological progress as a one-way staircase:

old → newer → newer → newer → future

But resilient systems look more like a network:

preferred pathway ↔ alternative pathway ↔ fallback pathway ↔ local pathway

The purpose of foresight is therefore not only to ask what replaces the old.

It should also ask:

What old capability might become useful again under a different future?

7. Context blindness can also happen with people

This is where the issue becomes uncomfortable.

Smart people can be especially good at building elegant explanations.

They see patterns quickly.

They connect evidence.

They create a coherent story.

And coherence feels like truth.

But a coherent explanation can still be incomplete.

For example:

Observed
“She keeps communicating with an ex.”
Inference
“She cannot move on.”
Possible hidden context
The person may share work, family, property, community or another unavoidable social context with the ex.

The inference could be true.

But the same observable behaviour can arise from different mechanisms.

This is why behavioural foresight needs more than pattern recognition.

The same behaviour does not always imply the same underlying state.

Context changes meaning.

8. Double standards can create context blindness too

There is another version that appears in everyday life:

Someone observes a behaviour in another person and immediately interprets it negatively.

Later, the same person behaves similarly themselves — but now they provide a different explanation.

This is not only hypocrisy.

From a modelling perspective, it can be a failure to apply the same contextual variables to both cases.

Case A:

“They did X, therefore they must mean Y.”

Case B:

“I did X, but my situation was different.”

Exactly.

The situation was different.

That is precisely why context belongs in the model.

9. The hidden-variable checklist I would add to foresight

Whenever a forecast looks suspiciously clean, I would stop before declaring victory.

Incentives
What reward, cost or risk changes behaviour?
Constraints
What resources, laws or infrastructure limit the pathway?
Interactions
What other trend or shock is moving simultaneously?
Institutions
Who has authority, veto power, protection or accountability?
Timing
Does the relationship change by season, lifecycle or sequence?
Alternatives
Can the same outcome be produced by a different mechanism?

10. A more realistic causal model

Instead of:

Signal → Outcome

try:

Signal → Mechanism → Conditions → Interactions → Actor response → Outcome

And then add:

What breaks the pathway?

11. This is why a forecast can be “correct” and still be useful to critique

Suppose a forecast predicts:

“Group X will probably behave in way Y.”

Then the real world produces something slightly different.

We should not immediately say:

> “The forecast was useless.”

Nor should we say:

> “The forecast was correct, reality was wrong.”

The better question is:

Which assumption connected the forecast to the actual outcome, and which condition changed?

This is a much more productive learning loop.

It turns forecast error into a discovery of hidden variables.

And sometimes the most valuable outcome of a failed forecast is not a better number.

It is a better model of the system.

12. Red teams, premortems and structured dissent already point in this direction

This idea is not asking foresight practitioners to invent criticism from scratch.

Recent OECD guidance for public administration recommends pre-mortems, calibrated forecasts, reference-class forecasting and Red Teams. The OECD describes Red Teams as adversarial collaborators that challenge assumptions, evidence and decision quality. It also describes a “Key Assumptions Check” and “Analysis of Competing Hypotheses” as examples of structured dissent.

There is an important insight here:

The purpose of dissent is not to prove the critic right. It is to expose assumptions that otherwise remain invisible.

That is exactly what a context-blind forecast needs.

13. The “annoying person” may therefore be a useful sensor

Almost every organization has one.

The person who says:

“Wait. What about…?”

Again.

And again.

Sometimes that person is simply difficult.

But sometimes they are detecting variables that the dominant model is not measuring.

The answer should not be:

> “They are always right.”

That would simply create another blind spot.

The answer is:

Convert the objection into a test.

“What assumption are you challenging?”

“What evidence would prove you wrong?”

“What evidence would prove the existing model wrong?”

“What variable are we not measuring?”

“Can we run the scenario?”

“Does the edge case scale?”

Now disagreement becomes an analytical instrument.

14. Living heritage gives us the same lesson from a different direction

UNESCO's framework places communities at the centre of identifying, maintaining, transmitting and managing living heritage. The Convention calls for the widest possible participation of communities, groups and individuals who create, maintain and transmit intangible cultural heritage.

That principle has an interesting parallel for policy and foresight:

If people live inside the system, they possess information about the system that an external model may not contain.

This does not mean every local belief is automatically evidence.

It does not mean every community practice is automatically efficient.

It does not mean experts become irrelevant.

It means that experience inside a system is a potentially important source of variables.

The person who maintains the boat knows the leak.

The farmer knows which “standard” schedule does not work after the first unusual rain.

The craftsperson knows which material substitution changes the whole behaviour of an object.

The frontline worker knows where the workflow breaks.

The community knows which policy assumption does not match lived reality.

That is not an argument against data.

It is an argument for more complete data about context.

15. The foresight loop I would use

16. A practical rule: forecast the conditions, not only the outcome

This is probably the biggest lesson I take from the whole problem.

When I hear:

“X will cause Y.”

I increasingly want to ask:

  • Under what conditions?
  • For whom?
  • At what scale?
  • At what time horizon?
  • Through which mechanism?
  • What other variables interact with it?
  • What would make the relationship fail?
  • What alternative pathway could produce the same outcome?

That is especially important for foresight because the future is not merely a continuation of a dataset.

It is a changing system of actors, incentives, technologies, institutions, environments and feedback loops.

17. The deeper connection with Living Heritage

And this brings us back to the title.

Why start a conversation about context blindness in foresight with living heritage?

Because living heritage reminds us of something modern systems frequently forget:

Knowledge does not only exist inside databases.

It also exists inside:

  • people who practise something;
  • communities that transmit something;
  • places where knowledge is embodied;
  • routines developed through repeated adaptation;
  • skills that become visible only when the normal system stops working.

UNESCO's own description of living heritage emphasises that it is dynamic and continually recreated as communities respond to their environment and history. That makes it conceptually interesting for foresight: the heritage is not only a record of what people once did; it is a record of capabilities that can continue to adapt.

That does not mean every heritage practice should be turned into a “resilience technology”. That would instrumentalise culture and ignore its meaning to communities.

The more careful argument is:

Living heritage can contain adaptive knowledge and alternative practices that foresight may overlook when it models only the dominant technological or institutional pathway.

18. The conclusion I keep coming back to

Good foresight is not merely:

“I predicted the trend.”

It is also:

“I understand the conditions under which this trend becomes consequential.”

And great foresight goes one step further:

“I know what could invalidate my own model.”

Because the future rarely announces:

> “Your data was wrong.”

It often says something much more subtle:

> “Your data was right. You just forgot something else was moving.”

Maybe that “something else” is an incentive.

Maybe it is an institution.

Maybe it is weather.

Maybe it is infrastructure.

Maybe it is another actor.

Maybe it is a hidden dependency.

Maybe it is a cultural practice that your model treated as background noise.

Or maybe it is the one person in the room who keeps saying:

“Wait… what if?”

That person is not automatically right.

But the question may be exactly what your foresight system was missing.

My working principle

Don't only ask what will happen. Ask what has to remain true for your prediction to happen — and what knowledge survives when those conditions disappear.

Try the idea yourself
Use the Horizon Scanning AI tool to stress-test a signal, assumption, hidden variable and possible disruption.
↗ Open Horizon Scanning AI

References & further reading

UNESCO — 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage.
https://ich.unesco.org/en/convention
Defines intangible cultural heritage as community-recognized knowledge, practices, expressions and skills that are transmitted and continually recreated; Article 15 calls for the widest possible participation of communities, groups and individuals in safeguarding and management.

UNESCO — About Living Heritage and Education.
https://ich.unesco.org/en/about-01159
Emphasises that living heritage is community-based and that communities are central to its creation, maintenance and transmission.

UNESCO — Living Heritage and Indigenous Peoples.
https://ich.unesco.org/en/indigenous-peoples
Discusses knowledge, practices and skills as living heritage and notes the importance of transmission and community vitality.

OECD — Applying Behavioural Science in the Italian Public Administration (2026).
OECD report
Discusses pre-mortems, calibrated forecasts, reference-class forecasting and Red Teams; the report describes structured dissent and Key Assumptions Checks for challenging policy reasoning.

NOAA — Understanding El Niño & ENSO.
https://www.noaa.gov/understanding-el-nino
Describes typical El Niño rainfall patterns and explicitly notes that teleconnections are likely, not certain.

NOAA Climate Prediction Center — El Niño / La Niña FAQ.
https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/ensostuff/ensofaq.shtml
Explains coupled ocean-atmosphere processes and the typical suppression of rainfall over Indonesia during El Niño.

ASML — EUV lithography and supply-chain capability.
ASML EUV programme · ASML strategy & supply chain
Used here to illustrate the broader point that advanced lithography depends on a complex technological and supply-chain ecosystem. The disruption scenario in this article is a thought experiment, not a prediction of an EMP event.

Horizon Scanning AI Tool.
https://horizon-scanning.org/tool.html

Terminology note: “Context Blindness” is used in this article as a working analytical label developed by the author, not as a claim that it is a standardized academic term.

item.title: I Thought Inclusion Was Only About Disability. I Was Wrong.
item.category: Living Heritage, Inclusion, Foresight & Disaster Risk Reduction
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: Inclusion is not only about access. It is also about correctly understanding who is standing in front of us. When misclassification erodes peace of mind, small incidents can become grievances; foresight can model the escalation pathway, while human-centred DRR seeks to interrupt it before friction becomes a larger crisis.
item.content:encoded:
I used to think inclusion was mainly about disability. Making spaces accessible. Making participation possible. Removing barriers that prevent persons with disabilities from taking part.

That is still a critical part of inclusion.

But after working across international settings, observing how people are treated differently because of appearance, assumptions, communication style, culture, behaviour, or simply because somebody did not understand who they were, I started to see a much wider problem.

Inclusion is also about correctly understanding who is standing in front of you.

Because sometimes the most dangerous exclusion does not begin with an explicit decision to exclude someone.

It begins with a misclassification.

We see something.

We interpret it.

We classify the person.

Then we treat them according to the classification.

If the classification is wrong, everything that follows can be wrong too.

Part I — I Thought Inclusion Was Only About Disability

My first mental model of inclusion was relatively simple:

Accessibility
Can the person enter?
Participation
Can the person contribute?
Accommodation
Can the system adapt?

These questions matter enormously.

But they are not enough.

We also need to ask:

Do I understand the person accurately enough to decide how I should respond to them?

That changes the problem from physical access alone to interpretive access.

Can I understand their context?

Can I distinguish appearance from identity?

Can I distinguish behaviour from intention?

Can I distinguish difference from danger?

Can I distinguish an unusual thinking style from inability?

Can I distinguish a genuine risk from a false positive?

And can I correct my interpretation when the person tells me that I am wrong?

Part II — A Very Small Experience in China

I once travelled to China for an international meeting.

There were rules.

There was migration control.

There were procedures.

And of course, rules matter.

But at one point, I urgently needed to use the toilet. 😅

The interesting part was not that the rules disappeared.

They did not.

What I remember is that the official apparently recognised a very simple fact:

There is a human being standing in front of me, and this person has an immediate human need.

The procedure was still there. But the response became humane: I was assisted and directed quickly rather than treated as if the procedure itself was more important than the person.

It was a tiny moment.

But it stayed with me.

Because it demonstrated something that I think policy designers sometimes forget:

Rules exist to organise human activity. Humans do not exist to satisfy the emotional comfort of a rule.

This is not an argument for ignoring security, immigration controls, or procedures. It is an argument for context-sensitive implementation.

Inclusion can sometimes look like a very small operational adjustment that preserves both the rule and the dignity of the person.

Part III — When Appearance Becomes a Shortcut

Another international meeting gave me a very different lesson.

During a meeting in Korea, I observed a situation in which a participant from Indonesia who happened to have a beard was subjected to questioning and additional scrutiny that felt connected to assumptions about his appearance.

Another participant from Timor-Leste with a beard also experienced pressure. The irony was obvious: appearance had become a shortcut for identity, even though appearance could not reliably tell us a person's religion, intention, nationality, or threat level.

At one point I joked with the Timor-Leste participant that he already looked “Muslim enough” and might as well try converting. 😅

The joke was silly.

The underlying lesson was not.

A visible characteristic can be real without the meaning we attach to it being real.

A beard is a beard.

It is not automatically a religion.

A religion is not automatically an ideology.

An ideology is not automatically a threat.

And a threat assessment should not be replaced by a visual shortcut.

This is where inclusion and foresight meet.

A good risk system should reduce dangerous false negatives.

But a system that generates too many false positives can also create harm: humiliation, delays, mistrust, reputational damage, resentment, and unnecessary friction.

Part IV — The Other Side of Misclassification

I have also seen examples, through public videos and stories, where a person was treated as suspicious because of skin colour or perceived origin, and cases where somebody who behaved or thought differently was treated as though they had a disability when the actual issue was simply difference.

I do not want to turn individual incidents from videos or anecdotes into a universal claim about an entire country, institution, or population. The important point is the mechanism:

When the observer's category becomes more important than the actual person, misclassification can become treatment.

And treatment can become experience.

Experience can become memory.

Memory can become grievance.

Grievance can affect trust.

And damaged trust can influence what people do next.

This does not mean every misunderstanding becomes violence, let alone war.

That would be an unjustified leap.

The foresight lesson is more modest and more useful:

Misunderstanding can be an upstream risk factor in an escalation pathway.

Part V — Inclusion as a Defence of Peace of Mind

This is where I started thinking about a phrase I call:

Working concept

Inclusion as a Defence of Peace of Mind

Usually, inclusion is framed around rights, equality, participation, accessibility, or dignity.

All of those are important.

But there is another systems-level interpretation:

Inclusion reduces the probability that we will make expensive mistakes about people.

If I understand the person correctly, I am more likely to:

choose an appropriate response
avoid unnecessary escalation
preserve trust
detect the real problem
use the right intervention
learn from the person affected

That is not simply kindness.

It is risk intelligence.

Part VI — Then I Remembered My Own Story

And yes, I have been on the receiving end of misclassification too. 😂

I like women.

I enjoy getting to know someone.

My preferred trajectory is fairly direct: if we are compatible, I would rather move toward marriage than spend years in an undefined relationship.

But imagine someone sees “man who approaches a woman” and jumps directly to:

“Predator.”

Without understanding the actual context.

Now imagine that assumption affects what happens next.

I was told to stay away for years because of that interpretation.

And eventually the interpretation turned out not to match reality.

The response later became something like:

“We misunderstood you. Sorry. You can continue getting to know her now.”

My response was basically:

“Now?” 😅

Because time is a hidden variable.

Three years do not disappear because somebody says sorry.

People change.

Situations change.

Trust changes.

Other options appear.

The opportunity that existed three years earlier may simply no longer exist.

That is another foresight lesson:

A correction can be accurate and still arrive too late to restore the original outcome.

Part VII — The Joker and Harley Quinn Thought Experiment

Now for the deliberately ridiculous thought experiment. 😄

Imagine two people are repeatedly misclassified.

One is treated as a threat when they are not.

The other is treated as something they are not.

Both lose trust.

Both become angry.

Both start interpreting the world through grievance.

Then they begin making decisions based on that grievance.

This is where my joke about “becoming Joker and Harley Quinn” comes from.

Obviously, real conflicts are far more complicated than a comic-book origin story.

But the metaphor exposes a useful foresight question:

What if today's small misclassification becomes tomorrow's grievance?

And what if repeated grievances accumulate?

Not every grievance becomes violence.

Not every misunderstanding becomes conflict.

But resilient systems should still ask:

What pathway could turn misunderstanding into escalation, and where can we interrupt it early?

Part VIII-A — When Peace of Mind Breaks, Risk Can Escalate

There is one part of this argument that I want to make much more explicit.

When people are repeatedly misunderstood, incorrectly classified, humiliated, or treated as a threat, the damage is not only practical.

It can affect something much less visible:

Working concept

Inclusion can function as a defence of peace of mind.

By “peace of mind”, I mean a person's basic sense that they can move through a system without constantly expecting to be misread, humiliated, targeted, or forced to defend an identity they do not actually hold.

When that sense is repeatedly damaged, a small incident can stop being “just a small incident”.

A misclassification can become a memory.

A memory can become a grievance.

A grievance can become a story about “what they always do to people like us”.

That story can spread through a group.

The group can begin interpreting later events through the same grievance.

Then the other side can respond to that reaction.

This is where feedback loops become more important than any single incident.

Misunderstanding does not have to directly cause violence to become a risk. It can create the conditions in which mistrust, grievance and reciprocal escalation become easier.

Research and operational guidance on conflict prevention similarly emphasise that exclusion, grievances, declining trust and weakened social cohesion can contribute to fragility and violent conflict, while inclusive, participatory and responsive institutions are part of prevention. That does not mean every exclusion or misunderstanding leads to violence. It means that these conditions belong in the risk assessment rather than being treated as irrelevant “soft issues”.

At the extreme end of this pathway, if grievances become group-based, mutually reinforced, politically organised, and institutional channels for correction or peaceful dispute resolution fail, a society can move toward serious communal violence or civil conflict. Civil war is an extreme scenario, not a deterministic endpoint of misunderstanding. The foresight value is precisely to identify the earlier stages where intervention is still possible: clarification, participation, dialogue, trusted institutions, mediation, and grievance resolution.

This is why I increasingly see DRR not only as “what do we do after the hazard appears?” but also as:

“Which relationships, assumptions and feedback loops should we strengthen now so that a future shock does not turn into a larger crisis?”

The mindset is preventive:

Before the incident
Understand people and contexts.
At the first misunderstanding
Clarify before categorising.
When grievance appears
Give it a legitimate channel.
Before escalation
Use dialogue, mediation and early warning.
During a shock
Protect trust while managing the hazard.
Afterward
Learn what the system misread.

In that sense, peace of mind is not merely a private feeling. At scale, it can become part of the social conditions that support trust, cooperation and resilience.

Part VIII — This Is Where Disaster Risk Reduction Gets Interesting

When I first learned to think about DRR, it was easy to picture physical hazards:

earthquakes, floods, tsunamis, droughts, storms, fires.

But disaster risk is not only the hazard.

UNDRR describes risk in terms that include hazards, exposure, vulnerability and the decisions that shape how societies organise and protect people and assets. UNDRR also emphasises people-centred approaches, participation, inclusion and accountability in risk assessment and disaster management.

That means human relationships and social conditions matter to risk.

And this creates a fascinating possibility:

Some risks can be reduced before they become “disasters” simply by improving how we understand the people inside the system.

For example:

Migration
Misread identity → unnecessary friction.
Security
Visual shortcut → false positive.
Workplace
Different thinking → mistaken as incapability.
Public services
Unusual behaviour → incorrect intervention.
Community conflict
Misunderstanding → grievance and distrust.
Disaster response
Generic assumptions → people unable to act on warnings.

UNDRR's people-centred early-warning guidance makes a similar operational point: warnings and protective actions need to be designed with the individuals and communities who will use them, taking into account the complexity of different groups' circumstances.

Part IX — Tepa Selira: The Living Heritage Connection

This is where I return to Living Heritage.

One contemporary 2026 systematic literature review describes tepa selira as the ability to place oneself in another person's position, respect differences, and maintain harmonious social relations. It identifies cognitive, affective and behavioural dimensions of empathy, and discusses its relevance to inclusive, culturally respectful relationships.

Another 2024 study explores tepa selira as an empathy-oriented cultural value for preventing bullying, emphasising respect, care for others, and attention to one's words and behaviour.

I am interested in taking the principle one step further.

Not simply:

“Be empathetic.”

But:

“Before I act on my interpretation of another person, I should test whether my interpretation is actually valid.”

That turns a cultural value into a foresight question.

Part X — Living Heritage Is Not Only About Preserving the Past

UNESCO's 2003 Convention places communities, groups and individuals who create, maintain and transmit intangible cultural heritage at the centre of safeguarding, including their active participation in management under Article 15. ...

That matters here because inclusion is not only something we do to communities.

It is also about recognising communities as holders of knowledge about their own realities.

This has a direct parallel with DRR.

UNDRR's work on traditional and Indigenous knowledge explicitly argues for bringing traditional knowledge into disaster risk reduction and for allowing traditional and scientific knowledge to coexist and inform decision-making.

And UNDRR has documented cases where community-based DRR struggled precisely because local knowledge and participation were not meaningfully incorporated.

So the connection is bigger than culture.

It is epistemological:

Who gets to tell us what is really happening?

If we only listen to the model, the institution, the database, or the external expert, we may miss the people living inside the system.

And if we miss them, we may also miss the risk.

Part XI — From Inclusion to Risk Intelligence

I now think the chain can be represented like this:

Working framework

Living Heritage → Tepa Selira → Inclusion → Better Interpretation → Better Foresight → Earlier Risk Detection → DRR

This is not a claim that tepa selira is an official DRR framework.

It is my working synthesis: a way of connecting a local ethical principle with contemporary approaches to human-centred risk.

The logic is:

Tepa Selira reminds us to consider another person's position.

Inclusion gives that person space to correct our assumptions.

Foresight asks what happens if our interpretation is wrong.

DRR asks how we can reduce the risk before an adverse outcome becomes severe.

Part XII — The Inclusion Test I Want to Use

Before acting on a classification, I would ask six questions:

1. What did I actually observe?
Separate observation from interpretation.

2. What am I assuming?
Name the shortcut.

3. Who could correct me?
Invite the person or community into the interpretation.

4. What if I am wrong?
Run the edge case.

5. What could escalate?
Think one or two steps beyond the immediate response.

6. What preserves trust?
Choose the response that reduces avoidable harm while still meeting the legitimate objective.

This is where inclusion stops being a decorative value and becomes an operational capability.

Part XIII — The Point Is Not “Always Be Nice”

This distinction matters.

Inclusion does not mean:

“Ignore security.”

“Ignore rules.”

“Believe every claim.”

“Never classify risk.”

“Everyone is harmless.”

That would be another form of context blindness.

The goal is more disciplined:

Keep the rule. Improve the interpretation.

Keep the security objective.

Improve the identification.

Keep the policy.

Improve the feedback loop.

Keep the risk assessment.

Improve the understanding of the people inside it.

Part XIV — My New View of Inclusion

I began with a simple idea:

“Inclusion means making sure people with disabilities are not left behind.”

I still believe that.

But now I would add:

Inclusion also means refusing to reduce a human being to the first explanation that comes to our mind.

A beard is not a threat.

Skin colour is not a crime.

Unusual thinking is not automatically disability.

Approaching someone is not automatically predation.

Difference is not automatically danger.

And a person who does not fit our mental model is not automatically a problem.

Sometimes the problem is our model.

Part XV — The Foresight Question

What if the first disaster is not the hazard — but our interpretation of the people experiencing it?

Maybe the next step in human-centred foresight is not simply to ask:

“What could happen?”

But:

“Whom might we misunderstand?”

“What would that misunderstanding cause?”

“Who could be harmed by our classification?”

“How could the grievance propagate?”

“Where can we interrupt the chain?”

That is where I see a bridge between Living Heritage, Inclusion, Foresight and Disaster Risk Reduction.

And perhaps the most practical lesson is the oldest one:

Before deciding what someone is, try to understand where they are.

Maybe that is not only empathy.

Maybe it is risk prevention.

Closing thought

Foresight begins before the forecast. It begins with correctly understanding the human being inside the system.

Key References & Reading

UNESCO — 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of Intangible Cultural Heritage
Article 15: widest possible participation and active involvement of communities, groups and individuals in safeguarding.
UNDRR — Inclusion
Inclusive resilience, vulnerability, participation, equality and accountability in disaster risk reduction.
UNDRR — National Disaster Risk Assessment: A Guide for National Practitioners
People-centred risk assessment, participation, inclusion and accountability annexes.
UNDRR — A human-centred understanding of disaster risk
People-centred design for warnings and protective actions.
UNDRR — Traditional and Indigenous Knowledges for DRR
Traditional knowledge as accumulated, locally adapted knowledge for disaster risk reduction.
UNDRR — Why community-based DRR fails to learn from local knowledge
Evidence and discussion of barriers to meaningful community and local-knowledge inclusion.
Hamidah et al. (2026) — The Dimension of Empathy in Tepa Selira Philosophy
Systematic literature review describing cognitive, affective and behavioural dimensions of tepa selira.
Widiyanti (2024) — Tepa Selira as a Solution for Bullying
Literature-based discussion of tepa selira, empathy, respect and prevention of aggressive behaviour.

item.title: When Effort Changes the Choice: An Analogy Between Relationships and Diplomacy
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: Why two options with similar baseline value can lead to different choices once trust, damage, effort, repair, opportunity cost and relationship history enter the picture—and how the same logic can be used as a diplomatic analogy, negotiation lens and interactive sensitivity model.
item.content:encoded:
Consider this simple situation. You have two options, A and B. They are equally attractive. Then A hurts you, while B does not. Later, both approach you. All else being equal, why would you necessarily choose A?

Many people intuitively understand the answer: you probably would not. You would likely pay attention to the fact that A created a negative experience while B did not.

But now change one variable.

A starts making a serious effort.

A shows up.

A changes behaviour.

A sacrifices time.

A accepts a commitment that was previously resisted.

A repeatedly demonstrates that the relationship matters.

The interesting part is that A did not necessarily become a different person.

A's original attractiveness may be unchanged. A's baseline characteristics may be exactly what they were before.

What changed was the relationship history.

At the beginning, A and B may have looked similar.

After several interactions, they no longer represent the same proposition to the decision-maker.

One now carries evidence of hurt, repair, consistency and commitment.

The other carries a different history.

That is the central idea behind this article:

People do not choose options based only on what those options are. They also choose based on what interacting with those options has become.

Although the example starts with relationships, the same conceptual structure can be used to think about suppliers, partnerships, negotiations, institutions and diplomacy.

1. Story first: why two “equal” options can stop being equal

Let's start with a deliberately simplified model.

Suppose A and B both have a baseline value of 8.

A = 8 B = 8

At this stage, they are equivalent within the model.

Then A hurts you.

A = 8 − 3 damage = 5 B = 8

Nothing about B had to improve for B to become more attractive relative to A.

This is an important point.

Sometimes an option does not “win” because it became better.

Sometimes the alternative simply acquired a relative advantage because the first option created a cost.

Now suppose A makes an effort to repair the relationship.

A = 8 − 3 damage + 4 repair = 9 B = 8

In this toy model, A becomes competitive again.

This does not mean that every form of damage is reversible.

It does not mean that enough effort gives anyone a right to another person's forgiveness.

It does not mean that a relationship should continue after every kind of harm.

It simply illustrates a more general mechanism:

When the inputs to a decision change, the relative position of the alternatives can change.

2. First distinction: baseline value is not final value

People often use a single adjective to describe an option:

“beautiful,” “smart,” “powerful,” “qualified,” “valuable,” “important,” “strategic.”

But those labels describe only part of the decision.

A decision-maker may care about:

Baseline value
What the option brings initially.
Trust
How predictable and dependable the interaction feels.
Effort
What the option is willing to invest.
Damage
What negative experience or friction has been created.
Cost
What maintaining the relationship requires.
Repair capacity
What happens when something goes wrong.

This gives us a more complete conceptual equation:

Final Value = Baseline + Effort + Trust − Damage − Cost

Again, this is not a scientific law.

It is a thinking instrument.

The purpose is to force us to stop collapsing a multidimensional relationship into one adjective.

3. Why choice is comparative, not absolute

Suppose A is still objectively “good”.

That does not mean A must be chosen.

Why?

Because most decisions are comparative.

The relevant question is not:

“Is A good enough?”

It may be:

“Given my available alternatives, which option produces the better overall position?”

This is why:

A = good B = good

can still produce:

A is preferable

or:

B is preferable

depending on the accumulated history.

A can remain attractive while becoming less attractive relative to B.

4. “A + effort” is not the same as “A says sorry”

This is where the word effort needs more precision.

LevelExampleWhat it may signal
Presenceshowing up, replying, accompanyingattention
Timerearranging a scheduleopportunity cost
Practical sacrificedoing something inconvenientinvestment
Behaviour changeending a repeated harmful behaviourlearning
Major commitmentchanging a significant planlong-term investment
Sustained consistencyrepeating the new behaviour over timecredibility

These are not interchangeable.

A ten-minute message can be meaningful.

But changing a major life plan can carry a very different opportunity cost.

The point is not that “bigger sacrifice = better person.”

The point is that a costly action can provide different information about priorities than a nearly costless statement.

5. Opportunity cost makes effort visible

One reason effort becomes meaningful is opportunity cost.

Imagine someone says:

“I care about you.”

That sentence may be sincere.

Now imagine the person also changes their schedule every week to make room for the relationship.

Now they are giving up something.

That does not automatically prove deeper love or better character. But it does provide additional behavioural evidence.

The same concept applies to organizations.

If a country wants another country to believe a commitment is serious, a statement may be less informative than an action that imposes a real cost on the state making the commitment.

That is why costly actions can matter in negotiation: they can reveal priorities more clearly than cheap words.

6. The commitment example

Consider a person who originally does not want marriage, while their partner does.

Later, the first person decides that the relationship matters enough to change that position.

The interesting variable in this framework is not whether marriage is inherently the correct outcome.

The interesting variable is the magnitude of the change.

Changing a previously stated long-term intention is different from sending an apology message.

It has greater opportunity cost.

It therefore represents a different level of investment.

Important boundary: effort is not entitlement. A person can make a huge sacrifice and still have no ownership over another person. Effort is evidence of investment, not a claim on another person's consent.

7. Damage changes the next round

Another important concept is path dependency.

Before A hurts you, you do not have direct evidence of that particular behaviour from A.

After the incident, you do.

Even if you forgive A, the information environment has changed.

The next interaction therefore begins from a different starting point.

This is why trust is cumulative.

It can be built through repeated positive interactions.

It can be damaged by negative interactions.

It can sometimes be repaired.

And it can sometimes be permanently altered.

8. Repair is not the same as erasure

This distinction is crucial.

Repair does not necessarily mean:

“Pretend it never happened.”

Repair can instead mean:

“The event happened, we understood it, and the system changed so that the next interaction is different.”

That is why a useful repair sequence is:

Acknowledgement → Corrective Action → Consistency → Rebuilt Confidence

An apology may be part of the first stage.

Behaviour change belongs to the second and third.

Trust is rebuilt through repeated evidence.

9. The surprising case: B is less attractive, but B invests

Now consider a different scenario.

A is very attractive.

A = 9

B is ordinary.

B = 6

But B invests heavily.

B = 6 + 3 effort = 9

Under this simplified model, the two options become comparable.

The conclusion is not that “effort always beats beauty.”

The conclusion is that decisions can depend on multiple dimensions simultaneously.

That same principle appears everywhere.

A product can have a lower technical specification but lower maintenance cost.

A supplier can be smaller but more reliable.

A partner can have fewer resources but stronger cooperation.

A diplomatic relationship can involve fewer strategic assets but lower friction.

10. Reverse the scenario

Now B has the lower baseline and also creates damage.

A = 9 + 2 effort = 11 B = 6 − 3 damage = 3

The lower-baseline option is now substantially less competitive.

This illustrates something people sometimes overlook:

Effort is not a magic multiplier. It is one variable in a system of variables.

If the negative history is large enough, a small amount of effort may not compensate for it.

If the baseline difference is large enough, the lower baseline may still remain lower.

If the damage is severe enough, repair may not restore the prior position.

11. One-time gesture versus repeated behaviour

Suppose A makes one spectacular gesture.

Then A returns to the same behaviour that caused the original problem.

Contrast that with B, who makes small but consistent positive contributions.

The two forms of effort provide different information.

A dramatic gesture has high intensity.

B's behaviour has high persistence.

Persistence may be more informative when the decision-maker is trying to predict what happens next.

This is one reason repeated behaviour matters.

A single gesture tells you what happened once. A pattern gives you more evidence about what may happen again.

12. SVG visualization: accumulated relationship value

13. The deeper model: accumulated relationship capital

We can now stop thinking about effort as a one-time bonus.

Instead, imagine that relationships generate a kind of relational capital.

Repeated positive interactions can increase it.

Repeated negative interactions can decrease it.

Repair can recover part of it.

Major breaches can impose unusually large losses.

This produces a dynamic system:

Starting Value → Interaction → Trust / Damage → Effort / Repair → Revised Relationship Position → New Choice → New History

The last step matters.

The system does not reset after every decision.

The outcome of today's interaction can become tomorrow's baseline.

14. Transition to diplomacy

Now we can translate the same structure to diplomacy.

States are obviously not people.

States contain governments, institutions, bureaucracies, militaries, economic actors and domestic political interests.

Diplomatic choices are constrained by laws, treaties, security considerations, formal procedures and strategic calculations.

So the relationship analogy should be treated as a conceptual lens, not a literal equation of state behaviour.

What transfers well is the idea that relationships accumulate history.

15. Diplomatic scenario 1: the accidental damaging statement

Scenario: State A makes a sensitive statement about State B. The statement may be accidental, poorly worded, inaccurate or misunderstood.

Whatever the intent, State B may now reassess the interaction.

The immediate damage could involve:

  • loss of confidence;
  • additional verification;
  • greater diplomatic friction;
  • requests for clarification;
  • greater caution in future negotiations.

The important point is not that every mistake causes a diplomatic crisis.

The point is that a mistake can become part of the relationship context surrounding subsequent decisions.

Diplomatic Position = Strategic Value + Trust + Cooperation − Damage − Friction − Risk

Repair then becomes relevant.

The repairing state may need:

  • clarification;
  • correction;
  • reassurance;
  • additional communication;
  • confidence-building actions.

The exact response depends on the context.

16. Diplomatic scenario 2: two partners request the same cooperation

Scenario: State A and State B both request cooperation from a third party. Both have strategic value, but their recent relationship histories differ.

A has recently created friction.

B has not.

It would be reasonable to model the difference as a potential difference in transactional friction, not as an automatic “winner” or “loser”.

The third party may need to consider:

  • formal eligibility;
  • legal obligations;
  • security;
  • operational feasibility;
  • strategic value;
  • political consequences;
  • existing relationship history.

This is an important refinement.

Relationship quality can influence the cost of cooperation, but it does not necessarily override formal rules.

17. Diplomatic scenario 3: “I can help bring you closer”

Now introduce a broker.

The broker tells two actors:

“I can help connect you. I can make cooperation easier.”

This creates value because the broker is reducing search costs, uncertainty and communication friction.

Then the broker makes a major communication error.

The damage does not simply affect the broker's reputation.

It can also affect the two actors the broker was trying to connect.

Broker Value = Access Created + Trust Built − Miscommunication − Repair Cost

Now the broker has a new task:

repair the bridge.

18. Diplomatic scenario 4: repair requires more than words

Suppose a diplomatic partner says:

“That was not what we intended.”

That may be useful.

But the other side may still ask:

“What changed?”

This is the diplomatic equivalent of asking whether repair is observable.

Depending on circumstances, credible repair can involve:

  • formal clarification;
  • corrective communication;
  • new safeguards;
  • confidence-building measures;
  • greater transparency;
  • behavioural consistency over time.

Again, this is not a universal diplomatic recipe.

The broader idea is simply that repair becomes more credible when the future behaviour changes, not only the explanation of the past.

19. The Suez Canal thought experiment

Consider a hypothetical example involving Suez.

Suppose State A and State B both seek a comparable form of canal transit or cooperation.

State A has recently created diplomatic friction with another actor.

State B has not.

The intuitive relational question is:

Could the difference in diplomatic history create different levels of friction around later requests?

That is a reasonable question as a relationship analogy.

However, Suez cannot simply be treated as a personal relationship.

The canal operates under formal navigation rules and international legal arrangements. The Suez Canal Authority publishes Rules of Navigation, while the Constantinople Convention establishes a legal framework for the canal.

Therefore:

Relationship dynamics may influence political context, but they do not replace formal legal and institutional rules.

This distinction is one of the most important safeguards in the analogy.

20. Diplomatic scenario 5: strategic value can still outweigh friction

Another subtlety is that damage does not necessarily dominate every decision.

A state may have a very high strategic value.

Even if cooperation is difficult, the expected benefit may still be large enough to justify the friction.

In our toy framework:

A = strategic value 10 − friction 3 = 7 B = strategic value 6 − friction 0 = 6

A may still be the more valuable relationship.

This is important because the model is not a moral score.

A difficult relationship can still be strategically important.

That is another reason why diplomatic decision-making is more complex than interpersonal preference.

21. SVG visualization: from relationship repair to diplomatic repair

22. Interactive simulation: what changes the choice?

The simulator is deliberately transparent.

It does not tell you which person to choose.

It does not predict which country will “win” a negotiation.

Instead, it asks a more useful analytical question:

Which assumptions are driving the relative position of A and B?

Option A

8
1
1
3
1

Option B

8
2
2
0
1
Final A
6
Final B
11
B is ahead under the current assumptions.

B starts from the same baseline but has more positive relational inputs and less damage.

How to use the simulation

Change one slider at a time.

For example:

  • increase A's effort and see how much damage it offsets;
  • increase B's trust and observe how much lower baseline B can compensate for;
  • increase A's friction and see when a high baseline stops being sufficient;
  • switch to diplomacy mode and reinterpret the same dimensions as strategic value, trust, confidence-building, diplomatic friction and risk.

The formula remains:

Final Score = Baseline + Effort + Trust − Damage − Cost

The important word is assumptions.

If you change the assumptions, you change the outcome.

That means the simulation is better understood as a simple sensitivity analysis than as a prediction machine.

23. Scenario matrix

ScenarioABWhat changes?
Equal baseline88Starting point is equivalent.
A creates damage8 − 38B gains relative advantage.
A repairs8 − 3 + 48A can recover in the toy model.
B has lower baseline + effort96 + 3The gap can narrow or disappear.
B has lower baseline + damage96 − 3The gap widens.
A has higher baseline + high friction10 − 58 + 1B can become competitive.
Both invest8 + 38 + 2A remains slightly ahead.

24. What the model does explain

Trade-offs.
Different attributes can offset one another under some assumptions.
History.
Two similar options can become different after different interactions.
Repair.
Post-damage behaviour can change the next decision position.
Opportunity cost.
Effort is more informative when we understand what it costs.
Comparative choice.
An option can remain good while another becomes relatively better.
Sensitivity.
Small changes in assumptions can change the relative position of A and B.

25. What the model does not explain

It does not explain everything.

Humans are not spreadsheets.

People have values, boundaries, emotions, memories, identities and changing preferences.

Relationships also contain variables that cannot easily be quantified.

Diplomacy is even more complex because formal rules and institutions impose constraints that a relational score cannot override.

Therefore, the framework should be used to ask better questions, not to pretend that human or diplomatic behaviour can be reduced to a single formula.

26. The deeper analogy: relative value under relationship history

At this point, the beauty analogy becomes almost unnecessary.

The more general structure is:

Relative Value = Initial Value + Interaction Effects + Relationship Capital − Friction − Cost

That can describe:

  • a romantic relationship;
  • a friendship;
  • a supplier relationship;
  • a business partnership;
  • an institutional collaboration;
  • a negotiation;
  • a diplomatic relationship.

The common mechanism is not romance.

It is accumulated interaction history.

27. “Better on paper” versus “better in reality”

This framework also explains a familiar paradox.

Sometimes A looks much better on paper.

A has more resources.

A has more credentials.

A has more money.

A has more strategic importance.

A has more impressive baseline characteristics.

Yet B is easier to work with.

B is reliable.

B communicates.

B does not create unnecessary friction.

B repairs mistakes.

B invests consistently.

The decision-maker may rationally prefer B even though B was not the stronger option on the first page of the spreadsheet.

This is not necessarily irrational.

The spreadsheet may have measured baseline value.

The decision-maker may also need to consider relationship value.

28. Closing: value is not static

So perhaps the real lesson is this:

When two options begin with comparable value, the way they interact with you can become part of the value calculation.

Effort can add value.

Trust can add value.

Damage can subtract value.

Repair can restore part of what was lost.

Consistency can make repair credible.

Opportunity cost can make effort more informative.

And a major commitment can matter because it demonstrates that the relationship is being treated as valuable enough to justify a real cost.

That is why “A was better on paper” and “B was chosen” are not necessarily contradictory statements.

One describes the starting position.

The other describes the position after interaction.

And that is the bridge to diplomacy.

A country can remain strategically important while becoming more difficult to work with.

A partner can create friction and then repair the relationship.

An intermediary can create access and then damage the trust that made the access valuable.

Formal rules can constrain what is possible, while relationship history can still influence the political and practical cost of cooperation.

The useful question is therefore not simply “Who is better?” It is: “Given the history, the costs, the effort, the trust and the constraints, how has the relative value of these options changed?”

This article is a conceptual framework and interactive simulation. The numerical values are illustrative, not empirically calibrated measures of attraction, trust, or state behaviour. They are intended to make the reasoning visible and testable rather than to produce objective verdicts.

item.title: The Shortcut Problem: Why Doping, Gambling, Cheating and Corruption Follow the Same Behavioural Logic
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: Doping, cheating, gambling, corruption and other shortcuts can look unrelated, yet many share the same behavioural architecture: a desired outcome, an uncomfortable process, an immediate shortcut and delayed cost. This article connects that pattern to COM-B, the Behaviour Change Wheel, EAST, present bias and implementation intentions, and introduces the conceptual SCALE framework plus an interactive Shortcut Pressure Calculator.
item.content:encoded:
Doping is one of the clearest examples of a much bigger human problem. A person wants the trophy. The legitimate route is slow, uncertain and painful. Then a shortcut appears: a substance that promises better performance now.

But the pattern does not belong to sport.

Take away the stadium and the same behavioural skeleton can appear in gambling, corruption, cheating, manipulation, fraud, get-rich-quick schemes, and countless everyday decisions.

Different behaviours. Different consequences. The same behavioural logic.

This is the question that started bothering me:

Why do people repeatedly choose the shortcut when the shortcut itself can create a larger problem than the one they were trying to escape?

Part I — The Doping Hook

Imagine an athlete who has trained for years.

Year 1Builds the basics.
Year 2Gets stronger.
Year 3Loses competitions.
Year 4Improves technique.
Year 5Still may not win.
ThenSomeone offers a shortcut.

The temptation is not difficult to understand.

The legitimate process gives a delayed and uncertain reward. The shortcut offers an immediate and visible reward.

The athlete is not necessarily thinking, “I want to become a dishonest person.”

The internal dialogue may be much simpler:

“I have trained so hard. I just need an advantage. I cannot afford to lose again.”

That is why reducing the problem to “bad people do bad things” can be analytically weak. It tells us almost nothing about how the behaviour becomes attractive.

Part II — The Same Pattern Outside Sport

DopingThe athlete wants performance now.
Hidden motorThe cyclist wants speed now.
JudolThe player wants money now.
CorruptionThe person wants wealth or access now.
CheatingThe student wants a grade now.
ManipulationThe person wants control or affection now.

Even supernatural or pseudoscientific shortcuts can fit the same structure. Someone who desperately wants another person's affection may seek a supposed “special method” rather than face the possibility of rejection or incompatibility.

The mechanism is not “all these behaviours are morally equivalent.” They are not.

The point is more precise:

At the behavioural-mechanism level, many of them share the same sequence: desired outcome → friction or uncertainty → tempting shortcut → immediate reward → delayed cost.

Part III — What Is a Shortcut, Actually?

A shortcut is not automatically bad.

Technology, process redesign, automation and good management are full of legitimate shortcuts. If a better tool removes unnecessary work while preserving the objective, quality and integrity of the outcome, that is efficiency.

GOOD
Reduces waste
NEUTRAL
Changes the route
RISKY
Bypasses a requirement
Efficiency: remove unnecessary friction.
Shortcutting: remove necessary friction.

Training an athlete better is efficiency. Using doping to bypass training is shortcutting.

Automating a repetitive report is efficiency. Fabricating the underlying data to make the report look successful is shortcutting.

Finding a faster legal route to build wealth is efficiency. Fraud or corruption to bypass the economic process is shortcutting.

Part IV — The Core Behavioural Formula

I wanted a simple way to represent the pattern.

Shortcut Pressure ≈ (Goal Urgency + Immediate Reward + Process Friction + Failure Aversion + Shortcut Access) × Present-Bias Effect − Future-Cost Salience

This is a conceptual working model, not a validated psychometric scale. I am using it as a systems-thinking tool: a way to make the mechanism visible and to ask where an intervention could change the system.

Goal urgencyHow badly is the outcome wanted now?
Immediate rewardHow attractive is the payoff today?
Process frictionHow difficult is the legitimate route?
Failure aversionHow intolerable does failure feel?
Shortcut accessHow easy is the shortcut to reach?
Future-cost salienceHow vivid and believable is the later consequence?

The sixth variable matters because humans do not always value immediate and delayed outcomes equally. Present bias and related time-dependent biases are well-established topics in behavioural economics and intertemporal decision-making.

Important: The calculators below are deliberately transparent. They do not “diagnose” a person. They show how changing one part of a system can change the pressure toward a shortcut.

Part V — Click the Model: Shortcut Pressure Calculator

Shortcut Pressure & Behavioural System Simulator

Use the sliders to diagnose why the shortcut is attractive. Then switch to the redesign panel and test how changing the system could alter the pressure.

Interactive teaching prototype
Current system
—
/ 100
Adjust the sliders, then calculate.
Primary driver: — Protective factor: —
Where should we intervene?Calculate the system first to identify the biggest leverage point.
0–49Lower pressure
50–74Moderate pressure
75–100High pressure
What-if redesign
Change the environment
REDESIGNED SYSTEM
—
Set the design sliders and simulate.
System diagnosis
Where is the pressure coming from?
Goal urgency
Immediate reward
Process friction
Failure aversion
Shortcut access
Interpretation
Target the largest gap first
High friction?Make the legitimate route shorter, easier or better supported before demanding more willpower.
High immediate reward?Create legitimate progress, recognition or small wins that can compete with the pull of “now”.
High shortcut access?Use proportionate friction, safeguards and better defaults around the harmful option.

Teaching prototype only. Equal weights are intentional for inspectability. The redesign simulator is an illustrative what-if model, not a validated predictive or diagnostic instrument.

Part VI — Why the Same Shortcut Appears in So Many Domains

Now we can see why the “this is all the same” intuition is useful.

The surface behaviour changes, but the underlying variables can remain remarkably similar.

Sport“I cannot afford another loss.”
Money“I cannot wait years to become financially secure.”
Relationships“I cannot tolerate rejection or uncertainty.”
Career“I need the promotion now.”
Education“I need the grade now.”
Social status“I need to prove myself now.”

The common factor is not the specific object of desire. It is the combination of time horizon + uncertainty + friction + perceived shortcut opportunity.

Part VII — COM-B Gives Us the Diagnostic Layer

This is where COM-B is particularly useful.

The Behaviour Change Wheel places Capability, Opportunity and Motivation at the centre of behavioural diagnosis. In a shortcut problem, I would invert the question and ask:

“Why is the legitimate pathway losing?”
C — CapabilityDoes the person have the knowledge, skills and capacity to perform the legitimate behaviour?
O — OpportunityDoes the environment make the legitimate behaviour possible, accessible and supported?
M — MotivationDo reflective and automatic processes make the legitimate behaviour attractive enough to occur?

Maybe the person lacks capability. Maybe the legitimate route is too difficult to access. Maybe the immediate reward is too weak. Maybe failure feels unbearable. Maybe the shortcut is sitting one click away.

Part VIII — Click the COM-B Bottleneck

PRIMARY BOTTLENECK
—

Move the sliders and diagnose the system.

The three slider values are a teaching aid, not a formal COM-B score.

Part IX — COM-B Is the Diagnosis. It Is Not the Whole Intervention.

Diagnosis and intervention design are related but not identical. COM-B helps identify what needs to change; the wider Behaviour Change Wheel helps select intervention functions and policy categories.

For shortcut behaviour, that means we should not immediately jump to “education”.

If the problem is opportunity, education may do almost nothing. If the problem is motivation, changing the form may do almost nothing. If the problem is capability, punishment alone may not build the skill needed to choose the legitimate route.

Low CapabilityEducation • Training • Enablement
Low OpportunityEnvironmental restructuring • Access redesign • Proportionate restrictions
Low MotivationPersuasion • Modelling • Incentivisation • Commitment strategies

Part X — EAST Explains How to Redesign the Environment

EAST turns behavioural insight into four practical questions: make the desired behaviour Easy, Attractive, Social and Timely.

EasyReduce unnecessary friction on the legitimate route.
AttractiveMake progress and legitimate rewards visible.
SocialMake the desired norm observable and credible.
TimelyIntervene at the moment the shortcut becomes tempting.

If a person is tempted at 11:47 PM, giving them a two-hour seminar on financial literacy tomorrow afternoon may be too late. The intervention has to meet the temptation in time.

Part XI — The Intervention Is Not “Make People Stronger”

There is a common mistake in behaviour-change programmes:

“We need to teach people self-control.”

Sometimes yes. But a robust system does not rely only on heroic self-control.

Make the good route easierRemove unnecessary steps.
Make the shortcut harderAdd appropriate friction and safeguards.
Make delayed benefits visibleShow progress and future gains.
Make immediate rewards legitimateCelebrate small wins now.
Prepare for temptationUse if–then plans.
Repair the systemLearn from each shortcut event.

Part XII — Present Bias: The Missing Time Variable

Imagine two options.

Option A: work for five years, uncertain result.

Option B: get a chance to win tonight.

Even when the long-term expected value of A is better, B can feel psychologically stronger because the reward is immediate.

Humans are not comparing abstract values in a vacuum. They are comparing time-stamped experiences.

Design implication: if the desired behaviour pays off only in the distant future, find a way to create legitimate feedback, progress, recognition or reward today.

Part XIII — If–Then Plans Protect the Moment of Choice

An implementation intention is an if–then plan that links a recognizable situation to a prepared response.

IF I feel pressure to get the result immediately, THEN I will pause, name the shortcut, and choose one legitimate action I can complete today.

The point is not magical wording. The point is pre-commitment.

Part XIV — My Synthesis: SCALE

I would combine these ideas into a practical sequence I call SCALE.

S — SignalWhat outcome is the person trying to get?
C — ConstraintWhat process, uncertainty or fear are they trying to escape?
A — AlternativeWhat shortcut becomes available, and what immediate reward does it promise?
L — Long-term costWhat later consequence is being discounted?
E — EnvironmentHow can we redesign the system so the legitimate route becomes easier and the harmful shortcut harder?

SCALE is not a published behavioural-science framework. It is my working synthesis for making the shortcut mechanism operational.

Part XV — What Actually Changes the Behaviour?

If the aim is to reduce harmful shortcut behaviour, I would not begin with a poster saying:

“DON’T CHEAT.”

I would begin with a behavioural diagnosis.

Define the legitimate target behaviour.
Do not define success merely as “not cheating”. Define what people should do instead.
Map COM-B.
Find out whether the bottleneck is capability, opportunity or motivation.
Map the shortcut.
Where is it available? What makes it salient? What reward does it give immediately?
Reduce legitimate friction.
Simplify the correct route before demanding more willpower.
Add proportionate friction to harmful shortcuts.
Make risky shortcuts less accessible, less convenient or less rewarding where appropriate.
Create legitimate immediate wins.
Give feedback, progress markers, recognition and small rewards before the distant outcome arrives.
Install an if–then response.
Prepare for the exact moment when the shortcut becomes tempting.

Part XVI — Example: From Doping to a Better System

Suppose an organisation wants to reduce doping risk among athletes.

A weak intervention might be:

“Doping is bad. Here are the rules.”

A stronger system would ask:

CapabilityDo athletes understand safe performance strategies, recovery and nutrition?
OpportunityCan they access coaching, recovery support and credible health advice?
MotivationAre progress, clean achievement and identity as a fair competitor rewarding enough now?

Then EAST can reshape the environment.

Easy: make legitimate support easy to access.

Attractive: make clean performance visible and prestigious.

Social: strengthen team norms and modelling.

Timely: put decision support near the moments of greatest temptation.

That is a much richer intervention than “be a good person.”

Part XVII — Example: The Same Architecture for Gambling

The same architecture can be used for gambling-related shortcut behaviour.

The behavioural objective is not simply “understand gambling harms”. It could be:

“When I feel urgency to recover money quickly, I pause rather than attempt to chase the loss.”
CapabilityTeach loss-chasing recognition and financial planning.
OpportunityReduce frictionless betting access and add cooling-off mechanisms where appropriate.
MotivationMake long-term financial stability more salient than the immediate fantasy of recovery.

The domain changed. The behavioural architecture did not.

Part XVIII — Measurement: How Do We Know It Worked?

Instead of measuring only the final outcome, measure the variables in the pathway.

Leading indicatorPerceived process friction.
Leading indicatorAccessibility of the shortcut.
Leading indicatorSalience of delayed consequences.
Behaviour indicatorUse of the legitimate route.
Behaviour indicatorTime-to-shortcut after a trigger.
Outcome indicatorRepeat shortcut events and downstream harm.
Do not wait for the bad outcome to appear before asking whether the behavioural system has changed.

Part XIX — The Deeper Problem: We Often Reward the Shortcut

Sometimes the environment itself teaches people that shortcuts work.

If someone cheats and wins, the social signal may be: “Look how smart they are.”

If someone becomes rich through questionable means and receives admiration, the signal becomes: “They figured out the game.”

If someone constantly bypasses process and gets promoted for producing visible results, the organisation may unintentionally train everyone else to copy them.

Now the problem is no longer an individual weakness. It becomes a reinforcement system.

People repeat shortcuts when shortcuts repeatedly produce rewards.

Part XX — The Rule I Keep Coming Back To

Do not ask only, “Why did this person take the shortcut?”

Ask: “Why did the shortcut become the most attractive option in this system?”

That question changes the intervention. It moves us from blaming the individual to understanding the behaviour. And understanding the behaviour allows us to change the environment around it.

Part XXI — The Shortcut Problem Is Really an Uncertainty Problem

The deeper commonality may not be laziness. It can be discomfort with uncertainty.

The legitimate path says:

“Work hard. Wait. Learn. Fail. Adjust. Maybe succeed.”

The shortcut says:

“You can know the answer now.”

It promises not merely speed. It promises certainty.

That is why the intervention should not merely say “be patient”. It should help people become more capable of tolerating uncertainty while still moving forward.

Part XXII — The Practical Formula for Behaviour Change

DIAGNOSE → REDESIGN → REWARD → PREPARE → MEASURE
DIAGNOSEUse COM-B to identify the bottleneck.
REDESIGNUse EAST to make the legitimate route easier, more attractive, social and timely.
REWARDBring legitimate feedback and progress closer to the present.
PREPAREUse if–then plans for moments of temptation.
MEASURETrack leading indicators, behaviour and downstream outcomes.
Companion tool
ImpactArchitect v3.3

Use Case: Social Program Design & Diagnosis

A digital canvas integrating Theory of Change (ToC) with the COM-B behavioral model. Enhanced by Google Gemini, it helps program designers stress-test logic, diagnose stalling results, and translate outputs into behavioral change.

Analisa lengkapnya bisa klik ini ↗

Part XXIII — The Point Is Not “Never Take a Shortcut”

Some shortcuts are innovations. Some are accessibility improvements. Some are simply smarter process design.

The real question is:

What exactly is the shortcut removing?

If it removes waste, simplify it.

If it removes unnecessary bureaucracy, redesign the system.

If it removes learning, fairness, safety or responsibility, stop and investigate.

Conclusion — Diagnose the System, Then Change the System

What began with doping turned into a much broader question about human behaviour.

Athletes, gamblers, students, employees, entrepreneurs and decision-makers may face completely different situations. Yet many shortcut decisions can share the same structure:

Desired outcome → uncertainty / friction → tempting shortcut → immediate reward → delayed cost.

COM-B helps us diagnose why the legitimate pathway is weak. Present-bias thinking helps us understand why “now” can beat “later”. EAST helps us redesign the environment. If–then plans protect the critical moment of choice. SCALE connects the pieces into a practical sequence.

And perhaps the most useful question is the simplest one:

Are we asking people to be more disciplined — or have we actually designed a system in which the right behaviour can win?

Because sometimes behaviour is not failing because people are weak.

The system may simply be rewarding the shortcut.

Working-model note

Shortcut Pressure and SCALE are conceptual synthesis tools created for this article. COM-B, EAST and implementation intentions are established behavioural-science frameworks/concepts; the interactive scores above are teaching aids and should not be treated as validated psychometric or clinical instruments.

item.title: How Living Heritage Teaches Us About Making a Policy
item.category: Living Heritage, Policy Design & Inclusive Systems
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: Tepa Selira is more than empathy: it can inspire a policy stress test. Before a policy is implemented, compare its assumptions with other people's realities, deliberately invite divergent criticism, and test the edge cases before reality becomes the reviewer.
item.content:encoded:
What can living heritage teach us about making a policy? More than we might expect.

We often talk about living heritage as something we should preserve. But living heritage can also be read as a repository of social intelligence: ways communities have learned to coordinate, restrain themselves, solve collective problems, interpret conflict, and live with difference.

Take Tepa Selira.

At a basic level, Tepa Selira asks us to place ourselves in another person's position — to compare our own parameter with the possible experience of somebody else before we act.
