Existing literature on Tepa Selira links the value to cognitive, affective and behavioural dimensions of empathy, while the UNESCO framework for living heritage emphasises that communities who create, maintain and transmit heritage must participate in safeguarding and managing it.

The shift

If Tepa Selira asks a person to compare their own perspective with another person's reality, why not apply the same logic to policy design?

Part I — A Policy Is Also a Point of View

Every policy contains assumptions.

Who is the “normal” citizen?

What resources do we assume they have?

What information do we assume they can access?

How fast do we assume they can respond?

What language do we assume they understand?

What behaviour do we assume they will have?

What happens to the person who does not fit the average?

Policy teams often become extremely good at answering these questions without explicitly saying that they are making assumptions.

Then the policy is launched.

And suddenly the edge cases become real people.

Perhaps many policy failures are not failures of intelligence. They are failures of perspective.

Part II — Why Do Some Policies Produce Conflict Even When They Look Rational?

Here is my deliberately provocative question:

What if a policy causes conflict because nobody was assigned to make the policy uncomfortable before it was implemented?

A room full of competent people can still produce a fragile decision when everyone is solving the same problem using the same assumptions.

The danger is not that convergent thinking is bad. It is essential for narrowing options, applying standards and making decisions.

The danger is convergence without adversarial testing.

Imagine a policy process like this:

1. Define the problem
The team agrees on what the problem is.
2. Build the solution
The team develops an intervention that matches that definition.
3. Validate internally
The same people review the same assumptions.
4. Implement
Reality becomes the first serious stress test.

That last step is expensive.

Because once reality becomes the reviewer, the cost is no longer a workshop.

It can become budget loss, public resistance, implementation failure, staff burnout, legal disputes, damaged trust, or social conflict.

OECD guidance published in 2025 explicitly recommends stress-testing public policies against multiple plausible disruptions and using tools such as red teams, premortems and structured dissent to challenge assumptions before implementation. The same guidance cautions that evidence for red teaming in public administration remains limited, so it should be treated as a promising practice rather than a magic solution.

Part III — The “Annoying Critic” May Be an Institutional Sensor

Now we arrive at the uncomfortable part.

In many workplaces, the person who keeps asking:

“But what if…?”

can become unpopular.

“Why are you making this complicated?”

“We already decided.”

“That's not how we usually do it.”

“You're always finding problems.”

“You're too negative.”

Sometimes the critic really is simply being unhelpful. Criticism is not automatically insight.

But there is another possibility:

What if the person who keeps saying “but…” is functioning as a missing sensor in the organization?

A divergent thinker often expands the possibility space rather than immediately collapsing it into one answer. In a policy environment, that can look like criticism because the job is partly to expose alternatives, contradictions, hidden assumptions and edge cases.

That does not make the divergent thinker automatically right.

It makes their dissent potentially useful data.

Part IV — The Real Asset We Keep Throwing Away

Organizations frequently talk about “talent” as if talent were a list of qualifications.

Degree.

Certification.

Years of experience.

Test score.

Interview score.

KPI.

Those things can be useful evidence.

But they are still proxies.

The dangerous moment comes when the proxy becomes the definition of ability itself.

If the instrument cannot detect a capability, the capability can start to look like it does not exist.

This is especially important for people whose strengths are exploratory, connective, systems-oriented, unusual or difficult to standardise.

They may not “fit” a single job family.

They may produce ideas before the organization has a category for them.

They may jump between disciplines.

They may challenge the framing before accepting the task.

They may be irritating in meetings.

They may also be exactly the person who sees the failure mode nobody else saw.

Part V — “Divergent” Is a Thinking Mode, Not a Personality Ranking

This distinction matters.

I am not arguing that divergent people are better humans, better employees, or better policy makers.

Nor does “divergent” provide a clinical diagnosis or an excuse for poor behaviour.

The useful distinction is functional:

Convergent mode
Which option best satisfies the criteria?
Divergent mode
What possibilities, variables, stakeholders or consequences have not yet been considered?
Integration
Can we generate alternatives, stress-test them, and then converge on a defensible decision?

We need all three.

Because divergence without convergence can become chaos.

But convergence without divergence can become institutional blindness.

Part VI — Tepa Selira as a Cognitive Stress Test

This is where the cultural principle becomes surprisingly practical.

Suppose a ministry proposes a new service requirement.

The convergent question is:

“Does the procedure achieve the intended administrative objective?”

Tepa Selira adds another layer:

“How does this procedure behave when experienced by someone who has a very different set of constraints from ours?”

Then divergent thinking pushes further:

What if the assumption is wrong?

What if the average case is misleading?

What if the user cannot comply?

What if the policy creates a new incentive that nobody intended?

What if people adapt their behaviour around the rule?

What if the “exception” is actually a large but invisible group?

What happens after six months?

What happens when another disruption occurs at the same time?

Now the policy is no longer being evaluated only for whether it works in theory.

It is being tested for whether it survives contact with different realities.

Part VII — Why Critical Dissent Matters

There is a subtle organizational mistake here:

We sometimes treat disagreement as friction instead of treating disagreement as information.

A useful critical voice does not have to be rewarded simply because it is critical.

Instead, the organization can ask:

What assumption is being challenged?

What evidence would prove the criticism wrong?

What evidence would prove it right?

What edge case is being exposed?

Does the criticism reveal a design weakness?

That is the difference between argument and stress testing.

OECD's recent public-administration guidance describes red teams as arms-length collaborators who challenge assumptions, evidence and decision-making through structured dissent. It even suggests techniques such as checking explicit and implicit assumptions and systematically attempting to disconfirm competing hypotheses.

So perhaps the question is not “How do we silence the critic?” but “Can we convert criticism into a testable hypothesis?”

Part VIII — The Most Dangerous Sentence in Policy?

“We have already decided.”

Because that sentence can quietly transform evidence into decoration.

Once a team becomes psychologically committed to a solution, contradictory information becomes inconvenient.

And the divergent thinker becomes even more annoying.

Which is precisely why they may be useful.

The best time to hear “this could fail” is before failure becomes expensive.

Part IX — Living Heritage and the Anti-Top-Down Lesson

This is where UNESCO's living-heritage framework becomes directly relevant to policymaking.

The 2003 Convention calls for communities, groups and relevant organisations to participate in identifying living heritage, and Article 15 calls for the widest possible participation of the communities, groups and individuals who create, maintain and transmit it. UNESCO decisions concerning policies that may affect intangible cultural heritage also stress active participation and warn against top-down approaches.

That is not merely a heritage-management lesson.

It is a policy-design lesson:

The people affected by a system are not merely “beneficiaries.” They are potential sources of intelligence about whether the system will work.

The community knows the loophole the policy designer never imagined.

The frontline worker knows where the workflow breaks.

The local practitioner knows what the spreadsheet cannot see.

The unusual employee knows which assumption everyone has quietly normalised.

The critic knows which sentence makes the whole thing uncomfortable.

And discomfort can be useful.

Part X — The Black Death / Cats Story: A Warning About the Metaphor

There is a famous story that Europe killed cats and thereby helped rats spread the Black Death.

It is a great metaphor.

It is also a poor historical fact to repeat without qualification. The popular story simplifies a much more complicated history, and the causal claim that mass cat killing drove the plague is disputed.

So I would use the story differently:

Imagine a society destroying a potentially useful asset simply because its value was invisible to the dominant belief system.

That mechanism is entirely plausible inside modern institutions.

We can discard a person because their value is not visible to our test.

We can discard a warning because it does not fit our narrative.

We can discard local knowledge because it does not look like formal expertise.

We can discard a critic because they are irritating.

And afterwards, we wonder why the system became less resilient.

Part XI — Google Is Actually a Useful Counterexample

And yes: Google is not a clean example of “one narrow test decides everything.”

Google has publicly described structured interviews, consistent evaluation criteria and efforts to reduce bias in hiring. Google has also described project-based assessments designed around real-world engineering work, rather than relying only on abstract technical puzzles.

That matters because the argument here should not become:

“All organizations are convergent and all tests are bad.”

That would itself be a convergent stereotype.

The stronger argument is:

Every organization should examine what its measurement system systematically makes visible — and what it systematically makes invisible.

Google is therefore a useful reminder that organizations can design broader assessment systems.

Part XII — A Better Architecture: Diverge → Stress-Test → Converge

Diverge. Expand the space of possibilities.

Stress-test. Invite structured dissent. Attack assumptions, not people.

Converge. Make the decision using evidence, explicit criteria and accountability.

Then repeat.

This resembles the logic of strategic foresight: explore disruptions, imagine interactions, build scenarios, test strategies and identify actions that remain robust across multiple possible futures.

Part XIII — So What Does Tepa Selira Actually Teach a Policymaker?

The policy translation

“Before I impose my parameter on society, I should test what happens when society does not share my parameter.”

That is Tepa Selira translated into policy language.

Not “be nice.”

Not “never disagree.”

Not “all perspectives are equally correct.”

Something much more operational:

Never confuse the parameter used to measure reality with reality itself.

Part XIV — The Provocation

So here is the question I would leave with policymakers, managers, recruiters and anyone who designs systems:

How many valuable people have we called “difficult” because our organization had no instrument for measuring what they were actually good at?
How many policies have failed because the only people allowed to validate them were the same people who designed them?
How many conflicts could have been prevented if someone had been paid to disagree before implementation rather than blamed for complaining afterwards?
And how many “exceptions” are actually signals that our definition of normal is too narrow?

Maybe the goal is not to make every person more convergent.

Maybe the goal is to build organizations that know when to converge and when to deliberately diverge.

Because a system without convergence cannot decide.

But a system without divergence cannot see what it is missing.

And a system without Tepa Selira may make a perfectly rational decision — from the wrong person's point of view.

One final thought

A critic is not automatically right. But an institution that never listens to critics may eventually discover that it has removed one of its own warning systems.

Living heritage is not only about remembering how people lived.

Sometimes it teaches us how systems should listen before they decide.

Key References & Reading

1. UNESCO — 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of Intangible Cultural Heritage
Community participation, national policy measures, and Article 15 on active involvement in safeguarding and management.
2. UNESCO — About Living Heritage and Education
Living heritage is community-based; communities are central to its creation, maintenance and transmission.
3. UNESCO — Decision 10.COM 14.a
Policies and programmes that affect living heritage should involve the communities concerned and respect ethical considerations.
4. Hamidah et al. (2026) — Tepa Selira and empathy
Systematic literature review connecting Tepa Selira with cognitive, affective and behavioural dimensions of empathy.
5. OECD — Behavioural Science in the Italian Public Administration
Pre-mortems, calibrated forecasting and red teams as practices for challenging assumptions and stress-testing public decisions.
6. OECD — Strategic Foresight Toolkit for Resilient Public Policy
A five-module process for exploring disruptions, building scenarios and stress-testing policies across possible futures.
7. Google — Structured decision-making and hiring
Google's public discussion of structured interviews and consistent evaluation criteria.
8. Google / Byteboard — Work-sample assessment
Project-based assessment designed around real-world engineering skills.
9. Historical caveat on the cat / Black Death story

The popular claim that mass cat killing caused the Black Death by increasing rats is disputed and should not be presented as settled history. In this article the story is used only as a metaphor for the broader risk of discarding assets whose value a dominant measurement system cannot see.

item.title: Living Heritage at Work: How Gotong Royong Can Help You Coordinate
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: What can living heritage teach us about coordination at work? This article explores gotong royong as a living cultural practice of mutual cooperation, shared purpose, complementary contribution, reciprocity, social accountability, and collective problem solving — and explains why focal points and trusted information matter when second-hand communication can drift.
item.content:encoded:
Living heritage is living knowledge. It is not simply an old object, costume, song, building, or ceremony. UNESCO describes intangible cultural heritage, also called “living heritage,” as inherited practices, knowledge, skills, expressions, rituals, social practices and other forms of knowledge that communities continue to transmit, adapt and recreate. Its meaning lives in the people who practice it.

The central idea

Gotong royong can be read as a living coordination practice: people contribute what they can, align around a shared need, help one another, and keep the collective task moving.

Part I — What Is Living Heritage?

When people hear the word heritage, they often imagine something preserved: a historical building, an archaeological site, an old manuscript, a traditional textile, or an artifact in a museum.

Living heritage is different.

It is heritage that is still practised, learned, transmitted, adapted and given meaning in everyday life. UNESCO explicitly describes intangible cultural heritage as traditional, contemporary and living at the same time. It can be found in oral traditions, performing arts, social practices, rituals, knowledge about nature, and traditional craftsmanship. It is also community-based: the communities, groups or individuals who create, maintain and transmit a practice are central to recognizing it as their heritage.

That distinction matters because a practice does not have to remain frozen in its historical form to remain culturally meaningful.

Inherited
Knowledge and practices have histories and are transmitted between people and generations.
Practised
People actually use, perform or apply the knowledge instead of merely displaying it.
Adaptive
Living heritage can change as communities respond to new environments and circumstances.
Meaningful
The value is connected to what the practice means to the people who carry it.

This is why living heritage can be relevant to a workplace. The point is not to turn the office into a museum. The point is to ask:

What useful social knowledge is embedded in the way communities already know how to live and solve problems together?

Part II — What Is Gotong Royong?

Gotong royong is commonly translated as mutual cooperation, but the phrase is richer than simply “teamwork.” It refers to forms of people helping one another and working collectively around shared needs and responsibilities.

Research on gotong royong describes it as a form of social cooperation that has been embedded in Indonesian community life and can involve sharing, participation, collective responsibility and mutual assistance. One study in the Heritage of Nusantara journal describes gotong royong as an intrinsic form of daily social cooperation in many Indonesian villages and discusses its continuing relevance for community participation and cultural heritage.

Other research describes gotong royong as a cultural practice associated with togetherness, social solidarity and cooperation in solving collective problems, while also noting that its forms and sustainability can change as social and economic conditions change.

So, for this learning page, gotong royong is not treated as one rigid formula that every Indonesian community follows in exactly the same way. Instead, it is used as a living cultural lens for understanding collective action.

The cultural elements that matter

Shared purpose
People understand what the group is trying to accomplish.
Contribution
People contribute labour, knowledge, tools, time, relationships or other resources.
Mutual assistance
The relationship is not purely transactional; people support one another because the collective task matters.
Reciprocity
Contribution can create a social expectation that support flows in more than one direction over time.
Participation
The work depends on people actually taking part, not only agreeing with the idea.
Social accountability
People can see that their actions affect others and the shared outcome.

These elements are particularly useful when translated carefully into modern work. The goal is not to copy village practices literally into an office. It is to identify the coordination logic inside the practice and ask where that logic can still be useful.

Part III — Why “Mouth-to-Mouth” Information Can Break Down

Imagine a simple instruction:

“Please send the revised report to the partner by Thursday afternoon and copy the programme focal point.”

Person A hears it.

Person A then tells Person B:

“The report needs to go to the partner on Thursday.”

Person B later tells Person C:

“We need to send the report Thursday.”

Person C tells Person D:

“The report is due Thursday.”

Notice what happened.

No one necessarily lied.

But pieces of information disappeared:

This is why second-hand information can be misleading even when every person is acting in good faith.

The hidden steps

Hear → interpret → remember → reconstruct → retell.

At every step, information can be compressed. A listener may omit something they think is secondary. A person may remember the meaning rather than the exact wording. Another person may add context from their own assumptions. The next person receives a reconstruction, not necessarily the original message.

This is closely related to the classic psychological idea of serial reproduction, associated with Frederic C. Bartlett's work on reconstructive memory. Later research comparing repeated and serial reproduction has found greater forgetting and distortion as material passes from person to person in a serial chain.

The critical lesson:

Misleading information does not require a liar. It can emerge from ordinary human communication when context, memory, interpretation and verification are weak.

Part IV — Why This Becomes a Workplace Problem

Now replace the children's “telephone game” with a real organization.

A project manager tells one team. That team tells a consultant. The consultant tells a local partner. The partner tells a field team. The field team makes a practical decision based on what they understood.

Suddenly:

Different interpretations
People believe they are following the same instruction, but they are solving different versions of the problem.
Duplicate work
Two teams unknowingly produce the same output because neither knows what the other has already done.
Missed dependencies
One team does not know that another team is waiting for its input.
Slower decisions
People spend time checking what was actually agreed.
Lower trust
People begin asking who said what instead of focusing on the problem.
Rework
A task gets completed once, then has to be completed again because the initial understanding was incomplete.

The irony is that everyone can be working hard.

Many organizations do not have a lack-of-effort problem. They have a coordination problem.

Part V — Where Gotong Royong Changes the Model

A purely linear information chain looks like this:

Every person depends on the previous person's interpretation.

A more coordinated model looks different:

The difference is not simply “more communication.” It is more structured coordination.

Gotong royong as a workplace coordination logic

In a workplace, the cultural logic can be translated into a few practical questions:

What is our shared goal?
Can everyone describe the intended outcome in roughly the same way?
Who contributes what?
Are roles complementary rather than duplicated?
Where does information live?
Can people return to a trusted source instead of relying on memory?
How do we verify?
Is there a feedback loop before assumptions become decisions?
Who connects the pieces?
Is there a person who can see across workstreams?
What happens when something changes?
Does the update reach everyone who depends on it?

Part VI — And This Is Where the Focal Point Matters

In complex work, collaboration does not mean everyone talks to everyone about everything.

That can create a different problem: communication overload.

One useful role is the focal point.

A focal point can act as a coordination node: not necessarily the boss, not necessarily the person who does all the work, but the person who helps connect information, people, decisions, timelines and dependencies.

A good focal point reduces the need for every person to maintain every piece of information independently. It can also reduce the risk of parallel teams making contradictory assumptions.

But there is an important caution: a focal point is not a bottleneck.

If every decision must wait for one person, coordination becomes centralized dependence. The goal is not to create one human database. The goal is to create a trusted coordination mechanism that keeps people aligned while allowing work to continue.

Part VII — Gotong Royong Does Not Mean “Everyone Does Everything”

This distinction is crucial.

People sometimes misunderstand cooperation as unlimited availability: “We are a team, so everyone should help with everything.”

That can produce exhaustion, duplicated labour and unclear accountability.

Gotong royong is more useful when interpreted as collective contribution toward a shared need, not as the elimination of roles.

Coordination ≠ everybody doing the same thing.

It means different people contributing different things toward an outcome they understand together.

A designer can contribute design. A finance officer can contribute budget control. A researcher can contribute evidence. A field officer can contribute local knowledge. A communications officer can translate results into public-facing messages.

The collective strength comes from complementarity.

Part VIII — The Difference Between Cooperation and Coordination

Two teams can be very cooperative and still be badly coordinated.

For example, imagine six people working enthusiastically on a project:

“Everyone is helpful. Everyone is busy. Everyone is producing something.”

But no one has checked whether all six people are producing the same thing.

That is cooperation without coordination.

Now imagine the same six people with:

Shared goal → clear roles → common information source → feedback → adaptation.

That is much closer to a functional coordination system.

Part IX — Second-Hand Information: “But I Was Only Passing It On”

One of the most common workplace sentences is:

“I was only passing on what I heard.”

That may be completely honest.

But honesty of transmission does not guarantee accuracy of information.

A second-hand statement can contain:

Compression
Some details were left out because they seemed unimportant.
Context loss
The reason behind the instruction was removed.
Interpretation
The listener filled a gap using their own assumptions.
Time drift
An old instruction continued circulating after circumstances changed.
Authority drift
A suggestion gradually becomes remembered as a decision.
False certainty
“I think this is what they meant” becomes “They said this.”

This is why strong teams create mechanisms for verification.

Instead of:

“Someone told me that the deadline is Friday.”

the stronger practice is:

“Let me check the agreed timeline before we act on that.”

That small shift protects both the person who heard the information and the people downstream who depend on it.

Part X — A Workplace Translation of Gotong Royong

Living Heritage LogicWorkplace Translation
Shared needShared project objective
Mutual assistanceSupport across workstreams
Different contributionsComplementary roles and expertise
Community knowledgeShared institutional and field knowledge
ReciprocityHelp is not one-way forever
Social accountabilityVisible ownership and follow-through
Collective problem solvingJoint troubleshooting and adaptation

Part XI — What a Focal Point Actually Does

If gotong royong is the cultural logic, the focal point can become one of the practical mechanisms that keeps that logic functioning inside a complex organization.

1. Align
Make sure different teams understand the same objective.
2. Translate
Turn technical information into something another team can use.
3. Connect
Know who needs to speak to whom.
4. Verify
Check whether an assumption is actually documented or agreed.
5. Surface gaps
Identify missing information before it becomes rework.
6. Close the loop
Make sure decisions travel back to the people who depend on them.

The focal point therefore does not have to be the person with the most authority. The role is about maintaining coherence across relationships and information.

Part XII — Why This Is Still Living Heritage

There is an important conceptual boundary here.

Calling something “living heritage” does not mean every modern adaptation of an old value is automatically a heritage element. UNESCO emphasizes that living heritage is community-based and that the communities, groups and individuals who create, maintain and transmit a practice are central to its recognition and continuity.

So this page is not claiming that a corporate teamwork workshop is itself a traditional Indonesian heritage practice.

The more careful proposition is:

The bridge

A living cultural practice can provide a lens through which modern problems are understood and discussed.

Gotong royong can therefore be used educationally to ask what modern teams can learn from a culturally rooted model of collective action: shared purpose, mutual support, complementary contributions, social responsibility and the importance of keeping relationships functional.

Part XIII — Gotong Royong Is Not a Replacement for Good Management

There is also a danger in romanticizing cultural values.

“Let us just have more gotong royong” does not solve unclear job descriptions, insufficient budgets, broken systems, poor leadership, missing data, unrealistic deadlines or unsafe working conditions.

Cultural values can support coordination, but they cannot magically repair structural problems.

Culture can strengthen a system. It cannot substitute for a functioning system.

A healthy workplace therefore needs both:

Good systems — roles, processes, records, tools, accountability, decision rights and resources.

Good social practice — trust, reciprocity, respect, willingness to help, knowledge sharing and the ability to repair misunderstandings.

Part XIV — The Practical Experiment

Take any current project and ask five questions:

1. Do we actually share the same goal?
If two people describe the project differently, coordination is already at risk.

2. Are contributions clearly divided?
If nobody knows who owns an output, “teamwork” can quickly become duplication.

3. Is there a source of truth?
Do people check the same document, decision log, dataset or agreed record?

4. Is information verified?
Can someone ask, “Where did this information come from?” without creating conflict?

5. Does feedback return to the system?
When reality changes the plan, does the updated information reach everyone affected?

Part XV — From Cultural Practice to Modern Capability

This is perhaps the most interesting bridge between living heritage and professional practice.

The value of living heritage is not only that it gives us something beautiful to preserve. It can also reveal knowledge that communities have developed through lived experience.

In the case of gotong royong, the knowledge is social and practical: how to mobilize people, how to distribute effort, how to maintain relationships, how to respond to shared needs, and how individual contributions become meaningful when connected to a collective purpose.

Those questions remain relevant in an office, a school, a community programme, a humanitarian response, a research project or an international development programme.

The bigger idea

Living heritage can be a source of coordination knowledge.

Not because the past has all the answers, but because communities carry practical ways of solving human problems.

Part XVI — The Focal Point: Where Coordination Becomes Visible

When a project involves multiple teams, partners and information streams, someone often needs to hold the connective tissue.

That person does not need to control everything.

They need to help the system remember what it is doing.

Who needs to know? What has changed? What has been agreed? Who is waiting? What still needs verification?

That is why the focal point matters.

In a well-functioning coordination system, the focal point is not merely a messenger. The role can become a place where fragmented information is aligned, clarified, connected and returned to the people who need it.

That is remarkably compatible with the broader logic of gotong royong: different people contribute different things, but the work only becomes collective when the contributions are connected.

Part XVII — A Simple Mental Model

Part XVIII — One Final Distinction

Gotong royong should not be confused with simply being “nice” at work.

It is not:

“Everyone is friendly.”

It is closer to:

“Everyone understands the collective task, contributes appropriately, shares relevant information, and helps the system move.”

That makes it especially interesting as a living heritage concept for work.

The cultural practice gives us a language for collective responsibility. Modern management gives us tools for making that responsibility operational.

The final thought

Gotong royong is not about everyone doing everything.

It is about making different contributions work together.

That is why the conversation about living heritage does not have to stop at preservation.

It can also ask:

What knowledge does a community already carry that can help us solve today's problems?

For gotong royong, one possible answer is coordination.

Different people. Different capabilities. One shared purpose.

And somewhere in the middle, a focal point helps make sure the pieces do not drift apart.

Key References & Reading

1. UNESCO — Frequently Asked Questions: Living Heritage and Education
UNESCO, About living heritage and education
2. UNESCO — What Is Intangible Cultural Heritage?
UNESCO, What Is Intangible Cultural Heritage?
3. UNESCO — Community-Based Living Heritage
UNESCO, About living heritage and education
4. Gotong Royong and Cultural Environments
Heritage of Nusantara — Enlivening Cultural Environments through Sharing and Gotong Royong (Mutual Cooperation)
5. Gotong Royong and Cultural Conservation
Indonesian Journal of Conservation — Pengembangan Nilai dan Tradisi Gotong Royong dalam Bingkai Konservasi Nilai Budaya
6. Gotong Royong and Contemporary Change
Humanities and Social Sciences Communications — Shifting collective values: the role of rural women and gotong royong in village fund policy
7. Serial Reproduction and Information Distortion
ScienceDirect — Bartlett revisited: Direct comparison of repeated reproduction and serial reproduction techniques

item.title: Living Heritage as Anti-Bullying: Tepa Selira, and Why We Can Be Hurt Without Anyone Meaning It
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: What can living heritage teach us about bullying prevention? This article explores Tepa Selira — the Javanese principle of placing yourself in another person's position — and asks a harder question: why some of the deepest hurt comes from things no one ever intended as an attack.
item.content:encoded:
One of the things I find fascinating about living heritage is that sometimes, our ancestors already had social principles that modern society is still struggling to practice. One of them is Tepa Selira — a Javanese value usually translated as "measuring against oneself," or the discipline of imagining how something would feel if it were done to you before you do it to someone else.

The central idea

Tepa Selira is usually discussed as a tool against deliberate cruelty. But some of the deepest pain in bullying and social exclusion is never deliberate at all. It comes from small, unintentional moments that accumulate — a joke, an eye-roll, an exclusion nobody meant as exclusion — until the person carrying them breaks, and everyone around them asks, confused, "but who bullied them?"

Part I — What Is Tepa Selira?

Tepa Selira (also spelled tepa slira) comes from Javanese and is often glossed as empathy, self-restraint, or "measuring one's own feelings against another's." A simple version of the principle:

If I do not want to be hurt, I should not hurt others.

Recent academic work treats Tepa Selira as more than a proverb. A 2026 systematic literature review by researchers at Universitas Negeri Surabaya examined Tepa Selira specifically for its empathy content and found that the philosophy contains three interlocking dimensions of empathy — cognitive (understanding another's perspective), affective (feeling with them), and behavioural (acting on that understanding) — and that these dimensions are reflected in values of harmony, mutual cooperation, patience, mindfulness and justice. citeturn1search0turn1search5

That same review notes something directly relevant here: the integration of Tepa Selira into practice is described as strengthening empathetic competence and helping prevent negative behaviour such as bullying. citeturn1search5

This is where living heritage becomes more than nostalgia. UNESCO describes intangible cultural heritage, or "living heritage," as inherited knowledge, practices and social values that communities continue to transmit, adapt and use — not frozen artefacts, but tools still doing work in the present. citeturn0search2turn0search1

Part II — Bullying Doesn't Always Begin With Something Dramatic

Sometimes it begins with:

"It's just a joke."
"It's just a small thing."
"It's just teasing."
"Why are you so sensitive?"
"Ah, cuma begitu doang."

And here is the part that makes this harder to talk about than ordinary bullying: not every wound is inflicted on purpose. Sometimes there is no villain in the story. No one who set out to hurt anyone. Just a comment made without thinking, a joke that landed wrong, an exclusion that was never meant as exclusion — and the person carrying it never said a word about how much it stayed with them.

The same words pass through different histories. The listener assembles the meaning; the speaker only sends a fraction of it. That is what makes Tepa Selira so relevant here: it is not only about restraining cruelty. It is about the discipline of imagining impact — even when we never intended harm at all.

Part III — The Problem With Looking at One Incident

We see one incident. The person on the receiving end may be experiencing a pattern.

One exclusion. One humiliation. One rejection. One joke. One comment. One more day of being treated as if they don't quite belong.

And eventually, the person reacts — or, more quietly, breaks. Then everyone asks:

Why is that person so angry? Who bullied them?

But sometimes that is the wrong question, because sometimes no one did — not deliberately. What happened was an accumulation of small, unintentional moments that no single person meant as an attack. Maybe we should ask a different question:

What has this person been carrying that we did not see — regardless of whether anyone meant to hurt them?

Part IV — What the Data Tells Us

This is not a trivial issue, and the region's own numbers make that concrete, even where they cannot tell us exactly how much of the pain was intentional.

In Japan, the government's confirmed 2025 figures show 538 elementary, junior-high and high-school students died by suicide — the highest number recorded since comparable statistics began in 1980, and the second consecutive record year. Officially recorded causes and motives (which are multiply counted per case) show "school-related problems" as the single largest category, at 251 cases — a broad grouping that spans academic pressure, career anxiety, and peer relationships, not bullying specifically. citeturn2search3turn2search1

In South Korea, a nationwide school-violence survey found the reported student victimisation rate climbed to 2.5% in 2025, continuing a steady year-on-year rise since 2020 (1.1% → 1.7% → 1.9% → 2.1% → 2.5%), with experts pointing to digital isolation and post-pandemic aggression among the contributing pressures. citeturn2search6

These numbers do not mean every case involves bullying, and they do not mean every hurt was intentional. But they should remind us of something very simple:

We do not always know how much pain a person is carrying — even the people who accidentally contributed to it.

And Indonesia is not an exception. The conversation around bullying here increasingly recognises that consequences can extend beyond the immediate incident, and that not every act that contributes to someone's pain was meant as an attack — which is exactly why prevention, empathy and early attention matter more than blame alone.

Part V — The Psychology of Accumulated Small Hurts

Psychology has a name for exactly this pattern, drawn from research that started outside the bullying literature but describes the same mechanism. A microaggression is defined as a brief, everyday, often unintentional interaction or behaviour that communicates bias or hostility toward someone — and researchers explicitly note that these occur unconsciously, not necessarily with intent to harm. citeturn3search3turn3search5

What matters for Tepa Selira is not the label "microaggression" itself but the finding underneath it: research summarised by the University of British Columbia's health psychology lab shows that repeated small negative experiences are associated with depression and poorer self-rated mental health up to twenty years later, along with impaired sleep, elevated inflammation and faster cellular ageing — and that while any single day's effect may look small, these effects accumulate over time to raise the risk of future depression. citeturn3search0

A separate, more recent strand of research studies this in real time. A 2026 award-winning study of everyday ostracism — the everyday experience of feeling ignored or excluded — followed hundreds of participants through smartphone-based experience sampling and documented close to 2,000 real-life ostracism moments. It found that even brief moments of being ignored can threaten a person's fundamental sense of belonging, self-esteem, control and meaning, and that when the threat feels severe enough, people are more likely to withdraw or react in ways that look, from the outside, like sudden anger. citeturn3search2turn3search6

No intent required
Both microaggression and everyday-ostracism research describe harm that occurs without anyone meaning to cause it.
Effects accumulate
A single small slight looks harmless. Repeated over months or years, the same slights are linked to depression and poorer health.
The reaction looks disproportionate
Because outsiders only see the final incident, the eventual response can look like an overreaction to "nothing."
The pattern is invisible from outside
No single observer typically sees the full accumulated sequence — only the person carrying it does.

This is, in other words, a scientific description of what Tepa Selira was already asking people to imagine centuries earlier: that the person in front of you may be carrying more than the one moment you are seeing.

Part VI — "I Was Only Passing On What I Heard" Is Not the Same as "I Did No Harm"

One of the most common defences people offer, once something has clearly hurt someone, is a version of:

"I didn't mean it that way."

That may be completely honest. But honesty of intent does not guarantee the absence of impact. A comment, a joke or an exclusion can carry:

Compression
The speaker leaves out nuance because it seemed unimportant to them.
Context loss
The listener has no way to know this was "just a joke" rather than a genuine judgement.
Prior weight
The listener's own history fills in meaning the speaker never put there.
Repetition drift
A joke told once is a joke. Told about the same person by different people over months, it becomes a pattern only the target can see.

This is why strong communities, schools and workplaces build in a habit of checking impact rather than only defending intent. Instead of:

"I was only joking, so it's not my problem how you took it."

the Tepa Selira version is closer to:

"Before I said it, did I imagine what it would feel like if it were said to me?"

Part VII — Rational Thinking (Nalar): Asking a Different Question

Don't only ask: Why did this happen? Who bullied them?

Ask: What happened between people that made trust hard to rebuild — even where no one set out to break it?

Don't just look at the final reaction. Look at the sequence. This is where nalar — rational thinking — matters. It is tempting to sort every situation into "bully" and "victim," because that framing is simple and satisfying to judge. But accumulated, unintentional hurt does not fit that frame cleanly, and refusing to see it because it is complicated is itself part of how it keeps happening.

Part VIII — Tepa Selira Does Not Mean No Boundaries

It is worth being precise about what Tepa Selira is not asking of anyone.

It does not mean you have to like everyone.
It does not mean you cannot have boundaries.
It does not mean you must accept every friendship.
It does not mean you cannot say "no."

It means:

Before I hurt someone — even by accident — I try to imagine what it would feel like if I were in their position.

And perhaps this is the part we have forgotten.

When something happens: "Ah, it's just a small thing."
When someone reacts: "Ah, why are you so sensitive?"
When someone finally breaks: "Why didn't they tell us?"
And when tragedy happens: "Only one person died." Or worse: "But no one bullied them, so it's not our fault."

No. One person is already one person too many. And intent does not change that.

Part IX — Where Tepa Selira Becomes a Practical Framework

If gotong royong is a cultural logic for coordinating collective work, Tepa Selira can be read as a cultural logic for coordinating collective care — a check that runs quietly before words and actions, not only after complaints arrive.

1. Pause. Before a joke, a comment or a quiet exclusion, there is a half-second where it can still be reconsidered.

2. Imagine. Not "would I find this funny," but "would I find this funny if I had already heard six versions of it this month, from six different people, and never said anything?"

3. Check impact, not only intent. "Are you okay?" costs one sentence. Assuming silence means agreement costs much more.

4. Repair when impact and intent diverge. "I didn't mean it that way, but I can see how it landed that way — I'm sorry" is a complete sentence that does not require anyone to have been a villain.

Part X — This Is Still Living Heritage, Not Just a Slogan

There is an important boundary to hold here. Calling something "living heritage" does not mean every modern adaptation of an old value is automatically heritage. UNESCO is explicit that living heritage is community-based — the communities, groups and individuals who create, maintain and transmit a practice are central to recognising it as their own. citeturn0search1turn0search6

So this is not a claim that a school assembly reciting "Tepa Selira" is itself a traditional heritage practice. The more careful claim is the bridge underneath it:

The bridge

A living cultural value can give modern institutions language for a problem that psychology is only now measuring precisely.

Tepa Selira does not replace anti-bullying policy, teacher training, or mental health support. Cultural values can strengthen a system; they cannot substitute for one. What Tepa Selira offers is a shared, locally rooted vocabulary for a habit that is otherwise easy to skip: imagining impact before intent has even formed into words.

Part XI — Instead of Asking Only "Who Is to Blame?"

Perhaps we should also ask:

Where did we lose our Tepa Selira?

Because preventing this kind of pain is not only about punishment after someone gets hurt on purpose. It is about learning to care enough to notice — even when no one meant any harm at all.

Tepa Selira.
Living heritage.
Empathy.
Inclusion.

And a simple reminder:

The person in front of you is a human being too — and you may only be seeing one page of a much longer story.

Key References & Reading

1. The Dimension of Empathy in Tepa Selira Philosophy and Its Implications for Multicultural Counseling
Hamidah et al., Jurnal Pandu Husada (2026) — systematic literature review on Tepa Selira and empathy
2. UNESCO — What Is Intangible Cultural Heritage?
UNESCO, What Is Intangible Cultural Heritage?
3. UNESCO — Community-Based Living Heritage
UNESCO, About living heritage and education
4. Japan child and student suicides, 2025 confirmed figures
nippon.com / Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare data via National Police Agency statistics
5. South Korea school-violence victimisation rate, 2025
Xinhua — S. Korea's school violence hits record high on digital isolation, post-pandemic aggression
6. Microaggressions — definition and unintentional nature
Derald Wing Sue, PhD — Evolution of Psychotherapy course description
7. Cumulative mental and physical health effects of everyday discrimination
UBC UPLIFT Health Lab — Daily Experiences and Health Study
8. Everyday ostracism in real life (experience sampling study)
Büttner et al., Journal of Personality and Social Psychology — Best Paper Award 2026, ISSEP
9. Original reporting context
BBC Indonesia

item.title: Guyub as Living Heritage: Reconciliation, Social Cohesion, and the Everyday Work of Staying Together
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: Guyub is more than gathering. This article explores how Javanese relational practices such as rukun, tepa slira, gotong royong and musyawarah can be understood as living heritage: everyday social knowledge that helps people remain in relationship, navigate disagreement, repair trust and transmit ways of living together across generations.
item.content:encoded:
Ambient Java Reflection — Guyub & Living Heritage
Tap play to begin

There is a kind of togetherness that can be seen from the outside: people gathering, working together, attending ceremonies, sitting in the same room, or appearing united. But there is another kind of togetherness that is much harder to see. It is the willingness to listen after disagreement, to apologise without losing dignity, to help someone after a difficult conversation, and to remain capable of cooperation when a relationship has been hurt.

In Javanese cultural language, guyub offers a powerful way to think about this. It is often translated as togetherness, communal solidarity, or social harmony. Yet the deeper question is not simply whether people are together. The question is whether the relationship that connects them is still alive.

This article explores a particular interpretation: guyub can be read as a living cultural practice that supports reconciliation—not because “guyub” is a formal peacebuilding mechanism, but because everyday practices associated with guyub can create social conditions in which relationships are repaired, trust is rebuilt, differences are negotiated, and collective life continues.

The Journey

  1. From Togetherness to Living Heritage
  2. Guyub Is a Relationship, Not a Crowd
  3. When Togetherness Breaks: The Space of Conflict
  4. Reconciliation as a Living Practice
  5. Rukun, Tepa Slira, Gotong Royong & Musyawarah
  6. What Guyub Is Not
  7. From Memory to Transmission
  8. Guyub in the Digital Age
  9. A Reconciliation Cycle for Everyday Life
  10. Conclusion: Keeping the Relationship Alive

1. From Togetherness to Living Heritage

Living heritage is not simply a collection of beautiful traditions from the past. UNESCO describes intangible cultural heritage as practices, knowledge, skills and expressions that communities recognize as part of their heritage and continue to recreate across generations. The point is not only preservation. The point is continuity through living practice.

That distinction matters for guyub. If guyub were only the memory of how people once lived together, it would belong to history. It becomes living heritage when people still enact it: helping neighbours, making space for elders and younger people, negotiating disagreement, maintaining relationships, sharing responsibility, and teaching others how to live together.

Seen this way, heritage is not frozen. The outward form can change. A community meeting can move from the village hall to a group chat. Gotong royong can involve digital coordination. A family conversation can happen across cities. What remains is the cultural logic: relationship has to be maintained through practice.

2. Guyub Is a Relationship, Not a Crowd

Not every gathering is guyub.

A room can be full and still feel lonely. A workplace can look harmonious while resentment accumulates. A family can eat at the same table while nobody feels heard. A community can repeat the language of “togetherness” while people are afraid to speak honestly.

Guyub points toward something deeper: a shared willingness to remain in relationship. There is a sense of belonging, mutual care, and responsibility. People do not merely occupy the same social space; they recognize that what happens to another person can affect the life of the whole.

This is why guyub sits naturally beside ideas such as rukun, tepa slira, gotong royong, ngajeni, and musyawarah. These are not identical concepts, but together they describe a social grammar for living with other people.

3. When Togetherness Breaks: The Space of Conflict

Every community experiences rupture. Someone says something hurtful. Trust is damaged. A misunderstanding becomes a personal accusation. A family member stops speaking. Colleagues become distant. A neighbour feels excluded. The problem is not the existence of disagreement; disagreement is ordinary social life.

The crucial question is what happens after the rupture.

There are at least two possible directions. The first is escalation: each side builds a story about the other, intent is assumed, dignity is threatened, and distance becomes identity. The second is repair: people create enough space to listen, acknowledge what happened, and find a way to relate differently.

This is where reconciliation becomes useful as a lens. Reconciliation does not mean pretending nothing happened. It does not require immediate forgiveness, and it does not erase accountability. It is better understood as a process through which a relationship—or the possibility of coexistence—is renegotiated after harm or serious disagreement.

4. Reconciliation as a Living Practice

Large-scale discussions of reconciliation often focus on war, political violence, transitional justice, or divided societies. Those contexts matter. But the social work of reconciliation also happens at ordinary scale.

It can begin with a simple sentence:

“Let us talk.”

Not to decide who wins, but to see whether the relationship can still carry the weight of truth.

From there, reconciliation may involve several practices: creating a pause before reacting; listening to another person's experience; naming harm without humiliation; taking responsibility where responsibility exists; apologising; changing behaviour; respecting boundaries; and slowly rebuilding trust through repeated interaction.

None of these practices is uniquely Javanese. What is culturally significant is the way Javanese concepts can provide a vocabulary for thinking about them. Guyub gives value to togetherness. Rukun gives value to relational order. Tepa slira encourages consideration of another person's feelings and position. Gotong royong turns solidarity into action. Musyawarah creates a social process for negotiating difference.

The important point is not to claim that these concepts automatically produce reconciliation. They do not. Rather, they can provide cultural resources that communities may draw upon when trying to repair relationships.

5. Rukun Does Not Mean Everyone Must Agree

One of the most dangerous misunderstandings of harmony is the idea that harmony requires sameness.

Healthy social cohesion does not require everyone to think alike. It requires people to develop ways of staying connected while differences remain visible.

That distinction is especially important in conversations about reconciliation. If “keeping the peace” means telling the hurt person to stay quiet, then the relationship may look peaceful while the wound remains active. If “guyub” means preventing criticism so that the group can maintain a good image, then the cultural value has been turned against the people who are supposed to carry it.

A more mature reading is different: rukun protects relationship without demanding silence. A person can say “I disagree.” Another can say “that hurt me.” Someone can ask for distance. A community can still create a path back to dialogue.

6. Tepa Slira: Learning to Measure from the Other Side

Tepa slira can be approached as a discipline of considering the experience of another person. Before judging behaviour, one tries to understand the social meaning it may carry for the other.

This becomes powerful in moments of cross-cultural or interpersonal misunderstanding. The same gesture, tone, silence, or directness may carry different meanings. A person may intend honesty while another experiences aggression. One person may intend humility while another reads avoidance.

Reconciliation becomes difficult when every side treats its own interpretation as objective reality. It becomes possible when people are willing to ask: “What did you experience when I did that?”

A practical question
“I know what I intended. But what did my action mean to you?”

That question does not surrender truth. It expands truth from one person's intention to the relationship between intention and impact.

7. Gotong Royong: Repair Through Shared Action

Reconciliation is often imagined as conversation alone. Yet relationships are also repaired through action.

Gotong royong shows this clearly. People build, clean, carry, cook, prepare, restore, and help together. Shared work produces more than a practical result. It creates repeated opportunities for people to experience one another again in a different way.

A person you once misunderstood may become the neighbour who helps you lift something heavy. A colleague you argued with may become the person who quietly solves a problem with you. A family relationship may begin to heal through ordinary acts before either side is ready for a grand conversation.

In that sense, collective action can become a bridge between apology and trust. Trust is not repaired only by saying the right words. It is repaired when later behaviour becomes consistent with those words.

8. Musyawarah: Making Space for Difficult Truths

Musyawarah offers another useful dimension: reconciliation requires a process in which people can speak, listen, negotiate, and search for a way forward.

Musyawarah should not be reduced to “everyone agrees.” Its strength is that it treats difference as something that must be worked through socially. The goal is not always victory. The goal is a path that allows collective life to continue without forcing every person into the same position.

This is close to a central principle of living heritage: communities must not be treated merely as audiences for an externally designed cultural solution. UNESCO's 2003 Convention emphasizes the active participation of the communities, groups and individuals who create, maintain and transmit their heritage.

In other words, reconciliation cannot be designed entirely from outside the relationship. Those living the relationship must have agency in shaping how repair happens.

9. What Guyub Is Not

Guyub is not forced agreement.

A community can stay connected while people hold different views.

Guyub is not forced forgiveness.

A person can need time, distance, accountability, or boundaries.

Guyub is not silence.

Problems that cannot be discussed do not disappear.

Guyub is not permanent self-sacrifice.

Healthy togetherness leaves room for personal limits and dignity.

The distinction matters because cultural values can be used in contradictory ways. The same language of harmony can support care, but it can also be used to pressure people into tolerating harm. A living interpretation must remain capable of self-correction.

10. From Memory to Transmission

Living heritage survives because people transmit more than vocabulary. They transmit ways of behaving.

A child learns guyub by seeing how adults handle disagreement. They learn whether an apology is mocked or respected. They learn whether an elderly neighbour is helped. They learn whether criticism is a conversation or a humiliation ritual. They learn whether someone who made a mistake is permanently expelled from the social circle or given a path to repair.

This is why living heritage is especially powerful as an educational idea. The heritage lives in repeated social behaviour. Transmission is not only “telling young people what guyub means.” It is creating situations in which they can practice it.

A school can teach reconciliation through cooperative projects. A community can document oral histories of how local disputes were repaired. A family can teach children how to apologise and how to listen. A digital community can build norms that reward clarification rather than outrage.

11. Guyub in the Digital Age

The spaces have changed, but the relationship work remains.

Today a WhatsApp group can function like a neighbourhood. A social-media community can become a source of belonging. A single forwarded message can create suspicion within minutes. Public embarrassment can spread faster than a face-to-face apology ever could.

Digital guyub therefore asks for a modern version of old disciplines: pause before reacting, verify before forwarding, correct without humiliating, disagree without dehumanising, and remember that there is a person behind the screen.

Eling lan waspada becomes particularly relevant here: be aware, and remain careful. The technology is fast. The relationship is slower.

12. A Reconciliation Cycle for Everyday Life

We can now put the argument into a simple cycle. Not a universal formula, but a practical way of seeing how a living social value can become a reconciliation practice.

  1. Pause. Do not let the first emotional reaction become the permanent story.
  2. Listen. Find out how the other person experienced the situation.
  3. Acknowledge. Name the harm, misunderstanding, or difference without turning the person into the problem.
  4. Repair. Apologise when appropriate and change the behaviour that caused the rupture.
  5. Reconnect. Rebuild cooperation through small, consistent actions.
  6. Transmit. Teach the next generation what was learned so the community becomes better at repair over time.

This is where the idea of living heritage becomes especially meaningful. A tradition is not alive merely because its name survives. It is alive when its social intelligence continues to help people navigate the present.

Conclusion — Keeping the Relationship Alive

Guyub is often translated as togetherness. But perhaps the more interesting question is what kind of togetherness it asks us to practice.

Not a togetherness that demands everyone become the same.

Not a harmony that depends on silence.

Not a social ideal that requires people to ignore harm.

Instead, guyub can be read as a cultural vocabulary for maintaining relationship: caring, helping, listening, negotiating, repairing, and finding a way to remain human toward one another when life becomes difficult.

That is why the concept fits so naturally into conversations about living heritage. Living heritage is not only what a community remembers. It is what a community continues to do.

If people continue to use practices of mutual care, dialogue, respect, collective action, and relationship repair, then the heritage remains alive—not as a museum display, but as a social capability.

The quiet lesson of guyub
A community is not defined only by how well people live together when everything is easy.
It is also defined by how they find a way to remain human toward one another when things become difficult.

Perhaps that is one of the quietest forms of reconciliation: not a grand ceremony, not a declaration that all differences have disappeared, but the repeated decision to repair what can still be repaired—and to leave enough space for future generations to keep practicing the work of living together.

Selected Heritage References

UNESCO — Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage (2003). Article 15 emphasizes the widest possible participation of the communities, groups and individuals who create, maintain and transmit living heritage.
https://ich.unesco.org/en/convention

UNESCO — Intangible cultural heritage and peace. UNESCO's Operational Directives encourage recognition of ICH practices that contribute to social cohesion, dialogue, peaceful conflict resolution, restoration of peace, reconciliation and recovery.
https://ich.unesco.org/en/decisions/6.GA/7

UNESCO — Sustainable development and living heritage. UNESCO notes that locally rooted social practices of dialogue, conflict resolution and reconciliation can promote peace and social cohesion.
https://ich.unesco.org/en/sustainable-development-and-living-heritage

UNESCO — About living heritage and education. Communities are the primary actors in deciding what constitutes their living heritage and are responsible for its creation, maintenance and transmission.
https://ich.unesco.org/en/about-01159

Concept note: this article interprets selected Javanese relational values as possible resources for reconciliation. It does not claim that “guyub” is a formal conflict-resolution mechanism or that all Javanese communities interpret the concept identically.

Why This Matters for Living Heritage

The value of guyub is not located only in a word, a ceremony, or a remembered way of village life. It can also be found in the repeated social skills through which people maintain relationship: listening, helping, negotiating difference, repairing harm, and making space for another person to return to the conversation. That is what makes a cultural practice living: people continue to use, reinterpret, and transmit its social knowledge in changing circumstances.

item.title: Living Heritage That Teaches Mental Models for Inclusive Preservation
item.dc:creator: Angga Conni Saputra
item.description: What can Husnuzan, Tepa Selira and other living-heritage practices teach us about divergent and convergent reasoning? A deep exploration of why some people diverge first, how hidden variables change our models, why knowledge-zero makes divergence expensive, and how to train a disciplined Diverge → Investigate → Converge → Close loop.
item.content:encoded:
What if living heritage preserves not only what communities do, but also how communities learn to think?

When we talk about Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH), we often talk about dances, songs, crafts, food, rituals, languages and ceremonies. But living heritage can also carry relational habits, ethical concepts and ways of making sense of other people.

This article explores that possibility through husnuzan, tepa selira, and a practical mental model for divergent and convergent reasoning. The central idea is simple:

Core Mental Model
DIVERGE → INVESTIGATE → CONVERGE → CLOSE

Divergence expands the hypothesis space. Investigation reduces uncertainty. Convergence closes the model when the evidence becomes sufficient.

1. Living Heritage That Teaches Mental Models

UNESCO describes intangible cultural heritage as practices, representations, expressions, knowledge and skills that communities recognize as part of their heritage and continue to recreate across generations. That means living heritage is not simply a collection of objects from the past. It is also a continuing social process.

So I started asking a different question:

What mental models are hidden inside living heritage?

One example is the combination of husnuzan and tepa selira.

Husnuzan is commonly understood in Islamic ethics as maintaining a good or positive assumption rather than immediately jumping to suspicion. Tepa selira is commonly associated with considering another person's position, feelings and circumstances before judging or acting.

I am not claiming that these concepts are formally defined by UNESCO as cognitive frameworks. Rather, I am exploring them as cultural resources that can encourage a particular discipline of thinking:

Before judging the person, investigate the situation.

2. The Same Observation, Two Different Reasoning Paths

Consider a simple observation:

“She still chats with her ex.”

A fast convergent interpretation might be:

“She has not moved on.”

It is fast. It may even occasionally be correct. But the observation and the conclusion are not the same thing.

A divergent thinker starts somewhere else:

“Why?”

Now the hypothesis space opens.

Fast convergence
Chatting with an ex → not over the ex.
Divergent first
Chatting with an ex → why?
  • Maybe unresolved feelings.
  • Maybe family connections remain.
  • Maybe work or practical obligations.
  • Maybe there is social or professional dependency.
  • Maybe they are genuinely friends.
  • Maybe there is a hidden variable.

Then we ask the person.

Suppose the answer is:

“I have already moved on. Our families are still connected. Sometimes the former partner is simply the person who connects us to another person we need for practical reasons.”

Now the model changes.

The original observation was accurate:

They still communicate.

But the first causal explanation was not sufficiently tested:

Communication ≠ automatically emotional attachment.

This is one of the most important distinctions in reasoning:

Observation ≠ Interpretation ≠ Causal Explanation

A data point can be real while the story we attach to it is wrong, incomplete, or premature.

3. Divergent Thinking Is Not the Absence of Convergent Thinking

I do not see divergent and convergent thinking as two mutually exclusive personality types.

Someone can be strongly divergent by default and still have a powerful convergent mode.

The difference is often which mode activates first.

My own default is closer to:

Expand → investigate → update → close

When something does not make sense, the first question is often:

Why?

Then:

What else could explain this?

Then:

What variable am I missing?

Only after enough evidence appears does the convergent move become:

“Okay. Now I understand. Close.”

So convergence is not absent. It is deliberately delayed until the explanation space has been explored enough.

4. What Happens When Knowledge = 0?

This is where the problem becomes interesting.

If your knowledge of a subject is close to zero, divergence can become very expensive.

A convergent thinker may find one plausible explanation and stop.

A divergent thinker may produce:

“Maybe this. Maybe that. Maybe another thing. Maybe a hidden variable. Maybe a second-order effect. Maybe something I haven't even considered.”

Now divergence can become endless.

So the solution is not:

“Always diverge as much as possible.”

The solution is:

Build enough knowledge to create a useful hypothesis space, then investigate, then converge.

That gives us a more complete learning loop:

1
BUILD BASE
vocabulary, components, obvious relationships
2
DIVERGE
generate plausible explanations
3
INVESTIGATE
find evidence and missing variables
4
CONVERGE
select the best-supported model
5
CLOSE
hold a working model

Knowledge gives divergence something to work with. Investigation gives convergence something to work with.

5. The Danger of Premature Closure

Premature closure happens when the explanation space is closed before enough information has been gathered.

Examples are everywhere:

“He did not reply, so he does not respect me.”

“She declined the invitation, so she does not like me.”

“He is late, so he is irresponsible.”

“She is quiet, so she must be angry.”

These sentences may contain a real observation followed by an unsupported causal leap.

Divergent reasoning inserts a small but powerful gap:

“What else could be happening?”

That question does not mean every alternative explanation is equally likely. It simply prevents us from treating the first explanation as a fact before testing it.

6. Husnuzan as an Epistemic Pause

Husnuzan can be understood as a discipline of maintaining a positive assumption rather than immediately selecting a suspicious or hostile interpretation.

For this article, I find an especially useful reading:

Do not automatically choose the worst explanation when the evidence is incomplete.

This is not the same as believing everyone is good.

It is not the same as ignoring evidence.

It is not the same as refusing to recognize harmful behaviour.

It is simply an epistemic pause:

Before judgment
“I know what happened. I do not necessarily know why it happened.”

That sentence is powerful because it separates event from causal interpretation.

7. Tepa Selira: Add the Other Person's Context

Tepa selira is often associated with empathy, restraint and considering another person's position before judging or acting.

From a reasoning perspective, that creates an important question:

What information might they have that I do not have?

Every person operates with a different:

Context
What is happening around them?
History
What happened before this moment?
Constraints
What limits their available choices?

Add information, relationships, incentives, fears, responsibilities, culture and timing—and suddenly the same behaviour can have a very different meaning.

Tepa selira therefore supports perspective expansion. It does not require us to agree with another person's interpretation. It reminds us that our own perspective is only one point in the system.

8. Living Heritage as Cognitive Infrastructure

This lens can be extended to other Indonesian living-heritage practices. The following are interpretive readings, not claims that UNESCO formally defines these elements as divergent-thinking methods.

Pantun

Can illustrate indirect, relational communication: the message and the relationship are considered together.

Angklung

Can illustrate distributed intelligence: one person holds only part of the musical system, while coordination produces the whole.

Pencak Silat

Can illustrate power with restraint: capability and necessity are not the same thing.

Jamu

Can illustrate context sensitivity: a similar problem label does not automatically imply the same response for every person.

Wayang

Can illustrate perspective expansion: social situations can be explored through different characters and viewpoints.

9. Inclusion Begins Where Premature Judgment Stops

Exclusion can begin with a very small cognitive shortcut.

We see a behaviour.

We assign a label.

We stop investigating.

Lazy. Difficult. Arrogant. Doesn't care. Not interested.

These may sometimes become reasonable conclusions after evidence. The problem is when they become conclusions before investigation.

What if there is:

  • a missing resource?
  • a different cultural expectation?
  • an inaccessible instruction?
  • a hidden responsibility?
  • a constraint invisible to the observer?
  • a different interpretation of the task?

This is why divergent thinking can matter to inclusive practice. It creates room for the person to be more complicated than the first label we placed on them.

Again, this is not relativism. Some explanations will be unsupported. Some behaviours will genuinely be harmful. Convergence is still necessary.

The point is:

Diverge before you decide what the person is.

10. A Practical Reasoning Loop

01
OBSERVE
What actually happened?
02
DIVERGE
What else could explain it?
03
INVESTIGATE
What information would distinguish them?
04
CONVERGE
Which model fits the evidence?
05
CLOSE
Set a working conclusion.
06
REOPEN
Update when new evidence appears.

The final step matters. Convergence should not become dogma.

A good working model is:

“This is what I currently think, given the evidence available.”

Not:

“This is the only explanation that can ever be true.”

11. How to Train: Divergent First, Convergent Later

Exercise 1 — Separate observation from interpretation.

Write one sentence describing only what happened. Then write the interpretation your brain immediately generated. Keep them physically separate.

Example
Observation:
“The message has not received a reply.”
Interpretation:
“They don't respect me.”

Exercise 2 — The 5 What-Else Rule.

Whenever your brain gives you a conclusion, generate at least five plausible alternatives. You are not trying to prove them. You are expanding the space before choosing.

Exercise 3 — Find the discriminating variable.

Ask:

“What information would help me distinguish these hypotheses?”

This is the step that turns divergence from endless brainstorming into investigation.

Exercise 4 — Converge explicitly.

Write:

“Given the evidence currently available, my working explanation is…”

Writing the sentence forces you to recognize when the transition from exploration to conclusion has occurred.

Exercise 5 — Reopen the model.

Write one piece of evidence that would make you reconsider your current explanation.

This trains flexibility without forcing permanent uncertainty.

12. Interactive Practice Case

Case

“My colleague did not respond to my message.”

01

Observe

Write only the facts.

02

Diverge

List 5 possible explanations.

03

Investigate

What question or evidence would separate them?

04

Converge

Choose the best-supported explanation.

05

Reopen

What new evidence would change your mind?

The exercise is deliberately ordinary. The skill should eventually become useful in ordinary life, not only in workshops or strategic planning rooms.

13. The Divergent Thinker's Trap

There is a danger on the other side too.

If you are highly divergent, you can become attached to the search itself.

Every answer generates another question.

Every variable creates another variable.

Every explanation opens another explanation.

That can become analysis paralysis.

So the divergent thinker needs a deliberate convergence trigger:

Convergence Trigger

“Do I have enough information to explain the observation and act appropriately?”

Not perfect information.

Sufficient information.

That distinction prevents the search from continuing forever.

14. From Mental Model to Inclusive Practice

Perhaps the deeper connection to heritage is this:

Living heritage can preserve not only content but social intelligence.

Ways of listening.

Ways of disagreeing.

Ways of helping.

Ways of interpreting another person.

Ways of regulating ourselves before acting.

Ways of repairing relationships.

Those capacities are not frozen in the past. They can be reinterpreted and applied to modern settings.

A WhatsApp group can become a new space for guyub.

A classroom can become a laboratory for tepa selira.

A team meeting can practice musyawarah.

A community project can operationalize gotong royong.

A difficult conversation can begin with the discipline of husnuzan:

“I should not assume the worst explanation before I understand the situation.”

And divergent thinking adds another layer:

“What else could be happening?”

Then convergence completes the loop:

“Now that I know more, what is the explanation best supported by evidence?”

15. The Final Mental Checklist

Before concluding

  • What did I actually observe?
  • What am I assuming?
  • What else could explain this?
  • What variable might I be missing?
  • What information would distinguish the hypotheses?

Before closing

  • What evidence supports this explanation?
  • Have I confused a pattern with a cause?
  • Am I closing because I understand, or because I am tired of searching?
  • What evidence would change my mind?
  • Is this conclusion sufficient for the decision I need to make?
Living heritage as a living skill
Maybe preservation is not only about keeping a tradition alive.
Maybe it is also about keeping the social intelligence inside that tradition usable for the next generation.

For me, that is where living heritage becomes especially interesting.

The object may change.

The technology may change.

The setting may change.

But a community can continue transmitting ways of thinking:

consider another perspective.
do not judge too quickly.
